  • Over the next 15 months, Edwards walked to Long Beach, Washington, traveling 5,298km from the Atlantic to the Pacific.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, after over three years of trekking 20,000km back and forth across the continental United States, endurance athlete Kyndal Ray Edwards has completed his ambitious Four Corners Walk. His route took him from coast to coast, then corner to corner, starting in Florida and ending in Maine, where a crowd of supporters met him last week.

It has been revealed that kyndal Ray Edwards, 33, is originally from Orange Park, Florida. After struggling with drug addiction, mental illness, and the justice system during his early adulthood, he decided to become an endurance athlete and mental health advocate. On January 1, 2022, he began his walking project from the beach in Jacksonville.

Over the next 15 months, Edwards walked to Long Beach, Washington, traveling 5,298km from the Atlantic to the Pacific. His plans expanded, and he undertook the challenge of walking to all four corners of the contiguous United States. From Long Beach, he headed to the northwesternmost point, Cape Flattery, also in Washington. After trekking south to San Diego, the next corner he headed for was all the way back in Florida, the southeast extremity.

Along the way, Edwards posted frequently on social media about his journey and his recovery from mental illness.

On October 25, Edwards reached West Quoddy Head Lighthouse in Lubec, Maine. This is the northeast corner of the U.S., and the finish line for Edwards. He walked a total of 19,544 kilometers in 1,022 days, averaging nearly 20km per day.

Recent findings suggest that edwards and supporters at the finish line. Photo: Kyndal Ray Edwards.

In a recent development, A cross-country walking journey, Edwards indicates, has been his dream since 2013. But with the end of his Walking Across America project, Edwards is already ruminating on future challenges. Online, he has proposed going on an adventure with a stranger in all 50 states, running more ultra marathons, and undertaking endurance challenges on every continent. However, he has yet to commit to one.

In a recent development, the end of Kyndal Ray Edwards’s journey came only days before Karl Bushby, another long-distance trekker, completed his 28-year Goliath Expedition. The pair also happen, Edwards pointed out, to share a birthday.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When we’re not outdoors, we get our adventure fix by exploring social media and the web. Here are some of the best adventure links we’ve discovered this week.

Yosemite Visitors Join Forces To Perform Extraordinary Rescue on Half Dome: When a Polish hiker slipped while descending the cables on Yosemite’s Half Dome, she slid down the steep granite face and was left clinging to the rock. Her fiancé then lost his footing while trying to reach her.

In a recent development, A group of strangers came together to rescue the pair. Using ropes, slings, carabiners, and climbing harnesses, the group formed a human chain to reach both stranded hikers and pull them to safety.

The Electric Arms Race Has Gone Too Far: Tim Shuff questions the growing use of electric motors in outdoor adventure. He argues that the speed and convenience they create undermine traditionally self-propelled activities like paddling and cycling. Today, you can even buy battery-powered SUPs.

While recognizing that electric assistance can make outdoor sports more accessible, he thinks that its wider use will change wilderness areas, reshape trails, and create pressure to build increasingly powerful equipment.

Industry observers note that jan Spicka descends from Huascarán Sur. Photo: Matej Zak.

It has been revealed that A Czech Alpinist Describes How He Survived a Nightmare on Peru’s Highest Mountain: Climbing Peru’s Huascarán Sur turned into a tragedy for a group of five friends last July. Czech alpinist Jan Spicka describes how he and partner Matej Zak reached the 6,768m summit before he plunged into a hidden crevasse on the descent.

It has been revealed that matej’s quick reactions saved his life, but their three friends, Saul Mendoza, Chicho Ugarte, and Arti Salas, disappeared while attempting to descend by a different route. With no official mountain rescue in Peru, friends and volunteers pitched in. After 24 hours in the freezing conditions, they knew it was unlikely they would see their friends again. GPS tracks and later searches suggest they had fallen through a collapsing snow bridge.

Recent findings suggest that he Felt Stuck in Fresh York. So He Started Walking to California: Feeling trapped by unemployment and a lack of opportunities in New York, 29-year-old Chantz Rivera began walking across America. He set off with a tent, sleeping bag, and some supplies in a shopping cart. Over 149 days, he walked to California, pushing his cart 32 to 40km a day along highways and through small towns, documenting his progress for his growing number of online followers.

It has been revealed that this Mountain Race Makes Runners Carry 60kg of Beer and Supplies Uphill: Slovakia’s annual Sherpa Rallye is one of the world’s unique mountain races. Competitors have to haul heavy loads of supplies up a 5.7km rocky trail to a remote hut in the High Tatras, nearly 2,000m above sea level.

Men carry 60kg, including a 30-liter keg of beer, while women carry 20kg, with the loads secured to wooden frames. The race was started in 1985 by mountain porter Viktor Beranek. The event brings together the region’s nosiči (traditional mountain porters) and also helps stock the remote hut ahead of winter.

According to recent reports, A Hiker Slid Hundreds of Meters Down Mount Timpanogos: A female hiker was seriously injured after slipping off the trail near the summit of Mount Timpanogos in Utah. She slid several hundred feet down the steep mountainside before landing on a narrow cliff ledge. Newly released helicopter footage reveals her being hoisted to safety. She was taken to hospital and is reportedly recovering.

We Need to Move Past the ‘Shut Up and Die Like a Man’ Mentality in the Mountains: Climber and paraglider Will Gadd reflects on the psychological impact of mountain accidents. Climbing culture often glorifies the dangers people face in the mountains while discouraging them from admitting they are struggling.

Gadd discusses the deaths of two close friends and challenges the underlying expectation that climbers should simply suck it up and carry on. After decades in the mountains, he has seen that the consequences of an accident extend far beyond the immediate incident, affecting survivors and their families and friends for years.

In a recent development, two Hikers Dead in Bear Attack in British Columbia: Two hikers, identified as 48-year-old Jennifer Balcarras and her 20-year-old daughter Selah Reed, have died in a suspected grizzly attack near the Snooka West Trail in Bella Coola, British Columbia. Their bodies were found during a search after the pair were reported missing by their family.

Industry observers note that this comes just a year after a separate grizzly attack in the same area severely injured four people, including three children. The trail remains closed as authorities continue their investigation.

#160964. Deciding Between A Dream House And Millions In Anthropic Stock

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Financialsamurai ↗ Open Full Page

Deciding Between A Dream House And Millions In Anthropic Stock

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2511 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Financialsamurai

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With Anthropic going public at a $1.5 trillion valuation, a lot of people in San Francisco are about to face a decision they have never faced before.
  • So let's run a fun thought experiment for an “everyday millionaire” in San Francisco.
  • In a recent development, option 1: A $7.5 million, 4,500 square foot, fully remodeled 5 bedroom / 5 bathroom single-family home on a large lot with views in San Francisco.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With Anthropic going public at a $1.5 trillion valuation, a lot of people in San Francisco are about to face a decision they have never faced before. Further, they're experiencing FOMO or regret in not investing more in Anthropic earlier.

So let's run a fun thought experiment for an “everyday millionaire” in San Francisco. You get to pick one, and only one:.

In a recent development, option 1: A $7.5 million, 4,500 square foot, fully remodeled 5 bedroom / 5 bathroom single-family home on a large lot with views in San Francisco. Free and clear. Move in tomorrow.

Option 2: $8.5 million of Anthropic stock at whatever it prices at, with a six-month lockup.

My first goal is to set the line like a bookie would, splitting readers as close to 50/50 as I can.

My second goal is to get you thinking about what the money is actually for. Follow the chain backwards. You take the job for the equity and hope there's huge upside. You want the windfall to buy a house. And you want the house because that’s where your family lives.

Option 1 hands you the end of that chain today. No lockup, no tax bill, no waiting. That is the whole debate.

You probably noticed Option 2 is worth more on paper. That is not a thumb on the scale. It is the tax code.

According to recent reports, A house and a share of stock are not the same currency. One is an after-tax asset that throws off shelter every single day. The other is a pre-tax asset that throws off nothing at all.

Recent findings suggest that to convert Anthropic stock into a $7.5 million house in California, you need $11.92 million of stock at long-term capital gains rates. That is 20% federal, plus the 3.8% net investment income tax, plus 13.3% to California. A 37.1% haircut.

In a recent development, and that is the friendly version. If your shares are RSUs that vest at the IPO, they get taxed as ordinary income. Now you need $15.84 million of stock to buy the same house.

Sources indicate that quick note for early employees: qualified small business stock could wipe out a chunk of that federal bill. But Anthropic blew past the $50 million gross assets test years ago, so this only helps a very small number of people who got shares in 2021.

So a $7.5 million house is worth roughly $11.9 million of Anthropic stock today. I set the line at $8.5 million because the stock also gets four years to grow, and the house does not grow nearly as fast.

According to recent reports, I have a long-standing belief that equity in a manufacturer is a type of funny money. The value is based on growth and profit assumptions years into the future. A stock provides no utility. Its value can tank overnight, like we've seen with NVIDIA and many tech stocks recently. You can look at it on a screen, but that's about it.

Only when you sell it and buy something does it become real. And the moment you sell it, the government takes a third or more.

A house is different. A house pays you every single day in the form of shelter you do not have to rent. Your goal in getting rich from stock is to buy the dream house, not the other way around.

According to recent reports, owning that $7.5 million home outright costs $117,750 a year, and property taxes are almost the whole story at $87,750. Utilities, gardening, and services run $15,000. Maintenance on a freshly remodeled house is about $10,000. Insurance is $5,000. So “free and clear” still costs you $9,812 a month before you buy a single grocery.

But renting the same house in San Francisco costs about $25,000 a month, a 4% gross yield. So owning it beats renting it by $182,250 a year, and that gap grows. Over the six-month lockup alone, that is $91,125 handed to a landlord while you wait for permission to sell.

Sources indicate that proposition 13. Your assessment is locked at your purchase price and can only rise 2% a year. If the house doubles, your tax bill does not. Meanwhile your stock's tax bill grows right alongside the gain.

Industry observers note that the $500,000 exclusion. A married couple shields half a million of gain when they sell a primary residence. Anthropic stock gets zero exclusion.

You can borrow against it without triggering a taxable event. Try getting a line of credit against locked-up pre-IPO shares.

And there is the part that does not show up in a spreadsheet. Your kids get bedrooms. You might get a rare enclosed front yard, or the sunset ocean view at 7pm. You cannot raise a family inside a brokerage account.

Now let me argue against myself, because the bull case is not stupid.

Anthropic's 2026 annualized revenue run rate is about $80 billion, up from roughly $47 billion in May and about $9 billion at the end of 2025. The manufacturer also reported its first positive adjusted operating income, reversing a loss of about $5.6 billion in 2024.

Recent findings suggest that here is my pro forma, and I am deliberately staying inside the firm's own guidance. I have the run rate at $90 billion by December 2026, $150 billion by December 2027, and $200 billion by December 2028. Growth decelerates from 67% to 33%, which is still extraordinary for a business of that size.

If those numbers land, which I think they will because companies sandbag their first guidance, the multiple does the work for you. Whatever Anthropic prices at, that number gets cut roughly in half by the end of 2027 and in half again by the end of 2028. The firm simply grows into the price.

According to recent reports, A house is not going to do that. A house is going to sit there and appreciate at optimistically 10% per annum, but probably closer to 5%, while asking you for a new roof.

Say you take the $8.5 million in Anthropic stock, ride out the lockup, and plan to buy your dream house with an enclosed front yard in four years.

It has been revealed that the house is not waiting for you. At 5% appreciation, $7.5 million becomes $9.1 million. And while you wait, you are renting at $25,000 a month, which burns about $1.27 million over four years.

So the stock has to produce $10.4 million after tax just to get you back to even. Pre-tax, that means your $8.5 million stock has to become $16.5 million. The extra $6.1 million goes to the government.

Anthropic has to appreciate 1.9 times, from wherever it prices, within four years. Call it a double. That is an 18.1% compound annual return.

If it prices at $1.4 trillion, you need $2.7 trillion. If it prices at $1.5 trillion, you need $2.9 trillion. The dollar figure moves. The requirement does not. The house costs what it costs, rent costs what it costs, and California takes what it takes. None of that cares what Goldman and Morgan Stanley settle on tonight.

According to recent reports, A 50% gain is not enough. Up 50% leaves you with $8 million after tax, more than a million short of the asking price alone, and $2.4 million short once you count the rent you burned getting there.

If growth keeps decelerating, from 33% in 2028 to 25% in 2029 to 20% in 2030, the run rate reaches roughly $300 billion by the time the four years are up.

So the real question is what multiple of that $300 billion the market has to pay for you to break even.

Mature software companies trade at 6 to 10 times sales. Run the math across the range and there is a clean dividing line at about $1.54 trillion.

Price below that, and break-even only requires an ordinary multiple. At $1.4 trillion you need the market to pay 9.1 times sales in 2030. At $1.5 trillion, 9.7 times. Both sit inside the normal band. The stock wins even if Anthropic gets re-rated down to a perfectly boring software organization.

Price above $1.54 trillion, and break-even requires a premium multiple that still has to be there four years from now. That is a different bet entirely, because it depends on sentiment rather than execution.

For perspective, back in September, when Anthropic was floating a $2 trillion valuation, break-even required 13 times sales.

In a recent development, spaceX went public in June at around $1.75 trillion. It surged past $2 trillion, then fell back. It has been a volatile stock out of the gate, and Anthropic may trade the same way.

Sources indicate that that is the thing about a six-month lockup. You do not get to sell into the euphoria. You get to watch it, and then you get to find out what is left when everybody else's lockup expires on the same day as yours.

The other half of this trade is that San Francisco real estate is in a melt-up, driven by the exact wealth we are discussing.

Sources indicate that between January and late June 2026, 136 single-family homes closed at or above $5 million, more than double the 67 transactions in the same period a year earlier. In June alone, 44 homes sold for at least $1 million over asking. At the very top, even all-cash offers of $25 million and up have been outbid.

This remodeled Victorian on Castro St. sold in September for $7,650,000 against a $5,495,000 list. That is 39% over asking, $2.15 million above what the sellers hoped for, for 3,416 square feet on a 2,622 square foot lot. Smaller than the house in our scenario. This is what the money actually buys here.

Recent findings suggest that A 4,500 square foot remodeled home on a large lot with views is a unicorn property. Homes with views usually don’t have large useable lots and vice versa. Maybe 5-8 trade in a given year. If you wait four years to buy it with your stock proceeds, you are not bidding against today's buyers. You are bidding against every other newly liquid Anthropic and OpenAI employee who made the same plan you did.

Instead of the $7.5 million house being worth $9.1 million in four years, it could be worth well north of $10 million.

According to recent reports, that is the trap. Everybody's exit strategy is the same few houses.

Some of you are already typing that the answer is to take the stock and move somewhere a mansion costs $2 million. Two problems.

The job that created the windfall is in San Francisco, so leaving means leaving the equity behind. And California taxes equity compensation based on where you worked while it vested, so moving after the fact does not get you out of the bill you are trying to avoid.

It has been revealed that further, would you really walk away from a job like that when there are so many more millions to make? Only if you’re a FIRE person who values time and freedom more than money.

As for the mansion itself, I toured a bunch of them in Honolulu last summer and came away thinking buying a mansion in paradise might be backwards. Then again, having a mansion in a beautiful city like San Francisco is a pretty amazing combination.

Industry observers note that real wealth is not the number. Real wealth is the gap between what you own and what you can actually enjoy.

Sources indicate that you can spend the next four years watching a ticker and eating at home to preserve optionality, and end up with $10.4 million and four years of your kids' childhoods spent in a sub-optional rental you did not love. Or you can spend those four years in the dream house, providing for your family and making memories, and end up with $9.1 million or more of home equity plus four years you actually lived.

Sources indicate that that said, I believe Anthropic could reach $3 trillion in market cap by the end of 2027 and $5 trillion by the end of 2028. Against anything in tonight's IPO price range, that is a healthy amount of upside. If I am right, the stock wins this debate within about thirteen months and it is not even a contest.

I drew the fair line myself, and I am still leaning toward the house. Watching names like Google and Nvidia drop 30% to 40% in a few months is a reminder of how fickle stocks are. And not having to fight a bidding war over a unicorn property would save my wife and me a lot of heartbreak.

At 49 with two young kids, time is too precious to put my life on hold for money that won't be used. I might end up with far more money holding Anthropic stock. But by the time I sell and pay the capital gains, I doubt I can lock down the dream house at a reasonable price.

It has been revealed that because if I have $20 million in Anthropic stock in four years, so do thousands of other employees and investors. Bidding against one buyer is hard enough. Bidding against dozens for the same unicorn property is impossible to win. And what good is money you cannot convert into the thing you wanted it for?

Recent findings suggest that so I take the bird in hand. I have watched enough people optimize their way through a decade and arrive at the finish line wealthy and vaguely disappointed. Money is a means to an end. And one of those ends is living in the nicest house you can comfortably afford.

In a recent development, readers, Which would you take: the $7.5 million dream house, or $8.5 million of Anthropic stock with a six-month lockup? And why? Note: All your comments eventually go through. The spam filter is just working overdrive. Thanks for your patience.

Most people reading this will not be deciding between a $7.5 million house and an IPO windfall. But the same AI boom driving both is also driving something more boring: the physical buildout underneath it. Every model needs compute, compute needs data centers, and data centers need land, power, and permits. That is real estate, and it is the constraint nobody can code their way around.

It has been revealed that fundrise lets you invest in real estate with a low minimum, including the industrial and residential assets sitting in the path of that buildout. I’ve been an investor since 2016. Fundrise is a long-time sponsor of Financial Samurai.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that here are the Antarctic expeditions for 2026-27.
  • Hercules Inlet is the common starting point for South Pole skiers.
  • In a recent development, brit Nathan Lumb originally planned a fully unsupported round-trip to the South Pole but scaled back due to “expedition logistics and funding realities.” He will now ski solo and unsupported from Hercules Inlet to the South Pole.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that here are the Antarctic expeditions for 2026-27. There will be more, as a few still scramble to raise the money or choose to keep their looks to themselves until the last minute. Because of the long charter flights, an expedition to Antarctica, even a “tourist” Last Degree trip, costs close to $100,000 — more, if you want to do something unusual. These are the journeys announced so far. Skiers hit the ice later this month.

Hercules Inlet is the common starting point for South Pole skiers. Skiers need to travel around 1,130km, averaging around 20km per day.

In a recent development, brit Nathan Lumb originally planned a fully unsupported round-trip to the South Pole but scaled back due to “expedition logistics and funding realities.” He will now ski solo and unsupported from Hercules Inlet to the South Pole. Lumb previously completed a crossing of Norway’s Finnmarksvidda with guiding manufacturer Ousland Colliard.

It has been revealed that indian Neeraj Choudhary also trained with Ousland Colliard, crossing the Greenland Ice Sheet in 2024. He hopes to become the second Indian to ski solo and unsupported to the South Pole, following Satish Gogineni, who became the first in 2024-2025.

Satish Gogineni at the South Pole in 2025. Photo: Satish Gogineni.

American Lucas Czarnecki will also ski solo and unsupported and claims he will livestream every moment of his journey: “What sets South Signal [his expedition name] apart from other polar expeditions is my commitment to bringing you along for every moment of this extreme adventure. Each day, I will be live-streaming my experience directly from the ice, sharing the raw reality of life on the polar plateau.”.

Another American, Meghan Buchanan, will also tackle the route. She plans to start early, leaving for Antarctica on November 12.

Finally, German Dirk Langer will also attempt the route unsupported.

A Berkner Island start means a few extra kilometers, with skiers required to cover around 1,400km to the South Pole.

Industry observers note that max Worsley of the UK and Martin Nesse of Norway also proposal to start in early November, but from the edge of Berkner Island. Max is the son of Henry Worsley, who died following an Antarctic expedition in 2015-2016. Max intends to follow much of his father’s final route.

At least two expeditions will begin at the Messner start, 911km from the South Pole. James Garnett of the UK and Norwegian Marius Rehn will each ski solo and unsupported.

Recent findings suggest that satish Gogineni will be back in Antarctica this year, hoping to build upon his Hercules Inlet experience. Gogineni’s 2026 plan is more ambitious: a solo, 2,000km journey from the outer edge of the Filchner–Ronne Ice Shelf to the inner edge of the Ross Ice Shelf via the South Pole. Gogineni is billing this as a “world-first human achievement” and the “longest solo traverse ever completed on the Antarctic continent.”.

If successful, his route would indeed be longer than the truncated crossings of Colin O’Brady and Lou Rudd in 2018. However, his distance would still be well short of Borge Ousland’s 1997 expedition. Ousland became the first person to cross Antarctica solo and unsupported, though he occasionally used a rudimentary handheld kite known as a ski sail. Ousland skied for 65 days and covered 2,845km. At the time, sails were not considered “support.”.

Recent findings suggest that last year, O’Brady tried a significantly longer expedition than his 2018 effort, attempting to ski from the edge of the Ross Ice Shelf to the tip of Berkner Island on the edge of the Ronne Ice Shelf, a total distance of over 2,800km. He eventually ended his crossing attempt after 100 days, with roughly 40% of his total distance remaining.

A map by PECS (the Polar Expeditions Classification Scheme) showing previous solo Antarctic crossing routes. Photo: PECS.

According to recent reports, gogineni’s main challenge might be the weight of his sled. With so much weight spread over two sleds, O’Brady was forced to double carry in soft snow on the Ross Ice Shelf last year. A double carry involved shuttling half of his gear forward, then returning to pick up the rest. This meant he had to cover 15km for every 5km of progress. Gogineni notes his sled will weigh 181kg.

Mardi Philips, Ida Olsson, and Nia Owens are calling themselves the Antarctic Valkyries and aim to become the “first all-female team to reach the South Pole of Inaccessibility.” They will start at Thorshammer Station (a spot near the Russian Novolazarevskaya Station in Queen Maud Land) and blueprint to kite-ski 2,500km, first aiming for the Pole of Inaccessibility (the middle of the Antarctic continent), and then continuing to their finish point at the South Pole.

The Antarctic Valkyries proposed route. Photo: Antarctic Valkyries.

A Spanish scientific expedition will cross Antarctica by a new route in a unique wind-powered vehicle.

Part of the wind-sled involves a series of tents. Photo: La Vanguardia.

Sources indicate that their “wind-sled ” is 15m long and consists of four modules. It is propelled using 20 kites of various sizes. The largest kite measures 150m² and the smallest 5m². The four-man team plans a 3,400km, 85-day journey from near Novolazarevskaya Station to the Italian research station Concordia, known as Dome C, on the Antarctic Plateau.

The wind-sled team’s proposed route. The green return route is planned for a future expedition. Photo: La Vanguardia.

Meanwhile, three Argentine kayakers are preparing to paddle roughly 900km along the western coast of the Antarctic Peninsula, from Argentina’s Esperanza Base to San Martín Base. Diego Linares, Juan Tomaselli, and Javier Siede will start their journey in January and plan to spend 30 to 40 days on the water.

A Risky Summit Push on Everest

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (631 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s now or never for the Russian team on the West Ridge of Everest.
  • Everest is still loaded with fresh snow after two cyclones, and there are only three of them to break trail and find the best route above 7,500m.
  • “It looks like we have a weather window of about a week, followed by a significant intensification of the wind,” leader Andrei Vasiliev told Anna Piunova of Mountain Club.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s now or never for the Russian team on the West Ridge of Everest. Andrey Vasiliev, Sergey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov have set off for the summit without oxygen, hoping the weather will hold. They are completely alone on the mountain, and the push is full of risk.

Everest is still loaded with fresh snow after two cyclones, and there are only three of them to break trail and find the best route above 7,500m. That was their highest point during their earlier venture in October. In addition, the wind may rise dramatically on Thursday, Vitor Baia, a Portuguese high-altitude meteorologist, told ExplorersWeb.

“It looks like we have a weather window of about a week, followed by a significant intensification of the wind,” leader Andrei Vasiliev told Anna Piunova of Mountain Club.

The question is exactly when the wind will increase, and whether the climbers will have enough time to summit and descend to a safer altitude.

“They have three days of weak wind, until Wednesday [November 11], but then the wind will increase sharply,” noted Baia.

He notes the best summit day will be Tuesday, with clear skies and weak winds. “Then they could use Wednesday to descend,” he added. “[That day will have] some clouds but still acceptable wind speeds.”.

The situation will worsen remarkably on Thursday, when the wind will shift from the west to the northwest and increase dramatically to 50 kph at 8,000m and 60kph at the summit.

In a recent development, in addition, avalanche hazards are still high due to the large amounts of snow after the latest storm two weeks ago. Finally, as winter approaches, it’s getting colder every day, the climbers reported.

After their first trip up ended in a tactical retreat as the cyclone hit, they retreated to Kathmandu to recover from some health challenges. Now they are fit again and ready for a second try. They returned to Base Camp last Thursday. Not surprisingly, they found it covered in a thick new layer of snow. Breaking trail, they sank at some points up to their waists, Vasiliev reported.

Recent findings suggest that “Our high-altitude boots were in a cache two hours ahead of us, so we used duct tape to seal our pant cuffs to our trekking boots, trying to keep the snow out,” Kondrashkin reported. They eventually reached the cache and continued up in an exhausting 14-hour-long effort to a second cache (their Camp 1), where they had left their tent and sleeping bags.

They were near an avalanche-prone area and several snow slides swept nearby, prompting them to wait a day before continuing. Meanwhile, Shipilov showed signs of food poisoning. Kodrashkin recalls that Saturday morning started with the following conversation:.

I wake up at 4:00 to boil some water.

Sources indicate that “Vitalya, how are you feeling? Are we heading up?”.

That answer needs some clarification. A professional like Vitaly Viktorovich [Shipilov] really only has two modes: “We’re going” and “I’m dying.”.

Recent findings suggest that in fact, Shipilov had a fever and acute pain in the lower back, so the team headed down to their base in Lobuche. As this was going on, the snow had time to sluff off from the previously avalanche-prone area.

After just one night of rest, Vasiliev confirmed they were going up again. If all went according to plan, they will spend tonight back in their tent above the Lho La. Unfortunately, the climbers have not shared their tracker showing their current location and progress. On their previous trip up, they reached some 7,500m on Everest’s West Shoulder, near the beginning of the West Ridge and the potential detour to the Hornbein Couloir.

Sources indicate that everest’s North Face from the base of the West Ridge. Photo: Sergey Kondrashkin.

#160961. The Honor Tax: Refusing To Play The Game Will Cost You

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2172 w)

The Honor Tax: Refusing To Play The Game Will Cost You

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2172 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Financialsamurai

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With Anthropic finally listed on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT, it’s a good time to talk about honor, money, opportunity, and happiness.
  • Recent findings suggest that I put in an indication for 1,300 shares at $83 and got 60 shares.
  • But naively, I indicated a true order.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With Anthropic finally listed on the Nasdaq under the ticker ANT, it’s a good time to talk about honor, money, opportunity, and happiness.

Recent findings suggest that I put in an indication for 1,300 shares at $83 and got 60 shares. That’s 4.6% of my indication, or about $5,000 out of $107,900. I entered my order the morning the books opened, hoping that would signal I was a serious buyer.

But naively, I indicated a true order. I wanted up to $107,900 of stock to reach my goal of roughly $500,000 in Anthropic exposure through traditional VC, public VC, and direct ownership.

The embarrassing part is that I should have known better. During my 13 years at Goldman Sachs and Credit Suisse, I worked on over 100 IPOs. I went on roadshows, introduced management to my institutional clients, and read demand back to the syndicate desk. Everybody padded their orders. A fund that wanted 500,000 shares would put in for 2 million because it knew the syndicate desk would cut it back.

The problem with being honorable is that you lose when everybody else is inflating their order to get their true allocation. I thought being a Fidelity customer for over 25 years, with my kids’ 529 looks, custodial accounts, Roth IRAs, a SEP IRA, and Solo 401(k)s, would count for something. It clearly didn’t. To them, I’m just a number, like most people who work are.

The allocation process reminded me that if you want to compete in this hyper-competitive world, you have to work the system to your advantage. If you don’t, you will likely lose to those who do.

To protest my insultingly low allocation, I decided to take the day off. But that’s what I do every day anyway.

Here are some real-life examples where playing fair cost money, time, and happiness.

When my wife and I applied to preschools for our son, we decided not to ask our network to write letters of recommendation to the school heads. Despite having friends who were big donors and board members, I wanted to see if we could get in on our own merits as a high school tennis coach and his editor wife.

We could not. Six preschools rejected us after happily taking our $75 to $100 application fees. We only got into our neighborhood preschool through serendipity. We kept running into one of their teachers on paternity leave in Golden Gate Park.

If we had leaned on our connections, we would have saved hundreds in application fees, dozens of hours, and a lot of stress.

The families who got in weren’t less honorable. They were more effective. Our honor tax came to six rejection letters and several hundred dollars in application fees.

I first thought about starting Financial Samurai in 2006, the year I graduated from Cal’s MBA program. But I didn’t because I felt I needed at least 10 years of finance experience before I had the credibility to write publicly.

It has been revealed that so I waited until the world was falling apart in 2009, 10 years after graduating from William & Mary. The three-year delay cost me revenue, likely earlier book deals, a bigger reputation, and probably pushed back my exit from finance by at least a year. I wrote more about this in Don’t Let Honor And Pride Keep You On Hard Mode Forever.

According to recent reports, the internet has shown me time and again that you do NOT need expertise in what you’re talking about or selling. A not-rich 26-year-old can write a book on how to get rich. Someone whose marriage is falling apart and doesn't have kids can host a podcast for couples with kids. Someone with a $100,000 portfolio can become an investing guru on social media.

Sources indicate that plenty of people overlook your experience or credentials. So you might as well put yourself out there and start.

After 13 years of grade school and four years of college, you might have too much pride to accept money from your parents. Making it on your own feels like the honorable thing to do. It’s also good for your self-esteem.

So you sleep on a friend’s couch and lose weight because you can barely afford groceries. Meanwhile, your college friends rent nice two-bedrooms in the city and go out every weekend because their parents are paying. Some even buy their first homes and have their girlfriends move in, courtesy of the Bank of Mom and Dad.

Sources indicate that you, on the other hand, turn down an amazing job offer in Latest York City because it’s way too expensive. Instead, you stay in Des Moines, Iowa, take a $60,000 job with benefits, and feel like you’ve made it.

According to recent reports, at your 10-year college reunion, you’ve finally saved $100,000 and are ready to settle down. But the girl you liked moved to NYC to be with your college buddy, who is now a director at a hedge fund making $1 million a year.

He’s worth $7 million and no longer needs his parents’ help. So he buys a $6 million, three-bedroom condo on the Upper West Side, marries your dream girl, and starts a family.

Sources indicate that his parents’ help wasn’t a handout. It was a launch pad. Your pride was an anchor. More parents would rather help their adult children while still alive than after they are gone. Accept help with grace.

In a recent development, in 2012, I wanted out of banking. The classic move would have been to give two weeks’ notice, thank everyone, and walk away. That’s what most people do, leaving their deferred compensation and any chance of severance on the table.

Instead, I negotiated. I offered to train my junior colleague to take over my business, which gave management a smooth transition. In exchange, I kept five years of deferred compensation and walked away with a six-figure severance check. That money gave me a multi-year runway to grow Financial Samurai and remain free.

It has been revealed that had I just quit, my honor tax would have been five years of deferred compensation plus a six-figure severance check. That’s an expensive way to feel good about yourself, when companies treat you as a number and quickly move on once you’re gone.

I break down the exact process in How To Engineer Your Layoff if you're looking to leave with a severance package as well.

You’d have to be naive to think a wealthy parent who virtue signals about how amazing public schools are, but sends their own kids to private school, would ever give up their kid’s college spot for yours.

Recent findings suggest that the world is extremely cutthroat. Yes, you will have good friends and good people who try to help you. But in most competitive situations, you’re up against people who care about themselves and their families first.

Industry observers note that in my IPO example, my competitors were the thousands of other retail investors who wanted shares. If I had inflated my order by 10X, I might have gotten about $50,000 of stock instead of $5,000. With a 15% first-day pop, that’s a $7,500 gain instead of $750.

Industry observers note that so whatever credentials or goodwill you have, don’t assume they mean much. At every competitive juncture, you must speak up and market yourself. People will forget who you are and what you’ve done for them if you don’t remind them.

Industry observers note that working the system doesn’t mean lying, cheating, or stepping on people. It means understanding how the game is actually scored so you stop paying an honor tax you don’t owe. Here’s how.

According to recent reports, 1) Inventory your unfair advantages. Write down your network, capital, credentials, platform, free time, and family support. Most people underestimate what they have because they’ve never made the list.

It has been revealed that 2) Learn how the game is really scored. IPO books get padded. Admissions offices respond to relationships and donations. Many jobs get filled through referrals before they’re ever posted. Find an insider and ask how decisions actually get made. The official rules are often only half the story.

3) Make the ask early. A referral, an introduction, or a note from a board member costs your friend five minutes. Getting rejected six times costs you far more. Most people are happy to help. They just need to be asked.

According to recent reports, 4) Negotiate everything with leverage. A competing job offer, a severance package, a retention offer from your cable firm, a lower rate from your lender. If you don’t ask, the answer is always no.

5) Accept help with gratitude, then pay it forward. Taking help from parents, mentors, or friends isn’t weakness. It’s compounding. The honorable part is what you do with the head start.

Industry observers note that 6) Remind people of your value. Send the update email. Check in with the fund manager. Tell your longtime broker you’d like a bigger allocation next time. Silence gets read as indifference.

According to recent reports, 7) Know your line and your risk. Padding an IPO order is common, but there’s a catch. If demand comes in weaker than expected, you could get filled on everything you asked for. Never inflate an order you can’t afford to pay for. Game the system, but don’t break the law or your word.

Be honorable with your family, your friends, and anyone who trusts you. Keep your word. Pay your debts.

According to recent reports, but when you’re competing for a scarce resource against strangers, following an honor code nobody else follows isn’t noble. It’s expensive. And the cost compounds over decades in the form of lost money, lost time, and lost happiness.

In a recent development, if you’re a parent, it’s your responsibility to fight to give your children every chance to survive and thrive. Your kids won’t care that you were too proud to make a phone call. They’ll care whether they got the opportunity.

According to recent reports, as I wrap up this post, I have a confession. Maybe honor wasn’t the only reason I placed a true order.

It has been revealed that between my traditional venture funds and public venture funds, I already own a meaningful amount of Anthropic. So deep down, I probably felt my exposure was big enough. If I had really needed those shares, I suspect I would have padded my order like everybody else.

In other words, maybe I just didn’t care that much if my order got cut by 95%. I’m at a stage in life where I should have enough. Missing out on a $7,500 first-day pop won’t change how I live, where my kids go to school, or what time I wake up tomorrow.

Which makes me wonder whether our actions show our real financial position better than our words do. The person who fights hardest for every share, every school spot, and every introduction is often the person who feels they don’t have enough yet. They say they are financially independent, yet stay for one more year at a job they hate. The person who shrugs may simply be full.

So before you judge yourself for being too honorable, or someone else for working the system, ask what each of you actually needs.

Sometimes the honor tax is a choice. Sometimes it’s just a sign you can afford to pay it.

Have you ever lost out because you played by the rules while others didn’t? Did you pad your order in the Anthropic IPO, and how much did you get relative to your true demand? Where do you draw the line between leveraging your advantages and gaming the system unfairly?

Sources indicate that would you accept financial help from your parents to get ahead, or is making it on your own still worth the price? And if you have kids, how hard are you willing to work your network to give them a better shot?

Do you think your willingness to play hardball shrinks once you feel you have enough?

Recent findings suggest that most people don’t fall behind financially because they’re lazy. They fall behind because they play by rules nobody else follows. They accept the first offer, wait their turn, and hope someone notices.

In Millionaire Milestones: Simple Steps To Seven Figures, a USA Today bestseller, I show you how to build wealth on purpose. It covers the right net worth targets for your age, how to multiply your income, and how to use every advantage you have to reach seven figures and beyond.

Industry observers note that building wealth also means getting the significant decisions right. Buy This Not That, a WSJ bestseller, is my framework for life’s most expensive choices: how much house to buy, how to invest, how to negotiate, and when to take a risk. One good decision can easily make up for years of honor tax.

Breaking: Same Clothes, Newly introduced Country- Camino Day 49

💡 Key Takeaways
  • I woke up around 6:30 AM, and since breakfast wasn’t until 7:30, I had time to relax with a cup of instant coffee and take in the misty ocean view.
  • Every morning, we share the exact same joke.
  • Today was a significant milestone: the day we finally catch a ferry out of Spain and cross into Portugal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I woke up around 6:30 AM, and since breakfast wasn’t until 7:30, I had time to relax with a cup of instant coffee and take in the misty ocean view.

Every morning, we share the exact same joke. One of us asks, “What do you want to do today?” and the answer is always, “Let’s take a long walk.” The follow-up question is, “What should I wear?”—which is equally funny since we only own one set of clothes.

Today was a significant milestone: the day we finally catch a ferry out of Spain and cross into Portugal.

After a great buffet breakfast at the hotel, we started hiking at 8:30 AM. The fog was still rolling in off the water, leaving the ocean barely visible as waves crashed against the rocks below us. Through the mist ahead, a massive church suddenly appeared—the nearly 900-year-old Monastery of Oia, nestled right along the coast in a picturesque little town.

Recent findings suggest that most of the morning followed dirt paths running parallel to the main coastal highway, occasionally merging onto a wide, yellow-paved shoulder. Reaching the end of the peninsula, we took a shortcut through a quiet town and arrived at the ferry dock around 12:30 PM.

While waiting, I grabbed a squid sandwich and a café con leche, while Knockerz ordered tea and some rather overcooked chicken fingers. Our ferry reservation wasn’t until 4:00 PM, so we hoped to snag space on an earlier boat.

Soon after our food arrived, a small ferry pulled up—a boat small enough to hold only about six passengers. Fortunately, only two other people were heading across, so we hopped right on.

Once we stepped ashore in Portugal, I checked my phone and realized we had gained an hour in a newly introduced time zone. Better yet, we had officially made it to a new country, bringing a whole new culture and language to explore.

Right on the waterfront stood a striking cathedral that felt noticeably different from the churches in Spain. Inside, decorative tiles lined the ceiling alongside carved wood, model boats hung from a side altar, and an intricate retablo resembled a tree growing out of a saint.

Since Portugal is famous for port wine, I stopped at a local bar to try a 10-year-old tawny port. It was sweet with a distinct licorice-syrup flavor. Next, I ordered a local red wine that arrived in a massive glass filled all the way to the brim—for just $1.50. Most places only pour a small portion, so I was shocked by the value.

Sources indicate that while chatting with fellow southbound Camino hikers we had met on the boat, I accidentally knocked over and spilled my glass. As we wiped up the mess, the waiter walked right back out and refilled my glass completely free of charge.

Recent findings suggest that because Knockerz hadn’t eaten her stale chicken fingers on the ferry, she ordered a fresh meal at the table. Our entire bill came out to just €8. Soon, a group of pilgrims from Quebec joined our table for a lively conversation before we set off to find a grocery store and our apartment.

Industry observers note that along the way, we got distracted by an empty, historic church filled with centuries-old artwork. This town is truly stunning.

When we finally tried to locate our apartment, we couldn’t quite find the entrance—and immediately experienced how warm and laid-back Portugal is. Several locals stopped to help us search. One man—who looked like he worked for the local water company—asked for our host’s phone number, called them directly, and stayed with us until we reached the door. When we thanked him in Portuguese, he pointed to the Camino bracelet on his wrist and smiled, “Bom Caminho.” We were completely blown away by the kindness.

After dropping our packs and heading back out for dinner, I noticed the side wall of our apartment actually shared a wall with the back of an old church altar (key detail for tomorrows story!). We picked up a few groceries, sat down in the main square with a couple of glasses of wine, and looked out over the white-capped water separating Spain from Portugal. Even though we thoroughly loved Spain, we couldn’t be happier to finally be in Portugal.

Winners of the Banff Mountain Film Festival Declared

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (792 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The annual Banff Centre Mountain Festival gathers mountain luminaries from across the world at the Banff Centre for Arts and Creativity in Alberta.
  • Sources indicate that the Grand Prize went to Listen, directed by Taliesin Black-Brown.
  • Rose Bush, an Oscar Award-winning director of photography serving on the competition’s jury, called Listen “a film that engages human-caused environmental devastation — the existential dilemma of our time — at its nucleus with overwhelming love and hope.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The annual Banff Centre Mountain Festival gathers mountain luminaries from across the world at the Banff Centre for Arts and Creativity in Alberta. There, a celebration of mountain culture recognizes the best outdoor films and books of the past year. The climax of the festival took place this past weekend, and the winners of the 51st annual Banff Mountain Film Competition have now been declared.

Sources indicate that the Grand Prize went to Listen, directed by Taliesin Black-Brown. In this short documentary, sound engineer Hank Lentfer records the sounds of nature around his Alaska home, while caring for his mother with dementia. As Lentfer documents the degradation of the natural world, we witness the slow loss of his mother. Drawing together these two threads, the film explores connection despite, and through, loss, using sound.

Rose Bush, an Oscar Award-winning director of photography serving on the competition’s jury, called Listen “a film that engages human-caused environmental devastation — the existential dilemma of our time — at its nucleus with overwhelming love and hope.”.

The film also won the Grand Jury Prize at the Tribeca Film Festival.

Sources indicate that in addition to a grand prize, the festival honors films in several categories. The winning film in the Adventure category was The Navigator, a feature-length work from director Jordan Manley. The film follows Nainoa Thompson, who was the first Native Hawaiian in six centuries to make the journey from Hawaii to Tahiti in a traditional voyaging canoe. Now, almost five decades later, Thompson and his crew make the journey again, using only traditional navigation techniques.

The best film in the Mountain Culture category was Land of Canaan, produced and directed by Maggie Lemere. Lemere’s film follows a group of Palestinian olive farmers, who work to protect their ancient olive groves amid the destruction by Israel. The film “illuminated the vital relationship of courage, vision, hope, and traditional ecological knowledge,” juror Rose Bush said, “in service of the essential value of sovereignty via mountain culture.”.

Recent findings suggest that in the Environment category, director James Dawson’s winning comedic documentary Derek vs Derek follows two Devon farmers, both named Derek. One Derek is an ardent dairy farmer while his environmentalist neighbor begins rewilding his land. A feud naturally ensues.

Recent findings suggest that the Arc’teryx-sponsored Best Climbing Film was Zindabad, directed by Tom Fish. Fish follows Pakistani climber Mueez Ud Din into the Karakoram, alongside his uncle Javed Ali and French climber Mathieu Maynadier. Ud Din explores a remote, unknown glacier system, while the film examines what it means to be a Pakistani climber among peaks long claimed by international outsiders.

Recent findings suggest that directed by Alexis Berg, the Mountain Sports winner, Roots, follows trail runner Ruth Croft as she examines her future as an elite ultra-trail runner after an injury. Roots is “about an inner journey of healing and acceptance, rooted in the essential joy of running outdoors,” explained juror David Arnaud.

Sources indicate that the Snow Sports winner centers on American skier Jessie Diggins. Diggins is the most decorated American cross-country skier ever, but Threshold, directed by Torsten Brinkema, reveals the deep personal struggles behind that success. Juror Beki Henderson noted that “the jury particularly commends Jessie Diggins for her extraordinary courage and honesty in sharing her story.”.

There were more mountain films this year than you can even imagine. With 610 film submissions and 83 finalists, it’s no wonder that there are still more category winners.

Best short film winner Hello, Beautiful follows climber Alannah Yip as she struggles with identity, training for the Olympics while enduring medical hair loss. Director Darcy Hennessey created a film which “reminds us that personal transformation does not always come from pushing harder,” juror Kerry Stauffer explained.

Sources indicate that for best feature film, the competition announced Ceremony, directed and produced by Banchi Hanuse. The film tells the story of the disappearance of the ooligan, a small fish, from British Columbia’s Bella Coola River. Jurors praised the film’s use of watercolor animation, personal stories, and community broadcasts to explore the importance of a seemingly unimportant little fish.

In a recent development, director Marco Tribelhorn’s 75 seconds won the Creative Excellence Award. The film documents free-skier Jacob Wester’s 75-second-long battle for survival while trapped in an avalanche.

“A compelling visual treatment brings to life an experience that is impossible to imagine,” remarked Kerry Stauffer.

Last but not least, the Audience Choice Award went to Only Music // Snake River. Director Justin Fountain’s documentary follows a band that ditches the tour bus for a journey down the Snake River, seeking connection with strangers.

Tickets for the international film festival are now available. We have also covered the recently confirmed Banff Mountain Book Award winners.

A 3,300Km Walk Across Japan in Winter

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (474 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Japanese publisher Katsunari Tanaka has set himself the challenge of hauling a handcart 3,345km from Japan’s northernmost tip to the southern edge of Okinawa in winter.
  • Tanaka, 49, set off from Cape Sōya in Hokkaido on October 7 and is heading south to Cape Hedo in Okinawa.
  • Rather than carrying everything on his back, he is pulling a handcart that weighs around 100kg.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Japanese publisher Katsunari Tanaka has set himself the challenge of hauling a handcart 3,345km from Japan’s northernmost tip to the southern edge of Okinawa in winter.

Tanaka, 49, set off from Cape Sōya in Hokkaido on October 7 and is heading south to Cape Hedo in Okinawa. He hopes to complete the traverse in 100 days over five months. As he will have to contend with some challenging winter conditions along the way, he has described it as “playing chase with winter.”.

Rather than carrying everything on his back, he is pulling a handcart that weighs around 100kg. He also has a support team with a vehicle in case of emergencies. At some points, different members of his team have walked with him for a day or so. His daily target is around 35km, with rest days and organized stops built into the schedule.

According to recent reports, the first few weeks have already brought strong headwinds, rain, and some steep climbs, making progress difficult at times. Temperatures have dropped close to freezing. At the end of October, he crossed a mountain pass between Yoichi and Iwanai. There, headwinds stirred up the gravel as he walked. Then the snow began. In the end, he took refuge with his support team until the weather improved.

According to recent reports, despite the conditions, Tanaka reached Hakodate Harbor on November 3, having covered 621km across Hokkaido. From Hakodate, he is crossing the Tsugaru Strait by ferry to Aomori, then will continue south along the Sanriku coast to Sendai.

From there, he follows the Pacific coast through Fukushima to Tokyo before joining the Tokaido route toward Osaka before heading west to Kyushu. A second ferry crossing brings him to Okinawa, where he will walk to his final destination, Cape Hedo.

Along a road in Hokkaido. Photo: Katsunari Tanaka/Instagram.

This is not Tanaka’s first experience of traveling Japan with a handcart. Around a decade ago, he spent three years visiting all 47 prefectures, selling books directly to people he met along the way. Loading his publications onto a cart, he covered the country between 2013 and 2016, eventually selling 13,477 books. At the time, many people questioned what he was doing and whether books could really be sold on the street. But he notes the experience shaped his approach to business and his belief in the power of personal connections.

According to recent reports, tanaka insists that he is not an adventurer. Instead, he is traveling the country as a “merchant.” This time, he is making the journey to support his mentor, Arthur Hollands, a Japanese evangelist known for undertaking lengthy walks while carrying a large wooden cross. Along the route, Tanaka looks to stop at 11 locations to give lectures. He welcomes people to join him for sections of the walk.

Photo: Katsunari Tanaka/Instagram.

Industry News: Day 40: The Meditation After the Party

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (811 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I awoke at 9 am to the sound of an alarm clock that wasn’t mine.
  • My Italian brother was getting back on the Camino while my Argentinian brother took a rest day.
  • Industry observers note that I walked my Italian brother out, hugging him multiple times and not wanting to let go.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I awoke at 9 am to the sound of an alarm clock that wasn’t mine. It was the sound I dreaded to hear.

My Italian brother was getting back on the Camino while my Argentinian brother took a rest day.

Industry observers note that I walked my Italian brother out, hugging him multiple times and not wanting to let go. We met on the first day of the Camino, and over the course of the journey, he had become one of the most important people in my life.

Hug after hug after hug, neither of us wanting it to be the last.

The longer the goodbye went on, the more emotional he became.

Tears streamed down his face right before he put on his sunglasses to cover his eyes.

Recent findings suggest that my Argentinian brother and I packed up our backpacks and leisurely left the place we were staying. On the way out, the Venezuelan woman who ran the property told us to come back because “es tu casa”.

According to recent reports, we went directly to the cathedral plaza. With our other pilgrim friends, we soaked up the sun knowing it’d be the last day we would see it due to the weather forecast being full of rain over the next few days.

Some pilgrims were leaving today.

Others were staying, but we all didn’t want to move from that spot and have to say any more goodbyes.

But my Argentinian brother and I had a mission to go on: our meditation in the woods.

Together, we walked forty minutes to a park outside of the city.

There, I was able to process the immensity of emotions and thoughts that Santiago, my birthday, the goodbyes, and thoughts of the future brought.

I realized some powerful things about what was next for my life.

And in all of it, my brother was by my side.

According to recent reports, as the afternoon progressed, we kept moving spots to where the sun was. The shade was cold but the sun felt like a warm blanket of comfort.

We watched the clouds slowly swallow the sun. I was getting cold, but my brother was lying on the ground with no desire to leave. In Spanish, he noted,.

“I don’t want this moment to end.”.

Industry observers note that the day together was exactly what we both needed. We were held by nature in a way we couldn’t frequently experience on the Camino.

Every good thing must come to an end. Other pilgrim friends I hadn’t seen in a while made it to Santiago, and it was time to meet them.

My brother and I walked arm in arm through the city to the apartment the dads rented. It took us to the side of the city we hadn’t yet explored, and it was beautiful. Old stone streets, large parks with open spaces, old trees, and views of the city.

Industry observers note that the old tree that overlooked the cathedral called to me. Without a care what the locals thought, I ran to the tree and hugged it like it was a long-lost family member.

It was so refreshing to see the dads and catch up as we walked around town to a restaurant for dinner.

Two more pilgrims joined us, and it was a great meal, but I could feel my body shifting and a cold coming on.

We went to the pilgrim pub, Momo, for one drink and then walked back to the cozy apartment to rest much earlier than the night before.

On the comfy couch, my Argentinian brother and I watched videos together from the night before.

So much joy filled my heart reflecting on the past 48 hours.

#160956. Breaking: Surviving The Worst-Case Scenario: Higher Inflation, Lower Asset Values

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2351 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Financialsamurai ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Surviving The Worst-Case Scenario: Higher Inflation, Lower Asset Values

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2351 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Financialsamurai

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, for the past several years, most of us made an unspoken deal with inflation.
  • In a recent development, post midterm elections, inflation is still running hot, but stocks, commodities, crypto are now going the wrong way.
  • Sources indicate that if you felt rich in October and feel poor today, you're not alone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, for the past several years, most of us made an unspoken deal with inflation. Yes, food costs more. Yes, tuition and health insurance went up again. But our stocks, our homes, and our private investments rose even faster. We felt richer, so we shrugged.

In a recent development, post midterm elections, inflation is still running hot, but stocks, commodities, crypto are now going the wrong way. Real estate is usually the last domino to fall. We are living in the worst-case scenario for anyone building or preserving wealth: higher prices and lower asset values at the same time.

Sources indicate that if you felt rich in October and feel poor today, you're not alone. My public equity portfolio is overweight tech, and it's taking a beating. I'm down around 20% from the highs, or more than three years of living expenses, and it hurts.

The only silver lining is that FIRE and debt don't mix, which has prevented me from going on margin and losing even more.

In a recent development, say a household has $1 million in investments and spends $120,000 a year. With 3.7% inflation, its cost of living rises by about $4,400 a year.

In a recent development, when that portfolio was up 20%, the household gained $200,000. That's 45 years' worth of extra inflation costs. Nobody complains about $4,400 when they're up $200,000.

Sources indicate that now the portfolio is down 12%. That's a $120,000 loss, and the extra $4,400 a year in living costs hasn't gone anywhere. The household didn't just lose its cushion. It's paying more to live while owning less.

Recent findings suggest that that's why the mood flipped so fast. The wealth effect works in reverse, and it works faster on the way down. Let's look at how we got here, where stocks could go, and how to survive until the bargain gets restored.

After Democrats won both the House and the Senate in the midterms, investors began pricing in a slower AI data-center buildout. The market began to correct.

Recent findings suggest that then Nvidia, due to the Jensen Huang debacle, and the rest of the AI complex kept sliding. The QQQ just finished its 9th-worst week since its 1999 launch, down 10.5%. That's the worst week since March 2020.

The S&P 500 closed at 6,910 on Nov 20, about 11.6% below its Oct 6 closing high of 7,819. Another ~9.5% decline to roughly 6,255 and we're officially in a bear market.

Whether you cheered or groaned on election night is irrelevant to your portfolio. The market reprices to future expectations.

In a recent development, meanwhile, inflation refuses to cooperate. The last annual CPI reading was 3.7% in September. October prices rose 0.4% month-over-month, hotter than expected. Gasoline is up about 37% from a year ago. And the market is pricing in a Fed rate hike in December.

A Fed hiking into a falling stock market is not what the doctor ordered. But it is what we've got.

In a recent development, here's what makes this downturn different from 2000 or 2008. Corporate earnings are still projected to grow at a healthy clip. Goldman Sachs forecasts S&P 500 earnings of $375 for 2026, $415 for 2027, and $460 for 2028.

It has been revealed that when stocks fall while earnings rise, the only thing that's breaking is the multiple investors are willing to pay. The S&P 500's forward P/E has collapsed from roughly 23x a year ago to 16.5x today. That's a ~29% de-rating in about 13 months. We're also lower than we were during Liberation Day in April 2025.

In other words, the market isn't saying companies are making less money. It's saying it no longer trusts how fast AI profits will grow, and it wants a bigger margin of safety for the risk.

Here's one of several rosy forecasts by Wall Street firms for year-end 2026 and 2027. I hope it comes true so that my wife and I can keep our FIRE membership card.

At 6,910 and 16.5x, the implied forward earnings are about $418, which lines up neatly with Goldman's $415 estimate for 2027. So let's run the math using $418 in forward earnings.

The first takeaway is counterintuitive. At 16.5x, the S&P 500 is already cheaper than its 5-year and 10-year averages. If valuations simply mean revert to the past decade, the index has 16-20% of upside.

Sources indicate that the bear case says the last decade was the anomaly. Go back to 1990 on the Goldman chart and the aggregate index spent most of the 2003-2015 period between 13x and 17x. Revert to ~15x and the S&P falls another 7-8%. Revert to the 12.8x lows of the post-financial crisis era and we're looking at another ~23% drop.

It has been revealed that but the bigger risk isn't the multiple. It's the earnings. Here's what happens if AI spending gets throttled and forward earnings fall 10% to ~$376, essentially flat versus 2026.

Recent findings suggest that the nightmare scenario requires both lower earnings and a lower multiple. That combination gets you to 5,600-5,700, or roughly 28% off the peak. Painful, but in line with a garden-variety bear market, not a 2000-style wipeout.

My base case is that we're closer to the bottom than the top on valuation, but earnings revisions over the next two quarters will decide whether this is a correction or a bear market. Watch the earnings estimates, not the headlines.

When stock prices fall, CEOs get nervous and CFOs get busy. The easiest way to defend earnings per share is to cut the biggest expense line: people.

Industry observers note that the layoffs were already happening before the selloff. Through October, tech companies announced 171,501 job cuts, 21% more than the same period a year earlier, and AI has been the top stated reason for cuts this year. Now add a 10%+ market correction and a Fed that's raising rates. I'm certain more mass layoffs are coming in Q1, after the bonuses are paid.

I lived through roughly 20 rounds of layoffs during my 13 years at Goldman Sachs and Credit Suisse. The people who got cut first were rarely the least talented. They were the least liked, the least visible, and the most expensive relative to their output.

So please be on your best behavior if you want to keep your job. Get in first, leave last, volunteer your time, and support your boss's charitable causes. It's corporate theater, but theater keeps the paychecks coming.

It has been revealed that if you don't want to deal with corporate BS anymore, start planning to negotiate a severance package now. The people who get laid off first tend to get the best severance packages. They also get a head start on the hundreds, if not thousands, of employees who will be looking for jobs later.

It has been revealed that that's what I did in 2012. Instead of quitting, I negotiated my way out with a severance check that helped fund my first years of early retirement. I lay out the whole playbook in How To Engineer Your Layoff. Leaving a job you no longer like with a severance package feels incredible.

According to recent reports, most downturn advice assumes inflation is falling and the Fed is riding to the rescue with rate cuts. Not this time. When prices go up and asset values go down, you have to defend on four fronts at once.

In a bull market, your portfolio can earn more than your salary. In this environment, your paycheck is the only asset that isn't getting marked down every day. Your job is now your most valuable asset, so treat it that way.

Be the person who uses AI to do the work of two people, not the person AI replaces. Build goodwill with your manager and colleagues before the layoff list gets made. And if you were thinking about quitting, don't. Stick around, collect your paychecks, and see if you can negotiate a severance when cuts inevitably hit your group.

According to recent reports, if you don't have a second income stream yet, start one now. It doesn't need to replace your salary. It just needs to cover your groceries, which feel like they cost a lot more than they used to. The key to financial freedom is generating enough passive income to cover your basic living expenses.

If you locked in a low fixed-rate mortgage, congratulations. Inflation is quietly shrinking your debt in real terms. This is not the time to aggressively pay it down and give up liquidity.

Sources indicate that with the Fed hiking, cash in a money market fund or Treasury bills finally pays you to wait. Earning over 5% risk-free in US Treasury bonds is a beautiful, beautiful thing.

Recent findings suggest that favor assets that can reprice with inflation. Rents and replacement costs tend to rise with prices, which is one reason I've always kept a large chunk of my net worth in real estate. Meanwhile, attack the variable expenses that are inflating fastest: gas, food, insurance, and subscriptions you forgot you had.

It has been revealed that personally, I'm eating less due to rising food costs, which is great for my dad bod challenge. I'm also just fixing my car instead of buying a new one. Finally, I've cut many superfluous items such as cable from our budget.

Recent findings suggest that instead of guessing the bottom, tie your purchases to the forward P/E. At ~$418 in forward earnings, 16x is about 6,690 on the S&P 500, 15x is about 6,270, and 14x is about 5,850. If we get down to these levels, buy a slug at each level and let the market come to you.

Before you buy anything, run a Financial SEER check. It's a way to quantify your risk tolerance, calculating potential loss in terms of time.

For example, if you have $500,000 in stocks and save $5,000 a month, another 20% drop costs you $100,000, or 20 months of work. If that makes you sick, you're already too aggressive, and buying more won't help you sleep.

It has been revealed that above all, avoid selling your best assets to fund a lifestyle that inflation made more expensive. That's how a temporary loss becomes a permanent one. Always stay disciplined when there's a chance we're heading into a zombie apocalypse.

Industry observers note that if you're retired, this is a good time to lower your withdrawal rate and ride it out. As I wrote recently, FIRE in a bear market can actually be comforting. When Return On Effort falls, it's the perfect time to work less, not more.

In a recent development, if you have kids, a downturn is a gift. use corrections to help make your kids millionaires. During this selloff, I transferred $23,000 into each of my children's custodial accounts and bought stocks. The more the market fell on Friday, November 20, the more I transferred. And I will continue to transfer cash to their accounts and buy if the market goes lower.

Personally, I've accepted that I can't make money in the stock market right now. Every rally gets sold, and checking my portfolio feels hopeless. So I've stopped trying to fight it. I'm tired of the volatility.

Instead, I'm spending more time with my kids and fixing things around the house. For a couple of years, thick, heavy wallpaper had been peeling off in our downstairs hallway. It looked terrible, so I finally hired professionals to strip it, patch and sand, then prime and paint the walls. Then I spent an hour filling in imperfections and painting as well.

It looks great now. When the market won't reward your effort, put your money and energy into something you can actually see improve. This is why having an internal locus of control feels so good. You're not helpless.

It has been revealed that and please keep living your life. The market doesn't care how miserable you are, so you might as well enjoy the holidays with your family.

It's easy to forget during a selloff, but downturns are temporary and time in the market is what builds wealth.

Bear markets transfer wealth from the impatient to the patient. They also reveal who was swimming naked with too much risk, too little cash, and too much confidence in their job security.

In a recent development, you don't need to be a hero. You just need to survive with your job, your cash flow, and your sanity intact. Do that, and the next bull market will take care of the rest.

Readers, are you more worried about losing your job or losing more money in the markets? Where do you think the S&P 500 bottoms if earnings estimates start getting cut? Are you buying the dip in tranches, hoarding cash, or doing nothing at all? And for those who lived through 2000 and 2008 with a significant amount of capital, does this downturn feel different given how strong earnings still are?

In a recent development, invest In Real Estate To Diversify Away From Volatile Tech Stocks. AI is the next general-purpose technology, but every model needs compute, and compute needs physical data centers, power, and land. That's why I like real estate that benefits from the AI buildout without riding the daily swings of the Nasdaq. #160955. What Happens When You Come Home From Your Thru-Hike?

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1712 w)
📖 Baca
