Happy Fails

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1514 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I set off on my final 4 day backpacking stint, what surprises does the trail have in store for me?
  • According to recent reports, spirits were high when I returned to Pen Mar Park in Maryland around 7:00AM.
  • Back at Pen Mar Park for the first time since July.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I set off on my final 4 day backpacking stint, what surprises does the trail have in store for me?

According to recent reports, spirits were high when I returned to Pen Mar Park in Maryland around 7:00AM. I felt prepared to finish off my double distance Appalachian Trail hike over the next 4 days. I said my traditional goodbye to my van and approached the pavilion perched above the incredible vista. I pictured myself stumbling back here on Sunday, exasperated but filled with a sense of having completed a once-in-a-lifetime endeavor. I turned south to assess the trail. I’d want a good idea of what I was signing up for. It didn’t take long before I found myself in a bit of a boulder field. That wasn’t ideal. I was supposed to leave the rocks behind in Pennsylvania, this section of trail was supposed to be relatively easy. After about 2 miles I began a climb up toward the High Rock overlook. The climb was no gimme either – plenty of uneven rocks, slippery leaves, and a decent grade. I would at least be going down this slope on my 4 state challenge attempt in a few days, but that was almost worse in a way. I’d have hiked 42 miles by this point, dealing with slippery downhill terrain seemed like a recipe for disaster. My resolve remained strong though, I’d find a way, just as I had over the 4,300 miles up to this point.

Back at Pen Mar Park for the first time since July.

Back to Pennsylvania you monsters!

Once I finished the climb I wandered around some of the rocks offering views West. Visitors have been quite active with graffiti, hardly a rock was left its original color. I continued along the short High Rock loop trail through the small parking lot and up to the main view point. I had the spectacular 180 degree view to myself. I realized the potential to hedge my plans a bit. If I wasn’t on pace to make it to the Pen Mar Park by sunset, I could watch it up here instead. Then I could take my time on the final 3 miles, relying on my headlamp again if needed. That felt like a fair compromise if the situation called for it.

View from the trail near High Rock.

View from the trail near High Rock.

Recent findings suggest that I continued south, enjoying the warm, clear day. The trail conditions improved, but were still less friendly than I expected. There are far easier sections of the AT than what I had been traveling through. I crossed Raven Rock Road, making note that I’d need to be back here by about 3:00PM on Sunday if I wanted to mark sunset at Pen Mar Park since it was about 6 miles north of the crossing. I stopped for water at a creek about a mile later, which is notable only because I had all but stopped filtering water along the trail. I had no trouble waiting until I was at camp, unless there happened to be potable water available along the trail. The trail continued to feature more elevation change than ideal. I was going to be in for a tougher day than I had been picturing. I pressed on, feeling like I needed to prove to myself that today’s 22 miles wouldn’t feel so bad by the end of the day and than I’d feel better.

It has been revealed that that crossover never arrived. I climbed up South Mountain without much hassle, but still wasn’t finding the going easy. I realized I was actually cutting it quite tight to get to the Washington Monument State Park by sunset. I tried calling them to confirm that I could arrive and camp after dark, but the call dropped before I could get a response. I checked the weather forecast to see if Sunday was looking any better in terms of cloudiness and what I saw just about stopped me in my tracks. About an inch and a half of rain was now expected to hit the entire area. The chance of rain was around 60-80% for nearly the entire day. What now? My margins were already incredibly fine assuming things went generally well. Now I had found the trail to be more challenging, my diet had been turned inside out, and I was going to have to do all this in the pouring rain?

My head fell as I continued along the mountain wondering if I even had a choice. I walked to the Black Rock Cliffs, noticing a tempting looking tent site. If this was an ordinary stint I might concoct an itinerary change so that I could camp here with a view of the sunset, but I shook the thought off and continued toward Washington Monument State Park.

I stopped by the Ensign Cowall shelter on my way south.

View from the Black Rock Cliffs.

On I wandered, re-checking the forecast hoping to see something different. Was I thinking straight? It was Thursday and I was being thrown off by a forecast for Sunday. I considered my options. If I pushed the 4 state challenge to Monday I would run out of food, but I could fix that by buying town food in Harper’s Ferry, I’d need to spend Sunday somewhere anyway. I looked at hostels but realized that this would completely solve my problem. To do the challenge on Monday, I’d need to be at the Virginia/West Virginia state line Sunday afternoon so I could pitch my tent and get some sleep right before beginning the attempt. The rain on Sunday meant that Monday was essentially out too. I looked up at a sign for a side trail to Annapolis Rock. I didn’t have time for a side quest, even if it was only a quarter mile off the trail. Even so, I read through the description on FarOut. A large campsite is located near the overlook…two privies…a spring nearby. My progress came to a halt. Ahead of me lay a mix of certainties and uncertainties. Rain, pain, and darkness were certain. Success was very much uncertain. Behind me was a nice sunset with two privies at my disposal.

I turned around and into the Annapolis Rock campsite. The view was spectacular, sunset would indeed be incredible. I found the spring, gushing water even now past the mid point of November. I walked through the entire campsite before winding up at the first campsite. Technically it was a group campsite but since I hadn’t seen anyone I figured it was probably safe to claim it and give myself a little room to spread out. My only complaint was the tent pads which seemed to have been constructed exactly 6 inches too short to pitch even a one person backpacking tent.

It was hardly 3:00PM. I felt guilty for not hiking through even second of daylight. I settled myself by acknowledging that I still had plenty of lee-way built into my shorter itineraries the next two days if the forecast improved and I wanted to get back on track for the challenge. After a restful podcast session in my tent I ventured back over to the overlook. The photos speak for themselves which is handy because I was left speechless. Suffice to say, this was the kind of sunset that made you feel like you’d make the correct decision. I enjoyed myself finding some creative positions amongst the rocks (after doing thorough copperhead) to take pictures from. I must have gotten too excited because I tripped over a rock, leaving a nice scratch in my phone screen. Under other circumstances I might have kicked myself, but I was too awestruck to care much.

Map of the Annapolis Rock Backpacking Campground.

Sources indicate that post-sunset at Annapolis Rock. The horizon was lit up with every color on the spectrum.

Total: 16.4 miles, 37,795 steps.

The buyer pays the same price as they would otherwise, and your purchase helps to support The Trek's ongoing goal to serve you quality backpacking advice and information. Thanks for your support!

To learn more, please visit the About This Site page.

Sources indicate that I’m See You Tomorrow (SYT), a 30-something hiker who loves hiking just for the thrill of seeing things that most people don’t. I have no problem eating the same things every day and, for me, over-analyzing everything is half the fun (sometimes more). I am new to backpacking but that won’t stop me from taking on an unorthodox hike of the Appalachian Trail in 2026. It’s not quite a yo-yo, but I have aspirations of hiking the entire trail twice in one year. For the rest of the story you’ll just have to start reading my blog!

Notify me via e-mail if anyone answers my comment.

Everest Winds Force Climbers to Retreat

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that despite weather forecasts of high winds on Everest, the Russian team gamely left for the West Shoulder today.
  • Recent findings suggest that “It’s calm right now, but the forecast is worrying,” leader Andrei Vasiliev wrote yesterday from a snow cave, where Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shiilov, and Vasiliev had sheltered for the night at 6,400m.
  • The three climbers had fixed three pitches above them, according to Mountain Club, and were hoping for firmer terrain as they approached the West Shoulder of Everest, en route to the West Ridge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that despite weather forecasts of high winds on Everest, the Russian team gamely left for the West Shoulder today. But in the end, they couldn’t fight the gale-force winds, which eventually forced them back to their tent at the base of the mountain.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s calm right now, but the forecast is worrying,” leader Andrei Vasiliev wrote yesterday from a snow cave, where Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shiilov, and Vasiliev had sheltered for the night at 6,400m. Late today, they confirmed that the weather forecast of powerful winds was unfortunately right.

The three climbers had fixed three pitches above them, according to Mountain Club, and were hoping for firmer terrain as they approached the West Shoulder of Everest, en route to the West Ridge.

However, as we previously reported after consulting meteorologist Vitor Baia of Portugal, conditions were good Tuesday and Wednesday, but winds rose dramatically today.

Recent findings suggest that on a previous foray up Everest, one of the climbers heads for the West Shoulder. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev.

It has been revealed that “The winds are very strong,” Vasiliev reported. “It is impossible to work higher on the mountain.”.

Recent findings suggest that vasiliev noted that his team is retreating to a tent at 5,600m. This is below the Lho La Pass, possibly on the Khumbu Glacier beside the vertical section leading to that col.

The question is whether the team will wait there for better conditions, retreat to their base in Lobuche, or call off the expedition.

Some charts still show a chance of variable winds tomorrow, before the jet stream hits the mountain with full force (see below).

Wind levels at around summit altitude on Everest this week, by meteoexploration.com.

Industry observers note that baia indicates the winds will remain high every day until next Tuesday. From Wednesday on, the winds should be weaker.

The Russians set off on their third trip up Everest last Monday, hoping to summit via the West Ridge without oxygen or external support, and with no one else on the mountain.

On Tuesday evening, they checked in with Mountain Club from their tent at 6,000m, where they spent the night. The hard trailbreaking through fresh snow had slowed their pace, but they expected better conditions on the following day, as they started up steeper terrain toward Everest’s shoulder. They knew the snow up there was harder and compacted. They could even see their trails from the previous trip up, so no new soft snow had accumulated.

The Russian team on Everest’s West Shoulder. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev.

Yesterday, Vasiliev noted that they had climbed four pitches on old fixed ropes, plus another eight pitches of their own. The team is fixing ropes at the hardest sections, but not entirely along the route. As expected, snow conditions had improved with the more vertical terrain, but as Vasiliev pointed out, “it’s not exactly easy walking yet.”.

According to recent reports, the Russian leader insists the route to the summit is doable. However, wind delays and a lack of time may ultimately end their attempt.

#160932. Breaking: Piolet d'Or Team Shares Insider Tips for Climbing in Peru's Huayhuash Range

📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Piolet d'Or Team Shares Insider Tips for Climbing in Peru's Huayhuash Range

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1295 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that marc Toralles, Ruben Sanmartin, and Bru Busom of Spain were awarded a Piolet d’Or for a highly committing fresh route on Yerupaja Grande (6,634m), the highest peak of Peru’s Huayhuash range.
  • In the last few years, the Andes have reportedly been affected by climate change.
  • “That means that climbers need to pick their route carefully [when judging] what lingers above them,” Buson explained.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that marc Toralles, Ruben Sanmartin, and Bru Busom of Spain were awarded a Piolet d’Or for a highly committing fresh route on Yerupaja Grande (6,634m), the highest peak of Peru’s Huayhuash range. ExplorersWeb asked the young climbers about the ascent and the unique character of the Andes. They offered some tips for climbers looking to add Peru to their list of high-altitude destinations.

In the last few years, the Andes have reportedly been affected by climate change. “The main effect is that the huge snow structures on the summits are exposed to warmer temperatures and become more fragile,” Sanmartin mentioned. “Basically, they fall down more easily.”.

“That means that climbers need to pick their route carefully [when judging] what lingers above them,” Buson explained.

It has been revealed that bru Buson, left, and Marc Toralles. Photo: Ruben Sanmartin.

This was especially noticeable last year on Siula Grande. “There was a snowfield midway up the face as we trekked by, and on our way back, it was not there anymore,” remarked Marc Toralles. “Somehow, the melting process in the Andes, with its 5,000m and even 6,000m [altitudes], is similar to what we are seeing every year in the Alps, where we all work as mountain guides.”.

For Toralles, the best thing in the Andes is how accessible the mountains are. “It’s so easy to go climbing there,” he stated.

There are no lifts or paved roads, but you can go, climb a peak, and return in three or four days. Something like that in the Himalaya would take weeks. All you need is to get to Huaraz by plane, bus, or car from Lima, where you may stay some days to acclimatize (there are many options), and then go to the mountains.

According to recent reports, if your planned peak is not in the right conditions, you will surely find some other one to climb. Also, the options are infinite for ice climbing, alpine climbing, rock, trekking, anything.

The team’s base camp. Photo: Spanish Yerupaja Grande team.

Recent findings suggest that red tape is minimal. There are no permits for peaks. Instead, climbers and trekkers pay a small fee to cross the comunidades (the areas) where they want to climb, and climbers can hire arrieros (riders with mules) to help carry equipment and supplies to base camps or higher. On this occasion, the climbers kept their logistics basic, with little beyond a slightly larger base camp tent.

With some of the more accessible places, it is advisable to have someone watching over your base camp while you are away climbing.

Sources indicate that once you leave the beaten track, you’ll be alone. “There are no crowds in Huayhuash,” Buson stated. Why aren’t they more popular? The climbers explained that Huayhuash peaks are typically more difficult than popular options in the Cordillera Blanca, also in Peru. But they note this lack of popularity is changing fast. “We are seeing much more people in recent years, both climbing and trekking,” they said.

Sources indicate that thanks to the many possibilities, the three Spanish climbers didn’t need to do much planning. “We know Huayhuash pretty well, we are familiar with the terrain and the climbing style, and we are aware there are always options,” said Toralles, who has climbed there four times.

That noted, the line the Spaniards climbed on Yerupaja last year was not improvised. They had that route in their mind for some time. “We heard of someone who had tried but called the attempt off, so the route was there to be climbed,” Toralles said. “In addition, it didn’t require a long time, and the timing worked for me, since I was traveling to Peru anyway to do some guiding.”.

Buson and Sanmartin joined immediately. To acclimatize, they had worked double shifts the previous weeks around Chamonix, where both are professional guides. “Working on the Mont Blanc massif intensively was great training and acclimatization,” they stated. “We were ready by the time we set foot on the mountain.”.

The best time to climb in Huayhuash is July, August, and the first half of September.

Recent findings suggest that once on the mountain, they carefully checked the conditions of the face and the line they would follow. “In the Andes, you have to assume that the summit ridge snow formations, the famous ‘mushrooms,’ the substantial cornices, and the seracs on the sides of the face are mostly in a delicate state. You need to assume that you will progress on deep, unstable snow, and the entire structure may have deteriorated and be prone to crumble,” Buson noted.

Industry observers note that to deal with them, the climbers used some custom-made tools: They attached alitas (little wings) to their ice axes for a better grip on foamy, loose snow. They also carried small snowshoes for some sections.

Ice axe with ‘alitas’ (wings). Photo: Nick Sheldon/Mountain Project.

Recent findings suggest that conditions in the Andean mountains are always variable. “You’ll find different terrain depending on the altitude and the orientation,” Sanmartin added. “This is why technical routes on these peaks require a high level of commitment, which, as happened on our route, may be even higher than the intrinsic difficulty of the pitches,” Toralles explained.

With this in mind, the Spanish team named the route they opened Essence of Commitment.

In a recent development, marc Toralles ready for the ridge, with large snow pickets and an ice axe with ‘wings’ attached. Photo: Buson/Sanmartin.

In this sort of terrain, it is paramount to stay focused and make the right call between subjective and objective factors. “There are countless reasons to turn around on climbs like this, but one must keep going, except for obvious reasons, such as an injury, a completely impassable section, or a really violent storm,” Sanmartin said.

According to recent reports, “That is why it is important to consider all options and potential issues before starting the climb. You need to be sure you like the line and want to climb it.”.

According to recent reports, asked whether they reached a point of no return during their climb, Buson admitted they did. “On reaching the ridge, we became aware that trying to downclimb the same route would be quite complex. However, we also saw the route upward was doable.”.

It has been revealed that the Spaniards did not count on a professional meteorologist. “We had our friends texting us the online, free forecasts over InReach,” they said. “One of the positive aspects of Huayhuash is that good weather periods tend to last for quite a while. Weather windows of five to six days are common.” During their climb, for example, they enjoyed acceptable weather, with some rain and snow but no high winds.

They warn that conditions in the Andes are changing rapidly. “You need to observe the mountains and adapt,” Toralles remarked. “Some people aim for a route based on the information in a guidebook printed 50 years ago, and find a totally different scenario.” He pointed out that Siula Grande looked different in 2025 than it did when he climbed it just three years earlier.

Recent findings suggest that sanmartin noted that conditions have also changed on normal routes. They are now drier, more complex, and often more hazardous. “In some cases, climbers are abandoning the normal routes up the glaciers and opt for ridges which may be more difficult but in better conditions,” he said.

It has been revealed that the climbers think the Andes will not get as crowded as the Himalaya, simply because the logistics are not as advanced — no refuges, no helicopters — and because they don’t have the sizzle of being the tallest peaks on Earth. “But they have incredible potential,” they noted.

Lucky Skier Survives Night in Crevasse With Two Broken Legs

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (288 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Thirty-nine-year-old Emeric Ossatte was ski touring alone earlier this week in the Savoie area of the French Alps, near the Italian border.
  • The Grenoble-area man, who wasn’t carrying a beacon or radio, doffed his backpack and crawled 100m through the crevasse, looking for a way out.
  • Sources indicate that according to a Facebook report by France’s CRS Savoie mountain-rescue unit, they saw the slide path but no immediate sign of Ossatte.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thirty-nine-year-old Emeric Ossatte was ski touring alone earlier this week in the Savoie area of the French Alps, near the Italian border. He removed his skis to posthole up a steep couloir in his boots and crampons when an avalanche swept him downhill, depositing him into a crevasse and breaking both his legs.

The Grenoble-area man, who wasn’t carrying a beacon or radio, doffed his backpack and crawled 100m through the crevasse, looking for a way out. But the sides of the crack were too steep, and there was no cell service where he was. He remained beside an air pocket in the crevasse overnight. Meanwhile, when he didn’t check in that evening, his family raised the alarm.

Sources indicate that according to a Facebook report by France’s CRS Savoie mountain-rescue unit, they saw the slide path but no immediate sign of Ossatte. The search continued until the middle of the night, when avalanche risk forced the rescuers to suspend their operations.

Industry observers note that the following morning, a large contingent of 28 ground rescuers, dogs, three helicopters, and a physician to tend to Ossatte, if they found him alive, converged on the site, according to France 3. They found his gear and dug for five hours until they heard him calling out.

Industry observers note that “He was really lucky,” said Major Yoann Haberey of the mountain-rescue team. “We knew he was under there. But we didn’t think we’d find him alive.”.

It has been revealed that by the time they extracted him, he had been there almost a day and a half. The hypothermic but lucky survivor was flown to the hospital for treatment and surgery on one of his legs.

#160930. The Pressure to Crush Miles Can Ruin Your Thru-Hike. Don’t Let It.

📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (832 w)
📖 Baca

The Pressure to Crush Miles Can Ruin Your Thru-Hike. Don’t Let It.

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (832 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • After years of planning, you’re finally doing the thing: you’re thru-hiking!
  • This anxiety is familiar to many thru-hikers.
  • I’ve observed this behavior in countless thru-hikers, including myself at times.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After years of planning, you’re finally doing the thing: you’re thru-hiking! It’s exhilarating, it’s liberating, and it’s … remarkably stressful. You knew the trail would be hard, but now that you’re actually out there living the dream, you’re scared you won’t be able to keep up. The other thru-hikers seem stronger than you. More experienced. Younger. What if you fall behind and the whole thing falls apart?

This anxiety is familiar to many thru-hikers. We all know long-distance hiking is challenging, but we tend to picture spending six months walking through nature as a relaxing activity. So why do so many of us succumb to our fear of failure and spend the whole trip stressing about our mileage?

I’ve observed this behavior in countless thru-hikers, including myself at times. We’ll get to a beautiful viewpoint and stop to take a break, and after a few minutes, my hiking partner is already fidgeting and checking their watch. Or we’ll cross paths with a long-lost hiking friend and pause to chat before we go our separate ways, knowing we might not see each other again on that journey — yet my mind is only half on the conversation. The other half is running numbers and wondering how much this unplanned break will set me back.

It has been revealed that southern Maine on the AT was a lot harder than I expected and it slowed me down. But I just kept plugging away at the miles and finished anyway.

It has been revealed that no one wants to still be stuck out on trail with miles to go before camp as darkness closes in — to say nothing of the fear of running out of food on the way to a planned resupply stop or not managing to complete the whole hike within that year’s weather window. As a result, there’s a tendency to rush.

Industry observers note that I sometimes feel I can’t fully relax until I’ve gotten to my planned destination for the day. If I get there early, that just means I can push on a few more miles to make it even easier to reach the next day’s destination. And if I get there early, I can start building up a buffer of extra days in my schedule in case something goes wrong later on.

It has been revealed that this instinct is arguably rooted in good sense. There are a lot of unknowns on a thru-hike and a lot of ways things can go wrong. But learning to live with the unknowns and adapt on the fly is also part of thru-hiking: in fact, I would argue that it’s one of the most crucial skills a thru-hiker must develop, full stop.

Sources indicate that A lot can indeed go wrong in the course of a six-month thru-hike. But a lot can also go right in that same six months. If you suffer a setback on trail, chances are you will be able to make up for it over time. The most important thing is to not panic.

Getting “ahead” in your schedule might temporarily make you feel more in control, but this is largely an illusion. Pushing too hard could just as easily result in a hike-ending or hike-delaying overuse injury. Better to learn to live with the uncertainty and not let it ruin your day-to-day.

Industry observers note that I’ve found that much of the joy and beauty of thru-hiking lies in the quiet moments of stillness: deep conversations shared with fellow hikers around camp, spontaneous fun on an unplanned zero day,  a particularly tasty snack enjoyed in solitude during a water break, a thousand spectacular sunrises and sunsets. If you’re so worried about the success or failure of your thru-hike that you have to sacrifice those moments just to feel like you’re still on track, what is even the point of being out there to begin with?

Remember: it’s OK to linger over a meal or enjoy a diverting side quest, even if it puts you behind your planned mileage for one day. Getting your miles in while the getting’s good is not a bad proposal. But don’t let it sour the journey along the way.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • As the title suggests, Behind the Climb brings viewers behind the scenes with Colin Haley and Tyler Karow as they take on the Southeast Ridge of Cerro Torre.
  • Sources indicate that as the short film opens, Haley introduces us to the route in voiceover, while on-screen, he and Karow make the approach, crossing ice fields and fording streams.
  • The Headwall section of Cerro Torre.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As the title suggests, Behind the Climb brings viewers behind the scenes with Colin Haley and Tyler Karow as they take on the Southeast Ridge of Cerro Torre. Colin Haley has tried the route, which he calls a modern classic, three times already without success. He hopes that by teaming up with Tyler Karow, the fourth time will be the charm.

Sources indicate that as the short film opens, Haley introduces us to the route in voiceover, while on-screen, he and Karow make the approach, crossing ice fields and fording streams. The route is divided into three main sections: the Haston Crack, Ice Towers, and Headwall. Haley was turned back twice by bad weather on the Ice Towers; neither of them has finished the Headwall.

The Headwall section of Cerro Torre. Photo: Screenshot.

Hoping to catch the Ice Towers still frozen and the Headwall still warmed by the sun, they wake up so early that the sun hasn’t actually finished setting yet. At that point, it seems more accurate to say that they took an evening nap and then climbed through the night.

Interspersed with clips of climbing, Haley and Karow review the footage, sharing the little logistical details and impressions of the climb. The Ice Towers, which Karow recalls attempting many years ago, have changed since he last encountered them. Once, as the name implies, thick with ice, much of it has now melted. “In another ten years,” Karow predicts, they will “look drastically different.”.

Sources indicate that ice or no, they complete the second section. This time, the weather cooperates. Haley takes over for the final section, the dastardly Headwall which has repeatedly eluded him. The climbing itself is going well, but melting snow above is making the rock run with water. This, he admits, is a significant disadvantage to their carefully timed proposal.

It has been revealed that despite the wet holds, Haley makes good progress. With only a few pitches to go, the self-described pessimist Haley admits that he finally thinks they’ll make it to the top. When he does finally reach the summit, grinning widely at the camera, voiceover reveals he has already started worrying about the descent.

According to recent reports, keeping with the promise to go behind the scenes, the video doesn’t stop at the summit, where they stand victoriously and admire the views. We follow the pair as they rappel down.

At the bottom, when asked how they feel about the adventure, both men reply simply that their hands hurt. Not all of us can be poets.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

What’s in My Pack…

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1379 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that well, let’s see.
  • I also have my astronomy and chemistry books in there.
  • I don’t expect to be calculating any derivatives out on the trail, though I suppose there could be some deep analysis on rates of change over time, especially involving hiking distances per day.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that well, let’s see. There’s raingear, gloves, hat, a blanket, sweatshirt, a calculus book, some water….

Hold up. What was that? A calculus book?

In a recent development, yes. I also have my astronomy and chemistry books in there. Back when I was in college – before the internet but after color TV was apparently invented – our college professors assured us we would all be using calculus in our engineering careers. I’ve wondered for decades when I would ever use this… material (putting it politely), other than to teach it to my son or other engineering students who struggled with higher-level math. So, after thirty-five years, I’ve finally found a use for it.

I don’t expect to be calculating any derivatives out on the trail, though I suppose there could be some deep analysis on rates of change over time, especially involving hiking distances per day.

For astronomy, I love looking at the stars. Sure, it’s engineering astronomy with lots of galactic calculations for weights, trajectories and distances, but it has a few very pretty star charts that would look great at night. Not so much at 10 a.m. on a random Saturday, but considering Michigan, the probability of unusual weather events is never zero.

What about chemistry? Its really more of a canary in a coal mine for me… or more accurately, a canary in my backpack. The only chemical reaction I’m investigating is whether the chemistry book turns out wet and its pages become more pulp-like, in which case I’ve learned something.

My pack liner is no longer waterproof.

I’d take my statistics book, which is a heavier, but I actually like that one. Yes, I know. I have a bit of a twisted mind to enjoy statistics. The other choice was my Engineering Project Management book. While hiking the AT is, in itself, an entire project management adventure, and I suspect Change Control may be a solid fireside topic while hiking, I still need that book for work-related activities.

A better question may be WHY do I have these three books in my pack?

It has been revealed that weight. They help my pack get up to 30 pounds, which I hope is my peak hiking weight when I’m on the trail next March. The calculus book is a whomping 5 pound and a touch over 15 ounces. Lots of “good times” in that book. Chemistry is another five pounds and almost 2 ounces while astronomy is in between with 5 pounds and 5 ounces.

Perhaps a better title for this post would be “How Am I Preparing for My AT Hike?” In which case, those books are involved, but no, they aren’t going on the trail with me in four months.

For preparing my body for the trail, there are three strategies I’m using:.

Recent findings suggest that southeastern Michigan doesn’t have mountains, and the hills are more bump-like, but they are there. Tossing a 30-pound pack on my back and hiking 5–6 miles is a decent warm-up. I’m trying to do that every week.

Right now, I just finished a five-day continuous stretch of doing this every morning, as I had some vacation time still to burn from work. I’m assessing how my body handles it, what that strange feeling is in my legs, why my ankles are sore, and trying to force myself to get up, out of a comfortable bed, and hike in sub-30-degree weather. It’s been challenging but so far, OK. I am glad, though, to take a break over the next few days and instead keep working on the other two strategies.

Besides just working on my body, I’m also testing how various software works while on day hikes – my Garmin In-Reach Mini has passed my previous checks and now has its subscription suspended for another few months until I really need it, but testing Day One (a journaling app), Grammarly (to well… help with my grammar) and hopefully, WordPress to see how a post or two work here when I’m coming off a hike when I tired, hungry and just want to start my drive home with the heat on full blast.

It has been revealed that what would be considered the easiest is actually one of the harder ones for me. A good workout at the gym is two hours. That’s enough time to get at least three miles on the treadmill (at 3.4 mph with a 6–7° uphill grade), core work, strength training, stretching and maybe finishing by laying on a hydro lounger at the end.

Sadly, my job takes up longer hours than I want to admit at times, but at least I enjoy doing what I am doing at the office as well as the people I work with. The problem comes at the end of the day. If I don’t leave early enough, I don’t get to the gym until after 5 p.m., in which case it’s impossible to get a decent work out and get home in time to cook dinner for my wife. I’m left wondering where the day went.

In a recent development, yes, it’s true I could get up earlier in the morning, but… that isn’t happening. Probably won’t happen on the trail either, to be fair. Getting up before the sun rises is something I consider a necessary evil to continue getting a paycheck. Getting up even earlier to willingly work out is far worse and would fall into the category of a malicious act of cruelty to my body.

Industry observers note that this is strangely enough, the easiest and most satisfying. I’m doing a routine of about thirty minutes with ankle strengthening, core work and stretching. It’s something casual to do while watching TV and the time just passes. It’s not the most useful, but hopefully it will help prevent something like an ankle sprain.

In a recent development, as for my actual gear list. Yes, I’ll post it. It will probably be right after the Christmas holidays, as I have some upcoming gear that absolutely needs to be weighed, manhandled and experimented with. My hope is less than 20 pounds base weight for starting in March, with a fully loaded pack of under 30 pounds. Whether I hit that target or not, is in jeopardy with the requirement of a bear can, but that’s another discussion….

According to recent reports, about me? Sure. I’m a native Detroiter and have lived my whole life in Michigan where I live with my wife – more than 25 years – and a couple of college-aged children. Well, technically the kids live off at college but they do come home to make the house look a natural disaster struck while we weren’t looking. I’m an engineer, working for one of the Big Three automakers and have well over 30 years of experience doing everything from breaking transmissions to quality improvements and even designing cooling systems for both trucks and cars. Outside of work, I love exploring and spending time outdoors. I’ve learned a lot about camping over the last few decades, including relearning wonderful lessons like not leaving an unlocked cooler in camp and proper flow directions on my water filter. Somewhere in there, I fell in love with backpacking and found a whole new world of mistakes I can learn from. Eventually, I discovered long-distance thru-hiking and convinced both my job and my family that taking a vacation from me for six months would be beneficial to them (suckers!). Catch me on a good day, and I’d be happy to talk about camping, backpacking, video games, books, music or just about anything else fun. Just don’t ask me about spreadsheets, checklists, FMEAs or change control meetings.

Tech Report: Escaping the Farting Ghost Hotel: 17.6 Miles into Portugal

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (883 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that we both thought the place we slept in last night was haunted.
  • When we left, my phone died as I tried to disconnect from the Wi-Fi.
  • Recent findings suggest that we headed out around 7:00 AM while it was still in the high 50s.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that we both thought the place we slept in last night was haunted. It was on the backside of a thousand-year-old church, with one wall actually serving as the back of the altar. We both woke up in the middle of the night feeling really hot and smelling a sewer odor. Knockerz had some strange dreams, as did I.

When we left, my phone died as I tried to disconnect from the Wi-Fi. After a restart, Knockerz’s phone suddenly started talking to her—something it never does.

Recent findings suggest that we headed out around 7:00 AM while it was still in the high 50s. We also lost an hour crossing the water: Spain keeps the same time all the way out, but when you drop into Portugal, the clocks go back an hour. A high-speed train barreled by shortly after we set off.

In a recent development, we’ve been navigating our own Camino route choices since entering Portugal, generally following the official routes. This has allowed us to get off the beaten path, explore the backcountry, and see areas untouched by millions of pilgrims over the centuries. Of course, self-made routes sometimes come with obstacles, like busy highways with no shoulder.

At one point, I pulled up a map and realized we were on the coastal route. We’ve been bouncing between the coastal route (slightly inland and more popular) and the littoral route (which hugs the coastline and isn’t on many maps) because they run so close together.

We stopped at a cafe for some caffeine and breakfast treats. The pastries here are different from Spanish treats—more layered, like a croissant, and only slightly sweet. I also noticed people saying “bom caminho” instead of the Spanish “buen camino.”.

In a recent development, the people here are very friendly, constantly greeting us with bom dia (good day). We’ve started practicing our basic Portuguese greetings:.

We bumped back out to the coast where the littoral and coastal paths briefly share a path. A cool coastal fog sheltered us from the sun as the air warmed into the 60s.

We enjoyed the littoral route past a wide beach featuring an old fort—its design looked remarkably similar to a fort we visited in St. Augustine, Florida. After that, we walked on a long boardwalk through a marshy area for several miles.

Near Âncora, we took a littoral path out to the coast that forced us to walk through heavy sand dunes. It was exhausting, so we decided to bail and take an alternate route along a busy road.

After walking about a mile of cars whizzing past on a narrow sidewalk (and climbing about 500 feet off the beach), I found a quieter parallel road winding through local villages.

At this point, we were starving, so we found a restaurant that served a wonderful, incredibly cheap meal. Afterward, we made our way back to the coast to rejoin the littoral route.

According to recent reports, we walked through farm fields on a narrow path paved with six-inch rocks, much like an old Roman road we traveled in Spain. Our path shifted through a mix of paved tracks, cobblestones, and large boulders. With the fog mostly burned off, the sun rays grew hot, but a constant, cold ocean breeze kept us comfortable. Most of the coastline here is rocky, dotted with tidal pools.

As we approached our final destination, we could spot a castle up on the hill and what looked like a grand structure on the same hilltop. It had been a long, 17-mile day, and we were both completely exhausted.

In a recent development, we finally arrived in Viana do Castelo, a very cool medieval town that happened to be hosting a massive medieval (and Renaissance) festival! We wandered around for a while, taking in all the people dressed and acting like historical figures.

Recent findings suggest that tired out, we found a place to sit, enjoy some Portuguese-sized glasses of red wine, and people-watch for a couple of hours. It was actually quite cold, even in the middle of June!

We finally headed to our room, which happened to be located in the basement. Honestly, it was perfect—we were so tired and ready for some rest. Especially Knockerz, who needed to sleep off the memory of the farting ghost hotel from the night before!

#160926. Breaking: Kayaking 3,700km Around Britain

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1708 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Kayaking 3,700km Around Britain

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1708 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that dominic Gribbin, 61, is more than five months into his attempt to circumnavigate mainland Great Britain by sea kayak.
  • Gribbin rolled out his expedition from Crinan Harbour in Argyll, Scotland, on June 2.
  • Industry observers note that the journey has not gone according to blueprint.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that dominic Gribbin, 61, is more than five months into his attempt to circumnavigate mainland Great Britain by sea kayak. But relentless weather delays and mounting costs have made the journey even more challenging than anticipated.

Gribbin rolled out his expedition from Crinan Harbour in Argyll, Scotland, on June 2. Paddling clockwise, he has covered 2,584km. From Crinan, he continued up the west coast of Scotland and around Cape Wrath and Duncansby Head before heading south along the eastern and southern coasts. His latest reported landing point is Cliff End, near Hastings, Sussex.

Industry observers note that the journey has not gone according to blueprint. Persistent Atlantic weather systems have cost him weeks of paddling time, while the financial demands of keeping the expedition moving have forced him to return to freelance television camerawork so he and his wife, Nicola, can keep it running.

In a recent development, while he paddles, she follows him in their motor home, offering shore support. He now hopes to complete the circle at Crinan in the spring of 2027. ExplorersWeb caught up with him to find out more about the journey. This interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.

How do you approach the daily distances on a journey like this?

In a recent development, given that circumnavigating the British mainland is at least 3,700km, I have aimed to do at least 40km per day. My longest day so far has been 64km. However, weather, tides and daylight length, particularly in autumn and winter, often curtail one’s best-laid plans. Some days have been necessarily shorter, forcing me to make an earlier-than-envisaged retreat to shore.

Sources indicate that but this is very much a journey, not a race, so we will continue into the spring of 2027. It’s an incredible opportunity to explore every nook and cranny of the GB coastline.

How much has the weather affected your progress?

Roughly 85% of delays have been due to poor weather, 5% to Ministry of Defense firing range timetable restrictions, and 10% to the need for very specific tidal windows to navigate particular sections safely and efficiently. I have never had a delay due to fatigue or the need for a break from the sheer physical nature of this endurance challenge. I have used days when I have inevitably been “weathered-off” to recoup my energy reserves.

Industry observers note that for most of the trip, it has been extremely rare to have more than four days of consistently good paddling weather. Setting off from Crinan on June 2 meant we did not enjoy the heat wave experienced in southern Britain. Instead, we lost at least six weeks to poor weather. Constant Atlantic westerly and northwesterly fronts brought wind, rain, and high seas that seemed to permanently batter northwest and northern Scotland throughout June, July, and even into early August. It was one of the great untalked-about weather phenomena of summer 2026. It wasn’t all heat waves…at least not in Scotland!

Are you camping or sleeping in the motorhome?

Northwest Scotland and its wild, deeply indented coastline often made road access to the sea impossible. Early on, we accepted that there would be long stretches when Nicola would not see me for over 24 hours. She was often doing double the mileage I was doing and negotiating some very hairy driving conditions on roads way off the beaten track. That resulted in many planned and unplanned wild camps along the coast.

It has been revealed that by the time we reached the north coast of Scotland, road access had improved dramatically, and Nicola and I were generally able to coordinate to meet at the end of each day. This has proved an invaluable motivator, especially when the going gets tough. Our little motorhome has been a blessed retreat each night since then: a warm, reassuring space to relax, gather one’s thoughts, and proposal ahead.

In a recent development, the route so far. The blue line indicates the paddling route, the red line shows the route taken by the support vehicle. Image: Dominic Gribbin.

What kayak are you paddling, and how much equipment do you carry?

I am paddling around Britain in a Rockpool Taran 16 sea kayak. It is a fast, beautifully handmade sea kayak, perfect for putting down the miles and handling heavy seas. The trade-off is stability, but it has a prodigious load capacity in its various watertight bulkheads.

I carry a kayak trolley permanently on the back deck. I have already worn out two and am constantly experimenting with new designs to better negotiate the challenges of gravel and sand beaches. As a minimum, I carry basic wild-camping equipment in case I need to spend an unexpected night ashore.

Recent findings suggest that food consists of pre-cooked rice bags, canned fish and vegetables, alongside plenty of snacks. I favor savory rather than sweet food. Coffee is my essential luxury, and I normally carry a can or two of beer!

It has been revealed that safety equipment is extensive. I carry a Garmin 86i Marine GPS with InReach satellite tracking, an ICOM marine handheld VHF radio with AIS and GPS, a spare VHF radio, flares and smoke signals, and a McMurdo personal locator beacon. I also carry a fully integrated Garmin Fenix 7 Pro watch, first-aid kit, spare paddles, compass, mobile phone, battery packs, head lamp, repair tape, and a Swiss Army penknife.

Recent findings suggest that the kayak itself weighs 24.9kg, but the overall weight, including my dry suit, buoyancy aid, clothing, and equipment, easily reaches 35kg or more. It is a significant challenge to negotiate all this weight over an often-unfriendly shoreline. However, the kayak benefits from the additional weight when afloat.

What have been the most memorable moments along the way?

We have had numerous encounters with sea otters, hunting pods of bottlenose dolphins, and close-up encounters with bottlenose mothers and calves. There have also been golden eagles and white-tailed sea eagles, the largest raptor in the UK. Some of the most sublime moments have been the inshore sea passages through the sheltered waters of the Inner Hebrides.

In a recent development, successfully rounding Cape Wrath was a truly intimidating but awe-inspiring milestone. Then there was rounding the infamous Duncansby Head and crossing the Pentland Firth near John O’Groats, finally seeing the compass turn south. The huge breeding seabird colonies off Caithness and much of Scotland’s northeast coast have been incredible. Literally tens of thousands of birds, a deafening cacophony of noise!

Right along the GB coastline, we have also met some of the warmest and most generous people.

Have there been any particularly frightening moments?

The huge seas off Strathy Point, Caithness, are probably the closest call yet. If something had gone wrong there while two kilometers offshore in those seas, I wouldn’t be writing this.

I have experienced plenty of rough and scary seas so far, but that occasion was another order of magnitude. They were enormous seas driven by Arctic swell and spring tides. They were the biggest seas I have ever paddled in. I am not in a rush to return there, despite its beauty.

According to recent reports, you have mentioned that you are now combining freelance work with the expedition. How are you managing the financial and logistical side?

We were able to make this happen because I am self-employed. We bankrolled the expedition using our savings. The motorhome for shore support was the biggest investment. We initially calculated finances based on finishing by mid-autumn, but those weather delays cost us dearly. We ran out of money by mid-September, so I have had to return to my freelance work as a TV cameraman and juggle that with keeping this Edge of Britain expedition going until we are finished.

There is no stopping this winter. Instead, we will take advantage of every weather window.

How did you first get into the sport?

I began paddling at age 11 when I permanently borrowed a friend’s old kayak and started exploring the ankle-deep waters of the River Ver and River Colne around St. Albans and Park Street, Hertfordshire. At 13, I started British Canoe Union training. This began my lifelong involvement with whitewater paddling on rivers around the world.

Sources indicate that back in the 1970s and 1980s, when I began, skills progression was funneled entirely through very actively encouraged participation in canoe slalom. Everybody who learned to paddle at club level was involved in slalom to some degree. I chose men’s C1 (Canadian singles) and competed at a national level, ranking 19th in Great Britain by the age of 18.

It has been revealed that university changed my orientation somewhat, and the allure of traveling to exotic whitewater rivers around the world took over. Expedition whitewater paddling then became my life, and still is, alongside expedition sea kayaking. Combining this with filmmaking ultimately led directly to my career as a television cameraman.

Why did you decide to take on a circumnavigation of Britain?

Sources indicate that the decision to attempt to paddle around the GB mainland is the culmination of a life spent kayaking. It is hard not to fall in love with the sheer beauty and allure of the world of the river and coastline, particularly here at home in the UK. This country has what is widely celebrated as some of the best sea kayaking in the world. To dream of exploring the whole GB coastline in as much detail as time and weather allow is, to me, a logical conclusion.

In a recent development, the actual decision came extremely late in the day, namely January 2026. This began a frantic period of organization ahead of our June 2 launch. Admittedly, April would have been better, but prior commitments meant we had to begin in June.

It has been revealed that I chose a clockwise route around Britain, thinking (naively) that the prevailing winds would vaguely be behind us for at least half the journey. I also wanted to tackle the potentially most technically demanding section of the northwest and north coast of Scotland early, in the height of what I envisaged as long summer days. How wrong I was!

  • In a recent development, “We are at Lobuche…resting, analyzing the weather forecast.
  • In a recent development, in a post on social media, member Sergey Kondrashkin recalls the latest trip up.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Last week, high winds forced the Russian team to retreat from their third trip up the West Ridge of Everest. Sergey Kondrashkin, Vitaly Shiilov, and leader Andrei Vasiliev were climbing without oxygen, with no one else on the mountain. Winter is swiftly approaching, but they have no intention of going home yet.

In a recent development, “We are at Lobuche…resting, analyzing the weather forecast. Still want to try again,” Vasiliev texted to ExplorersWeb over the weekend. The climbers had not intended to reach the summit on that latest attempt up the West Shoulder of Everest via the Lho La Pass. Vasiliev explained that they were not yet acclimatized enough to reach the top without bottled oxygen. They did expect to reach higher than before, but high winds made that impossible.

In a recent development, in a post on social media, member Sergey Kondrashkin recalls the latest trip up. On November 11, the team set off from their tent at the base of the West Ridge, fixing ropes in bitterly cold temperature. Contrary to forecasts, winds were light. The climbers pitched their tent at 6,500m and still had time to fix some ropes above them.

It has been revealed that on the following morning, however, the gusts were too strong. After waiting in vain for the gale to abate, and with a forecast of even stronger winds the following day, Kondrashkin returned to the ridge, trying not to be blown away. He advanced between gusts and retrieved his two ice axes and the rope he had left behind the day before. They would need that gear for the descent.

In a recent development, once at the bivouac, the climbers retrieved their tent, cached some food and fuel, and downclimbed to their Camp 1 at some 5,600m. It lies on the steep section between the Khumbu Glacier and the Lho La. Here, they pitched their tent again.

On Friday, the Russian team rappelled down to the glacier, on a “relatively safe” line to the right, where an avalanche fell as they descended.

It has been revealed that today, the team sits at their lodge in Lobuche and looks intently at weather forecasts. “We have not yet decided when to return to the mountain,” Vasiliev told Explorersweb. “It’s all about the weather, and the forecasts announce high winds on November 20-21.”.

Officials Blame Climate Change for Glacier Collapse That Killed 17

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (344 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Russian authorities are now attributing the September 6 disaster on 5,047m Mount Mizhirgi in the northern Caucasus to climate-related destabilization of a hanging glacier.
  • According to recent reports, A half-million cubic meter avalanche struck a military group undergoing mountain training, killing 17 and injuring 10.
  • It has been revealed that the impact generated a powerful blast of displaced air that reportedly threw some victims 200m to 300m down the slope before burying them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Russian authorities are now attributing the September 6 disaster on 5,047m Mount Mizhirgi in the northern Caucasus to climate-related destabilization of a hanging glacier.

According to recent reports, A half-million cubic meter avalanche struck a military group undergoing mountain training, killing 17 and injuring 10. Another 10 were unharmed and made it down the mountain on their own.

It has been revealed that the impact generated a powerful blast of displaced air that reportedly threw some victims 200m to 300m down the slope before burying them. As we reported at the time, helicopter pilot Alexander Davydov caught the avalanche on video.

Sources indicate that eldar Khashkhozhev of the Russian Ministry of Emergency Situations explained that warmer temperatures melted the protective blanket of snow, exposing parts of the glacier. This weakened the ice support that had glued enormous masses of snow and ice in place for decades.

A helicopter inspection of the region’s snow conditions the month before found no cause for concern, and some officials insist the catastrophe was unpredictable. However, climber Dmitry Polyakov, who was in the region at the time, disputed the idea that the glacier posed no danger. He said climbers had long recognized its instability and generally avoided approaching it in large groups.

Recent findings suggest that the Mizhirgi Glacier against Mizhirgi East and West peaks, site of September’s catastrophic glacial collapse. Photo: Shutterstock.

The key points of Khashkhozhev’s explanation were:.

Rising temperatures have raised the altitude of permanent snow cover.

Previously protected sections of the glacier became exposed, weakening the supporting ice beneath the hanging masses.

Eventually, gravity overcame that support and triggered a collapse that struck the training group.

This was the largest climbing disaster in the country since 2002, when another glacier collapse in North Ossetia, located between the Black and Caspian Seas, killed 125 people, including local residents.

With major landslides in summer and the possibility of glacial collapse at other times of the year throughout the world, mountaineers will have to adjust their behavior, as previously safe areas become potentially deadly.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Despite a forecast of high winds on November 21 and 22, Andrei Vasiliev, Sergey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov have decided to begin a new attempt on the West Ridge of Everest on Sunday.

The three stubborn Russians will again proceed via the West Ridge without bottled oxygen, support, or any other living soul on the mountain.

Recent findings suggest that the forecasts warn of very high winds all weekend. Nevertheless, they will start up on Sunday, November 22, although that is the day with the strongest winds forecast.

“That day, we will remain low on the mountain and climb to our Camp 1 at 5,600m,” Sergey Kondrashkin wrote. “From there, we will push upward when the weather improves and the winds die down, aiming to descend around November 28.”.

It has been revealed that this means the team does not intend to summit quite yet. The goal is to acclimatize by reaching 7,500m and then return to their headquarters in Lobuche.

“The question is, will we manage to complete the summit push within the time frame of our permit, which expires on December 15, and will the weather cooperate?” mentioned Kondrashkin.

The fall season on Everest usually lasts until the end of November, since December 1 marks the start of Nepal’s winter climbing season. However, the permit dates may have been extended for this team, which is climbing off the normal route.

Once winter settles in, it will be the turn of Jost Kobusch of Germany, who will attempt to solo Everest in winter along the same route the Russians are now attempting.

It has been revealed that on their third and latest trip up the mountain so far, the team only reached 6,700m before hurricane-force winds up to 130kph forced them down, according to former team member Natalyia Belyankina. Belyankina had to leave the expedition for health reasons but has stayed in touch with the others.

Tech Report: Jost Kobusch to Train For Everest on Difficult, Dangerous Lhotse Shar

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (606 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that jost Kobusch of Germany has moved to the Khumbu Valley to finish his acclimatization before attempting to solo winter Everest, beginning on December 22.
  • Sources indicate that kobusch is now in Chukhung village, from which he climbed 6,165m Island Peak (Imja Tse) yesterday.
  • Kobusch’s climb on Island Peak as shown in his tracker today.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that jost Kobusch of Germany has moved to the Khumbu Valley to finish his acclimatization before attempting to solo winter Everest, beginning on December 22. His preparations include reaching 8,000m on a different peak.

Sources indicate that kobusch is now in Chukhung village, from which he climbed 6,165m Island Peak (Imja Tse) yesterday. He spent the night at 6,000m, topped out again today, and went back down, as shown in his live tracker. He told ExplorersWeb that he will now rest for a few days in Lukla and then hike up the valley again to inspect conditions on his next acclimatization goal: the difficult Lhotse Shar (8,383m).

Kobusch’s climb on Island Peak as shown in his tracker today.

“My plan is not to summit but to tag 8,000m up its flank, before heading for Everest,” he said.

Lhotse Shar is one of the main points of the Lhotse ridge, and it is climbed from south side of the mountain, with Chukhung as the starting point. The main options are to climb the southeastern flank of the Shar itself or try a direct line up the formidable south face of Lhotse.

Neither of them is easy, and the upper sections are statistically dangerous. According to Wikipedia, Lhotse Shar has the highest fatality rate of all principal or secondary 8,000m peaks. For every two climbers who summit, one person dies attempting to.

Recent findings suggest that lhotse and its various points, as seen from the south. Graphic by Gorskie Mapy.

In a recent development, the Austrian expedition that first reached the summit of Lhotse Shar (from the Southeast Ridge) in 1970 set four altitude camps, the uppermost at 7,600m. They used supplemental oxygen on their summit push. “Almost the whole of the route from below Camp 1 to Camp 3 was fixed with rope, as climbing was very difficult,” they reported in the AAJ.

Kobusch will not have to deal with the nearly vertical terrain and cornices near the summit, but will have to face difficult mixed terrain and uncertain conditions if he wants to venture up to 8,000m. He will not use bottled oxygen, and as far as we know, he will climb on his own.

Kobusch aims to reach the base of Everest on December 22 and solo the mountain in winter without oxygen, via the West Ridge — the same line currently being attempted by a Russian team.

In a recent development, this is Kobusch’s fourth attempt, and he is willing to try to reach the summit this time. However, when asked about it, he admits he does not know if such a feat is actually possible. “Every expedition, every training session, every difficult decision has been part of preparing myself for what I know will be the biggest challenge of my life,” he admits.

Industry observers note that kobusch’s is not the only confirmed climb this winter. Denis Urubko of Russia is reportedly preparing to climb Broad Peak in winter, possibly starting at the end of this year and continuing through January and February. On social media, Urubko mentioned he will be climbing with Vitaliy Skel. However, details of his route have not been confirmed.

Simone Moro of Italy has not decided whether to try Manaslu again this winter. He told ExplorersWeb he is still considering his aims while observing the “crazy weather this season.” Moro attempted Manaslu in fall to acclimatize and become familiar with the terrain. However, like every other team, he had to call off the attempt due to dangerous conditions following extremely heavy snowfall. Moro wants to climb the peak in alpine style.

‘I Tried Not Looking at the Rack.’ Indiana Hunter Tags 199-Inch Buck on State Park Land

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (814 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Avery Fisher of Delphi, Indiana, and his best friend since high school, Nathan Van Dokkenburg, put in for an Indiana parks draw hunt on the recommendation of a buddy.
  • Indiana has special limited-draw, short-term deer hunts on about 25 public parks around the state.
  • Neither Fisher nor Van Dokkenburg had ever walked the park they drew to hunt, which they declined to name.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Avery Fisher of Delphi, Indiana, and his best friend since high school, Nathan Van Dokkenburg, put in for an Indiana parks draw hunt on the recommendation of a buddy. Both drew the two-day Nov. 16-17 firearms season.

Indiana has special limited-draw, short-term deer hunts on about 25 public parks around the state. The hunts help manage the burgeoning deer herds, and most allow sportsmen to take three deer per hunt, with a limit of one buck. The number of hunters drawn for each park varies, but about 150 hunters are typically allowed on a park for each two-day hunt.

Neither Fisher nor Van Dokkenburg had ever walked the park they drew to hunt, which they declined to name. But they spent a lot of time figuring out where they should be on the property well before the hunt.

According to recent reports, “We studied a lot of Google Maps and onX to get an idea where we should hunt far back in the park well away from other hunters,” Fisher tells Outdoor Life. “It’s rolling hills with major creek drains and draws … I’ve hunted that kind of land previously, and I had a good idea where to go early that Nov. 16 opening morning.”.

According to recent reports, the hunters checked in when the park opened at 5 a.m. and were prepared for an all day sit with packs, gear, and food.

Sources indicate that “We got far back into the park, about one and a half miles from the road,” says Fisher, 25, who works as a financial advisor. “We stayed on ridgetops, and about one mile in, Nathan and I split up.

Fisher went about another half mile, hiking by the light of his headlamp.

“In the dark I spotted a tree line that had a lot of buck rubs. Then I saw a doe, and I figured it was a pretty good place.”.

He climbed about 30 feet off the ground and settled into his saddle with his coffee and snacks his favorite .44-cal Ruger, a gift from his father years ago.

It was cold early that morning, and he heard something in a nearby ravine around 7:45 a.m.

“I thought I saw a buck and put my binoculars on it, and it was one with a good spread and nice tines about 100 yards away.”.

He raised his rifle and rested it against the tree for support while looking for the buck in his scope.

“But my breath kept fogging the scope,” he indicates. “I kept cleaning it with my gloves, and the deer kept getting closer … I tried not looking at his rack as he turned uphill and then I saw his sticker points as he was rubbing trees.”.

Fisher found the shoulder in his scope and squeezed the trigger. The buck ran uphill past Fisher, wobbling as it went. When the buck stopped at 60 yards, Fisher shot again. The buck dropped.

Fisher texted Van Dokkenburg and told him he’d shot a nice buck, but to keep hunting because they were allowed to shoot up to three deer apiece.

It has been revealed that “A group of does came in at about 9 a.m., and I shot one and it fell,” Fisher says. “I decided not to shoot any more deer that morning.

“We had to bone and pack out two deer like we were on a Western hunt. I figured that was enough for us to lug out of there that day.”.

Van Dokkenburg saw nothing to shoot and met up with Fisher about 11 a.m., filming Fisher as he first walked up to his buck and realized how huge it was.

“I was speechless at the size of his rack,” notes Fisher. “I knew he was massive, but not a rack like that. I’m grateful and thankful to the Lord.”.

Using a wheeled cart and backpacks, the two hunters hauled both deer back down to their vehicle.

“I think my pack with deer and gear weighed over 100 pounds, and I had to stop and offload more from my pack to the wheeled cart,” Fisher says.

They then drove to check in their deer with park personnel.

Fisher’s 13-point buck has been measured with an unofficial green score of 199 5/8 inches. It turned out Fisher’s second shot had been unnecessary, since his first had struck the heart.

Read Next: ‘Complete Shock.’ Long-Haul Trucker Hunter Tags 227-Inch Nontypical During State Park Hunt.

The two buddies returned to the park to hunt the next day, though Fisher states they were exhausted from the previous day’s hunt.

“We saw some deer, including another far-off buck, but we didn’t shoot another deer that second day,” he says. “Nathan is drawn for another two-day park hunt later this year, so he still has a good chance of taking deer, maybe even a huge buck.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A heavy-antlered 12-point buck materializes on the trail. He’s only five steps from bow range, but then he throws his nose in the air, goes rigid with nervousness, and waves the white flag. Game over. That’s all, folks.

We all know that any successful deer hunt starts with not getting busted by a whitetail’s incredibly powerful sense of smell. And today there’s a whole collection of gear that’s marketed as being able to beat a deer’s nose. Many of the scent control gear and strategies are gimmicks, but some are not.

With careful scent control, you can give yourself a slight edge that just might mean the difference between getting busted and getting a shot. Here are scent-reduction efforts that work, with 15 steps that hunters can use to minimize scent before, during, and after the hunt.

Hunters must understand they will never completely neutralize the scent they emit. Furthermore, they will never completely beat a whitetail’s nose. However, a hunter can minimize their scent.

Industry observers note that this won’t keep a deer from smelling you, but it might buy you a little extra time or a few more yards. It can also make all the difference in a non-target deer just moving along rather than alarm snorting.

It has been revealed that you don’t have to use all of the following strategies just to shoot a deer. But, implementing at least some of them will certainly make you more effective in the stand.

Deer hunters should consider a long-term scent control mentality. Rather than just preparing the day of the hunt, start mitigating scent long before. During hunting season, consider cutting the smelly shampoos, soaps, colognes, deodorants, and aftershaves out of your routine. This will help keep your clothes smelling more natural, too.

Washing your hunting clothes is the next step. Treat with scent-reduction laundry detergent. Such laundry detergent doesn’t remove all scent, but it knocks out a lot of it and it doesn’t add unnatural scents. (Also, on a deer vision note, ensure that the detergent does not contain UV brighteners.).

Once your hunting clothes are clean, store them in a dedicated container. A portable plastic tote that has a place at home, but easily loads into a vehicle, is the best choice. This should help minimize odors that might contaminate the garment fibers. A lot of hunters like to put a pine branch in their tote to keep clothes smelling fresh and piney (and not like plastic).

It has been revealed that in addition to hunting clothing, hunters should also clean their other gear. Backpacks and boots absorb the scents around them. So, store these and other hunting items in areas that aren’t stinky. Use a dedicated storage bin for this gear, too.

The day of the hunt, take a shower with shampoos and soaps that are designed to reduce human odor without adding artificial scents. This should help neutralize some (but not all) of the existing surface scent on your hair and skin.

Brush your teeth, but not with a super-smelly toothpaste. Instead, use something with a natural scent, or no scent at all. Then, eat an apple to help further mitigate scent that might originate from the mouth and throat. Avoid strong-smelling drinks and foods, such as coffee or spicy grub which lead to bad breath.

It has been revealed that A lot of hunters use ozone in the field (like Ozonics), but it’s also applicable for treating hunting clothing. Some products are designed to work in conjunction with boxes to clean clothing and remove unwanted scent.

Used improperly, Ozone can destroy clothing. So Wildgame innovations recently introduced a ZeroTrace tote and device that is designed to treat gear without destroying it.

Read Next: Does Ozonics Actually Work? Here’s What 5 Independent, Diehard Deer Hunters Say After Field Testing.

To minimize unwanted scent particles from making it onto your hunting clothes, consider dressing once in the field. This keeps away scent from handling pets, visiting gas stations, or other stops between home and the hunt. Getting dressed in the field during a cold or rainy day can be a hassle, but it’s worth it.

Rubber boots can contain some scent, but they only achieve this if kept uncontaminated from foreign scents. Don’t wear your deer hunting boots around town where they might pick up unwanted odors.

Read Next: Best Rubber Hunting Boots.

Hunters have many reasons for field wipes. But in terms of scent control, wiping off sweat with a field wipe will certainly help. Just make sure the version you use is scent-free.

Industry observers note that even better than wiping away sweat, is to not break a sweat at all. Sweat just adds an entire fresh new layer of scent. In the field, do everything possible to prevent or reduce sweating. Wait to put on your coat until you get to your stand.. Walk slowly. Remain in the shade. Take more time to get settled in the treestand.

Perhaps the most crucial aspect of scent control is managing the direction that your scent travels. This means choosing good entry and exit routes, and ensuring your wind doesn’t carry over into areas that deer frequent (especially bedding areas and core feeding areas).

Sources indicate that those who hope to minimize scent even further should deploy hunting blinds that are completely enclosed. Those which have completely sealed doors and windows can hold most, if not all, scent within the blind. Keeping windows closed until it’s  time to shoot is an excellent way to bottle up scent.

Some hunters might cleverly use wind blockers, which are land features that keep deer from getting downwind. Examples include hunting along the edge of a bluff, river, hinge-cut, or lake. Similarly, you can make a mock scrapes on either side of your scent cone, which might stop a buck just long enough before he gets downwind of you.

The rising and falling thermals can be helpful or a huge pain in the butt. When used wisely, and with the right stand locations, thermals will carry scent up and away from deer. For example, hunting up high on a ridge when morning thermals carry scent upward makes it very difficult for deer to smell hunters. Likewise, hunting down low in a bottom when afternoon thermals carry scent downward can achieve the same result.

Industry observers note that remember, no matter how far you take scent control strategies, deer will eventually smell you. It’s key to take all precautions, and implement each step outlined above. Ultimately, careful stand selection that puts the wind in your favor will be the most important step for not getting busted.

Recent findings suggest that but don’t get discouraged when the inevitable happens. Just keep hunting. After all, you can’t really beat a deer’s nose, and it wouldn’t be fun if we won every time anyway.
