‘No Dad, This Is Your Deer.’ Hunter Gets a Second Chance at a 200-Inch Blackpowder Buck

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (800 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • During Virginia’s muzzleloader season last year, Mike Shifflett got a chance at a giant buck.
  • “I was worried I might have hit him,” Shifflett tells Outdoor Life.
  • Virginia had a very harsh winter last year, says the 50-year-old farm manager from Crozet, and he was concerned the buck wouldn’t survive.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

During Virginia’s muzzleloader season last year, Mike Shifflett got a chance at a giant buck.

“I was worried I might have hit him,” Shifflett tells Outdoor Life. “But we looked hard and found no evidence he was hit. I sat in a blind later looking for him and eventually spotted him on trail cameras and he was fine. I completely missed him.”.

Virginia had a very harsh winter last year, says the 50-year-old farm manager from Crozet, and he was concerned the buck wouldn’t survive. But he started seeing the whitetail again on trail cameras — then found its sheds.

“I’m sure glad I missed him, because when I started getting trail camera photos of him this summer, his rack had just exploded. His antlers had added at least 30 inches.”.

In a recent development, shifflett monitored the buck through summer and early autumn on trail cameras in the rolling green hills of northern Virginia. He concluded the deer was very much a loner.

“He wasn’t aggressive at all,” Shifflett explained. “He completely avoided other bucks. If there was another buck in a field edge I hunted, he’d never come out.”.

Recent findings suggest that he started hunting the deer during this blackpowder season, which opened Oct. 31 and is Shifflett’s favorite time to chase whitetails.

He got trail camera photos of the buck and saw him once, far away at dusk.

Industry observers note that on Nov. 6, Shifflett waited for his 16-year-old daughter, Chloe, to get home from school, then they rushed to their blind. The hardsided redneck sat  on a field edge near the top of a mountain, with deer trails feeding into the field.

According to recent reports, A little after 5 p.m., the buck stepped out at 200 yards. There were some does in the field, and he began working toward them.

Recent findings suggest that “He worked a scrape and kept walking a few steps at a time toward the does. He was locked on those does, but it took him at least 15 minutes to get to them.

Then the buck, now at 90 yards, started pushing one doe around.

“He was in range and I offered my gun to my daughter to shoot him, but she said ‘No Dad, this is your deer.’”.

Shifflett raised his scoped .50-cal T/C and fired.

Industry observers note that “The air filled with smoke when I shot, and when it cleared the buck had its tail up, and went into the woods. It was surreal, like he wasn’t hit at all.”.

But Chloe had filmed her dad shooting the buck, and the video showed the deer mule kick at the shot.

“But I still didn’t like the way the deer acted as it left the field and into the woods,” claims Shifflett.

The two quietly climbed out of the blind and left, planning to return the next morning to track the buck. They returned early the following day with Shifflett’s wife, his son, and a few other helpers.

The search party didn’t initially locate much of a blood trail. But 40 yards into the woods the blood became easy to see. Soon they found the buck dead about 100 yards from the hit site. Shifflet’s bullet had passed through both lungs.

“There was a respectful, silent reverence among us — almost like being in a church.”.

Once they got the buck home, Shifflett and his buddies measured its rack.

“I’m no trophy hunter, and when we started scoring him at home I realized it was a really significant buck,” he claims. “I had entered a local big buck contest earlier this year and they scored my deer at 194 inches. It’s leading the contest with a $1,000 gift card as top prize.”.

He got in touch with Virginia Buckmasters scorer Tyler Turner, who measured the 16-point whitetail slightly bigger (Buckmasters has a different scoring system than some traditional record keeping organizations, including Boone and Crockett and Pope and Young). His spread was 19.6 inches and taped out at 202 ⅛ inches.

“Tyler says it’s the biggest Virginia buck in their ‘Regular Deer’ category that’s ever been taken by bow, blackpowder, or gun. He also told me it’s the ninth largest Buckmasters deer in that rack category nationwide.”.

In a recent development, it’s been a whirlwind of congratulations since news of his great buck spread. But one thing he says he’ll always remember is when he and his family walked up to the buck that morning.

Recent findings suggest that “When we found him, everyone became real quiet,” he states. “There was a respectful, silent reverence among us – almost like being in a church.”.

#160902. Breaking: ‘Get Out of the F—ing Tree!’ The Police Raided Our Deer Hunt

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1218 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: ‘Get Out of the F—ing Tree!’ The Police Raided Our Deer Hunt

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1218 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that WHAT STARTED as a normal morning in the deer woods turned out to be the scariest day of my life.
  • Our state has an extended urban antlerless season that ends in late March, and this particular hunt occurred right after the state of Virginia confirmed the “Stay at Home” order during the early Covid-19 pandemic.
  • We were hunting in a neighborhood of multimillion-dollar homes on three- to five-acre lots, and the property we were on that day was a double lot of 10 acres total.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that WHAT STARTED as a normal morning in the deer woods turned out to be the scariest day of my life. It was March 2020, and my friend Billy Phillips and I were hunting one of the suburban properties we have permission on in northern Virginia.

Our state has an extended urban antlerless season that ends in late March, and this particular hunt occurred right after the state of Virginia confirmed the “Stay at Home” order during the early Covid-19 pandemic. That particular order allowed you to leave home for a couple of reasons, and hunting was one of them.

We were hunting in a neighborhood of multimillion-dollar homes on three- to five-acre lots, and the property we were on that day was a double lot of 10 acres total. In our world, that’s humongous.

According to recent reports, we parked at the end of an old driveway and walked a short way to our hunting spots. We climbed into our trees to set up about 100 yards from each other, with Billy closer to the trucks than my stand. Then, just as daylight broke, I spotted the lights of a car near where we parked. I looked through my binos and saw that an older Ford Taurus had pulled up. I remember thinking, Oh, this is kind of odd.

In a recent development, I texted Billy. “Can you see the cars?”.

“Yeah, I’m looking at them,” he texted back.

Then I saw Billy’s truck bed light turn on.

“He’s in my car,” Billy texted again. “I’m getting down.”.

Industry observers note that at this point the sun was fully up and we could clearly see our surroundings. As Billy descended his tree, I saw a police officer in full uniform coming down the little hill toward us with an M4 in his hands. I pulled out my phone to record footage, the kind of video that states, Look at the unusual things we deal with while hunting in the suburbs.

Then I realized the cop had his weapon shouldered and was pointing it at Billy. He was screaming at him.

“Get on the ground! Get on the fucking ground!”.

What he was saying was concerning, but the tension in the officer’s voice was worse. Billy was packing up his sticks as the cop approached. If Billy had turned around while holding the sticks or if he still had his crossbow in his hands, I don’t even want to think about what might have happened.

Sources indicate that “Where’s your buddy?” the cop started yelling, getting even more aggressive. “Where’s your buddy?”.

And I’m like, “Sir, I’m over here.”.

“Get out of the fucking tree,” he yelled.

“OK,” I replied, “it’s going to take me a minute.”.

Sources indicate that “I didn’t ask for feedback. I told you to get down here.”.

Industry observers note that the cop screamed at both of us the whole time it took me to get down. When I walked up to the cop, he spoke into his radio.

“You can take the guns off them now.”.

We were obviously perplexed, and he explained that he had snipers in the woods with their rifles trained on us.

Sources indicate that “What is going on here?” I asked. “What is happening?”.

“Shut up,” he told me. “I’m asking questions here. Hands on your head and turn around.”.

I kept persisting with questions, trying to figure out why we were being searched at gunpoint and who this police officer was. The man wouldn’t tell us anything and proceeded to pat us down.

Industry observers note that “I’m not a regular cop,” was all he said. “I’m a special cop.”.

Read Next: The Best Tree Saddles, Tested and Reviewed.

When the officer asked us what we were doing at this property, we explained that we are deer hunters and that we had permission to be here. I pulled up the signed permission slip from the landowner and highlighted it to him. Then I asked again what he was doing here. The officer told us that they spotted us on a UAV — an unmanned aerial vehicle. He was suggesting he had a military drone 30,000 feet above us, which is completely ridiculous for our county or most any police department.

“This is Fairfax County,” I said. “What are you talking about?”.

His demeanor shifted and he got less aggressive — especially when I asked him why he was going through our vehicles.

According to recent reports, “You had a wire on the floor, and I thought it was a bomb,” he said to Billy. Billy explained that he works in landscaping, and that he has sprinkler-head components in his truck.

Industry observers note that by now we were starting to get nervous, and I noticed the officer’s uniform didn’t look quite right. There was something off about him. We kept asking why he was searching our cars without cause, and why he was on private property.

According to recent reports, he didn’t give us his card or an explanation, and no other officers indicated up. After the adrenaline of having a gun pointed at us wore off, Billy and I ran through what had just happened.

I told Billy that I thought the guy must be impersonating law enforcement, because the whole interaction just didn’t sit right with me. Billy and I mentor several police officers who are learning to hunt, and we’re huge supporters of police in general. Mind you, this was when Covid lockdowns were at their peak, and there was mass civil unrest throughout the country. The last thing we wanted to do was blast the police.

Recent findings suggest that still, we needed answers. We sent the short video clip I had recorded to a few of our police officer buddies, and one called me right away. He explained that it didn’t look right, and that what happened is not standard police procedure. He asked where we were and made a few phone calls to see if he could find out any details for us.

When my buddy called me back, he was laughing so hard he could barely speak. The man who had just ordered us down from our trees at gunpoint was indeed a police officer known as the department’s Tackleberry. (In the Police Academy movies, Tackleberry is a tryhard who’s overzealous in his enforcement.) This particular police officer had been on desk duty and was sent out on patrol as a result of scheduling issues caused by Covid.

Recent findings suggest that my buddy learned that the officer had gotten turned around, thought he was at a park, and that we were doing something illegal. Billy and I had a meeting with the guy’s captain, who apologized profusely. We decided to leave it at that.

Read Next: Deer Hunting Every Day in the Suburbs of Virginia.

It was a terrifying and confusing ordeal while it was happening, but now that a few years have passed, it’s just another crazy story from our time hunting the D.C. suburbs. Here’s this guy who thought he was busting the biggest crime ring of all time and instead ended up nearly arresting a couple rednecks in camo.

This story first ran on March 17, 2023.

#160901. Industry News: The Paradox of Seeking First Ascents in Western Nepal

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1256 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: The Paradox of Seeking First Ascents in Western Nepal

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1256 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that western Nepal has plenty of unclimbed 6,000m peaks, and Fredrik Strang of Sweden and Sindre Kolbjornsgard of Norway went there planning to climb one.
  • According to recent reports, what I remember most clearly about that narrow summit is not the grade, the exposure, or the possibility of being first.
  • In a recent development, sindre Kolbjornsgard, left, and Fredrik Strang.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that western Nepal has plenty of unclimbed 6,000m peaks, and Fredrik Strang of Sweden and Sindre Kolbjornsgard of Norway went there planning to climb one. In the end, they settled for a slightly lower but equally memorable experience. It indicated again that adventure goes beyond first ascents.

According to recent reports, what I remember most clearly about that narrow summit is not the grade, the exposure, or the possibility of being first. It is the silence. No helicopters. No voices from a fixed-rope queue. No machinery, no aircraft, no distant sound of a settlement. Only the two of us, a serrated horizon, and an unfamiliar feeling that the mountain had asked a question rather than supplied an answer.

In a recent development, sindre Kolbjornsgard, left, and Fredrik Strang. Photo: Fredrik Strang.

In a recent development, after 18 expeditions to 8,000’ers and witnessing the evolution (or devolution) of climbing on these peaks’ normal routes, Strang and his partner knew they wanted something different. Quoting Ed Viesturs, Strang noted: “The point is to climb, not just to summit.” With that in mind, the climbers set four criteria for their objectives:.

Several route options face the climbers’ base camp tent. Photo: Fredrik Strang.

Industry observers note that strang noted that there are many unclimbed peaks left in Nepal, but they were looking for a compelling climb, not just a dull summit for the record. They finally found one that satisfied their criteria, but then, as with so many other teams in Nepal this fall, harsh weather put their original objective out of reach. Not to mention that traveling Western Nepal is anything but simple.

According to recent reports, “Our intended destination was in the Nyalu Lek area north of Simikot,” Strang revealed. “We planned to cross Nyalu La, a pass around 5,000m, with a support party that included porters and pack animals.

In a recent development, “Getting from Surkhet to Simikot took two rough days by road, with landslides having damaged or obliterated sections of the route. At Simikot, we learned that Nyalu La was probably impassable. Even reaching the place where we planned to start trekking had been uncertain.”.

Recent findings suggest that when they did reach the area, they confirmed that their planned peak was not an option. Hiking further down the valley, they pitched their tent at Phendol Kermi Camp. Snow had covered the trails beyond, but they simply had no time or money to move to some other region in Nepal. Instead, they decided to explore whatever was close to their camp.

In a recent development, during their stay, they encountered Mick Fowler and Victor Saunders of the UK. Bad weather had likewise spoiled the British pair’s blueprint to attempt an unclimbed 6,000m peak farther east, known only as Peak 6010, according to Mount Everest Foundation.. This would have been their second attempt on that peak. Ironically, dry conditions spoiled their 2025 attempt. This time, too much snow forced them back. Read more on the British climbers’ adventure here:.

In a recent development, on October 6, Strang and Kolbjornsgard made their first acclimatization climb on a 5,177m peak at 30°20′49.82″N, 82°03′54.82″E. They found no records of any previous ascent.

“From base camp, the mountain looked straightforward, and lower down, it largely was,” Strang recalls. “Steep grass, mud, and broken rock led toward the upper slopes. But at about 4,500m, the route disappeared beneath knee-deep snow, then waist-deep snow, and every step became a small excavation.”.

In the following days, they scouted and flew their drone down side valleys, looking for possibilities. Their second peak was 5,227m in altitude, located at 30°07′50.86″N, 81°41′56.58″E. Again, there were no records of previous ascents. Parts of it were far from fun.

Sources indicate that “Below 4,500m, progress was tolerable, but above that, we were back to forcing our way through knee-deep, sometimes chest-deep snow,” Strang wrote. “A tremendous amount of work for very little enjoyment.”.

Luckily, the climb improved once they reached the summit ridge, on relatively easy mixed rock and ice, which they assessed at PD+.

“Fowler and Saunders climbed the mountain several days later and found an easier way to descend and reascend the step on its western side,” Strang noted. “Their solution was a reminder that the first line a team takes is not necessarily the best one.”.

Still, the peak that most drew the climbers’ attention was a remarkable 5,337m tooth of rock above Yangchya Lake at approximately 30°07′09.36″N, 81°41′21.15″E.

“We began calling it Daara Peak — a name inspired by the Nepali word for a projecting tooth or fang and by the mountain’s striking shape,” Strang noted. He notes that the name is provisional while they await a response from the authorities about their suggestion.

According to recent reports, strang describes the peak as “a saber-toothed tiger’s canine protruding from a mass of rock. The terminal pinnacle was about eight meters high, overhanging and sharply defined against the sky.”.

Recent findings suggest that the climbers about to reach what they called Daara Peak. Drone photo: Brizendra Bhattarai.

Industry observers note that the problem was approaching the peak in deep, heavy snow from Yangchya Lake. They failed on their first attempt to tackle its northeast headwall. After waiting out another snowy spell, the climbers returned for a second attempt on October 17-18.

The climbers dealt with 250m of rather poor rock, a complex approach to the headwall across a bergschrund with soft snow, and the uncertainty of moving on unfamiliar terrain. They had no idea of the difficulties ahead or whether they could protect the passages ahead on their way to the summit. The route included vertical granite walls, with cracks adequate for cams, some mixed terrain with the crux at M6, a steep couloir, and then the summit ridge: a granite edge with some 30cm of snow on top.

Climbing terrain on Daara Peak. Photo: Fredrik Strang.

Recent findings suggest that rather than technical difficulty, the section was delicate due to exposure and a lack of comfortable belay stations. Yet, the climbers reached the summit on October 18, including the top of the final pinnacle, thanks to a crack in the rock.

Industry observers note that strang admits that the climbing details suggest a rather straightforward ascent: a 5,337m summit via its northeast side in five pitches with difficulties up to M6. However, Strang judges the climb on a different scale. “The technical crux was behind us, but it was the part I remember most vividly,” he explained. “It was the silence.”.

It has been revealed that strang and Kolbjornsgard’s route up Daara Peak. Photo: Fredrik Strang.

On many of the 8,000m peaks I have climbed, the human presence has become part of the landscape: camps, radio calls, fixed ropes, queues, and the distant sound of aircraft. Up here, none of that reached us. Mountains extended in every direction. There was no audience, no ceremony, no one to confirm that we had accomplished anything at all.

Sources indicate that strang also reflects on the paradox: They enjoyed the wild terrain but, if every climber chases solitude by visiting these last remote valleys, the character of these places will inevitably change. For Strang, the question is not to ban access. However, he says:.

Perhaps some summits should remain untouched — not because we lack the skill or courage to reach them, but because future generations deserve to inherit mountains that have not all been reduced to objectives.

According to recent reports, the climb from the ridge. Photo: Fredrik Strang.

#160900. I Hunted Ducks and Geese During the Glory Days of Earthquake Lake

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 14m • 📚 Deep Dive (2900 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

I Hunted Ducks and Geese During the Glory Days of Earthquake Lake

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2900 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, it was a good day for waterfowl hunters.
  • I slid the overhead hatch back and stuck my head up and out of the blind.
  • According to recent reports, the blind was one of the biggest I had ever seen, and it was also almost invisible.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, it was a good day for waterfowl hunters. Wisps of fog seeped out of the melting landscape, and the sky was so low and solid that the geese—if they came—would be close to the deck. And it was cold. Two days before, a savage cold wave had swept across Tennessee, plastering trees and highways with ice and freezing ponds thicker than anyone could remember. Ducks and geese had been sitting it out, but on this third day, the ice was melting, and they would fly.

I slid the overhead hatch back and stuck my head up and out of the blind. Earlier it had been too dark to see how we were situated. I found that we were in a soybean field of perhaps 300 acres, already plowed for the spring planting. There was sparse timber on all sides. To the south, the way hunters faced when standing in the blind, the timber was not so tall or thick, but there was the heavy undergrowth that grows at water’s edge. The lake is closer than I thought, I remarked to myself. It’s only 100 yards or so away.

According to recent reports, the blind was one of the biggest I had ever seen, and it was also almost invisible. From a duck’s overhead view, it no doubt looked like a rush-covered finger of land surrounded on three sides by timber, water, and waterfowl decoys—hundreds of them.

Thus oriented, I closed the camouflaged hatch and placed my feet near the gas heater. Sheer luxury! Being there almost made up for all those miserable days I have spent crouched in freezing mud holes. Perhaps a time or two before, in Texas and Louisiana, I’d been in more luxurious shooting stands, but they were small houses built on stilts above the water. This was a blind dug into the ground, lined with concrete, and covered with earth that had been planted with suitable cover. The blind’s eyes on the outside world were 12 sliding hatches.

Sources indicate that inside, the padded theater seats were as comfy as easychairs. Theater seats! I thought. Who in hell would have thought of putting theater seats in a duck blind? But it was perfect! The spring-loaded bottoms snapped up out of the way when you rose to shoot. That gave a man more foot and leg room and eliminated bruised shins if he turned around for backyard shots. I’m forever scraping my shins on the sharp-edged board benches found in most blinds.

Industry observers note that as the light increased, so did the yipping of the Canada geese rafted up on Lake Isom just beyond the brushy boundary. A few minutes before, the even din of honking had changed pitch when a raft of Canadas took wing. Moments later another flight heaved into the morning fog.

In a recent development, our lookout Jerry Jones made no sign that geese were coming our way, but the atmosphere inside the blind was becoming so charged with excitement that you could almost touch it. Feet shuffled, experienced hunters quaked with anticipation, and hands rattled shotshells in jacket pockets to make sure fast reloads were ready. Overhead and close by, there was a whistle of teal. Jerry’s eyes followed their crossing flight, but he did not signal us to shoot, because he didn’t want to spoil our chances for the significant honkers that could be only minutes away.

Sources indicate that from the lake came another din of geese taking off, and Jerry pulled his head lower and tightened his grip on his Browning autoloading magnum. Then he crouched even lower, eyes level with his lookout hole, and said, “They’re ours boys. Get ready—now!”.

In a recent development, shotgun barrels poked out of the blind, and there was ragged fire at eight or nine geese that were angling by to our left. The closest bird went limp in midair, but the one I fired at twice merely did the double wobble of a wise old goose that knows he’s being shot at.

Long ago I learned that in each flight of waterfowl there are one or two obvious birds. They are closer or bigger or out in front, and they tend to draw fire. When I’m sharing a blind with other hunters, I therefore pass up the obvious targets and go for a more obscure member of the flight. That bird is all mine, and I know for sure if I hit or miss. This time the obvious bird did draw most of the fire and was the only one to fall. Happily there was no chorus of “I got him!” that sometimes mars such events. These men, most of whom I’d met only that morning, were too experienced and too polite for that. Instead, each one claimed to have missed by several feet and that the goose must have been felled by the youngest member of the party, 15-year-old Charlie Lawrence.

It has been revealed that “I did?” he whooped in wide-eyed amazement. “And that means you’ll have to fetch it,” Charlie’s father almost managed to say before the young hunter was out of the blind and sprinting after the prize, his rubber boots going flub-flub and launching dollops of river-bottom mud from the Mississippi in all directions.

It has been revealed that whoever first said that you can tell a lot about a man’s character by hunting with him really knew what he was talking about. Settling back into my posh seat, I knew I had learned a lot about my fresh acquaintances already and had a feeling that we would all be good friends before the day ended.

The only one of us who hadn’t pulled a trigger on the geese was Ralph McDonald, the well-known wildlife artist. His sliding hatch had stuck when the action started, so he had to sit out the first round. But Jerry Jones fixes that in a hurry by leaving the hatch open and covering the opening with a layer of cane that could easily be pushed aside. I liked that arrangement better than moving the hatch, so he fixed me up the same way. It gave me a better look at incoming birds.

Industry observers note that in addition to Jerry, Ralph, and myself, our shooting party included H. Lea Lawrence, his teen-aged sons David and Charlie, country-music star Jim Ed Brown, plus Bill Morrison and Tom Callery. Lea, who lives in Nashville, is an outdoor writer whose name is familiar to readers of OUTDOOR LIFE. Morrison and Callery are field and legislative assistants to U.S. Senator William Brock of Tennessee. When I met Morrison and Callery that morning and learned of their political connections, I made a mental note to bend their ears about pending firearms legislation.

But there was no time for that now—ducks were coming, and Jerry was making seductive sounds on his big-barreled duck call. I couldn’t see the incomers from my angle, but it was easy enough to pinpoint their position by watching Jerry’s eyes. As they came closer, he crouched lower in the blind, and I knew they were within range even before he whisper-shouted, “Now!”.

About 10 spoonbills were winging low and fast from right to left in front of the blind. I swung my 12-gauge double, a Model 21 Winchester, through one of the trailers, but before I could press the trigger the bird’s head kicked back and he collapsed in midair. Then I was aware of three or four other ducks tumbling out of the formation, but my attention was concentrated on another spoonbill. I swung the barrels ahead by about two feet and pressed the trigger. The load of No. 4s folded the spoonbill so cleanly that there was no need to think about a follow-up shot, so I chased the barrels to the next closest bird and gave him the remaining round. It was a straightaway shot, and the range was rapidly increasing with each beat of his wings. For a moment it looked like a miss, but then the spoonbill did a turnover and went into a power dive before thumping hard on the semifrozen field. At 60 yards, perhaps more, it had been a lucky shot, but all eyes had been on me, and the welfare of my ego was at stake.

While David and Charlie fetched the downed waterfowl, I made the innocent mistake of asking Ralph if he had scored on the spoonbills. Though he is a leading wildlife artist whose paintings have twice been featured on the cover of the Ducks Unlimited magazine, he has a well-earned reputation as a hard-luck waterfowl hunter. On his goose hunts something always goes wrong, and he was still looking to shoot his first honker.

Jerry, who owns and operates Sunset Court and Dock on Reelfoot Lake, is one of those old-fashioned guides who believes that a day not spent hunting or fishing is a day wasted. Just to make sure that he and his customers get in plenty of both, his fees for a guided goose-and-duck hunt—including lodging, a heated blind, decoys, transport to the blind, plus some of the finest duck calling and yarn spinning you’re likely to hear anywhere—are no more than you’d expect to pay to spend the night in a rundown Fresh York hotel.

While I was hunting the Reelfoot and Lake Isom area, the local waterfowl population was estimated at some 70,000 geese and about a quarter of a million ducks, mainly gadwalls and mallards.

Historic Reelfoot Lake is well known among waterfowlers and it is an easy day’s drive from many large Midwestern and Eastern cities. Lake Isom, however, remains distinctly undiscovered, even though it is only a few miles away (see map, page 89).

Industry observers note that hunting seasons run from December into January. The duck limit is based on the point system. Some ducks, such as pintails and spoonbills (shovelers), are rated at only 10 points each, so it is possible to bag 10 ducks plus two geese in a single day. That’s a lot of shooting.

Ralph was about halfway through a lengthy explanation of how he had failed to get off a single shot at the geese when Jerry shouted “Get down!” at the two young Lawrence brothers, who were still gathering ducks. Another flight of spoonbills had just cleared Isom’s boundary and were coming directly at us. Charlie had left his shotgun in the blind, but older and wiser David had his pump ready and neatly dropped a drake.

Industry observers note that the first half-hour had produced a goose and a half a dozen ducks—rich promise of a good day of shooting—but by midmorning the action tapered off to only an occasional shot at a passing duck. For some reason known only to themselves, the geese had decided to leave by the western side of the lake. We could hear their comings and goings, but none came within half a mile. Over a breakfast of ham and eggs cooked in a subterranean kitchen attached to the blind and complete with gas stove, we discussed the sagging action. Jerry allowed that we could move to a blind closer to the flyway the honkers had selected that day. Jerry owns or has access to 15 blinds.

Industry observers note that after a quick scouting sortie, he asked for volunteers to try another blind situated where the honkers seemed to be heading, but he also told us the road was bad and we’d have to walk a ways. Jim Ed Brown, Lea Lawrence, and I volunteered, but not without some misgivings on my part.

Ralph McDonald elected to stay where he was, because, as he put it, he’d “… had a vision that the geese would soon come that way.”.

It has been revealed that even before we got to our new blind, there was no doubt that Jerry was right. While walking about a quarter of a mile through a sparse stand of scrub timber, we spotted three flights of geese skimming low over a field of winter wheat. They landed almost in the new blind.

Industry observers note that “Holy catfish!” said Jim Ed in the soft Southern accents that have made him a favorite of Grand Ole Opry fans. “All I need is two.”.

In a recent development, just then six or eight more honkers slipped in low over the wheatfield, wings cupped to land. Before they touched down, the leader thought better of it, and they flared hard left, leveled off treetop high, and headed straight at us. We were almost through the scrub brush by then, and there wasn’t much cover, but we ducked into what concealment there was.

According to recent reports, “Get ready,” Jerry whispered just an arm’s length to my left. Like me, he was half hidden in a honeysuckle bank. Just then Jim Ed and Lea opened up, and two honkers dropped at once. A third, hit hard, scaled overhead, and Jerry or me, or both of us, hit him at less than 30 yards and folded him cleanly.

Sources indicate that the rest of the formation had swerved violently when Lea and Jim Ed started shooting, and they were out of range before I could come to bear with my second barrel. The geese were still reasonably close to Jim Ed, and with the last shot in his Model 12 Winchester pump, another Canada pitched down, wing feathers humming in the rush of the fall.

“Friends,” drawled Jim Ed, “this is what I was brought up to call good goose hunting. I’ve got my limit, and we ain’t even in the blind.”.

In a recent development, the timing was perfect, because less than an hour later Jim Ed was scheduled to leave by charter plane to tape his popular “Nashville On The Road” TV show. So he and Jerry took the four honkers back to the truck while Lea and I went on to the blind. Jerry got back as promptly as he could.

Recent findings suggest that we had no more than settled ourselves when a flight of perhaps 20 geese came soaring up the field. Jerry called, and they began to circle. When we stood to fire, they flared sharply and momentarily gave us that near-motionless target goose hunters love. I shot at a bird on the far right end of the formation so there would be little chance that Lea and I would double on the same target. The Canada spun and fell without a flutter.

Meanwhile Lea was doing the same with a honker he had cut out of the flight.

In a recent development, that evening we feasted on lake-country froglegs, catfish, hush puppies, and tart cole slaw. It had been a great day for everyone except Ralph McDonald.

“I was sure my hunch about those geese was a good one,” he lamented, pouring himself a stiff snort of Reelfoot tea, “but I never got a shot. My record is intact.”.

Read Next: I Gave Up My Duck Blind to Hunt Where the Mallards Actually Are.

Reelfoot Lake in far western Tennessee was formed by the New Madrid earthquakes of 1811-12. The catastrophe depressed some 50,000 acres that were later submerged by water from the Mississippi River. The surge was so great that the Mississippi is remarked to have flowed backward for a while. Due to siltation, plant succession, and drainage, Reelfoot Lake now covers about 18,000 acres.

It has been revealed that A colorful legend accounts for the lake’s name. A Chickasaw chief suffered from a deformed or club foot and reeled when he walked. Chief Reelfoot could not persuade any of the Chickasaw maidens to become his wife, so he and his warriors kidnapped a Choctaw maiden named Starlight. Her father, who would not allow the marriage because of Reelfoot’s deformity, was so angered that he ordered his medicine men to bring down a terrible vengeance on Reelfoot and his people. That, the legend has it, was the cause of the earthquake.

According to recent reports, lake Isom, scene of the waterfowl hunt in this story, was isolated from the major lake when a road was built around the southern end of the lake. A water-control structure and a ditch aided in draining the land that lies between the lakes today. The lake was given a name when the site was acquired for a waterfowl refuge from the Isom family.

Industry observers note that reelfoot’s excellent waterfowl habitat made it one of the most famous hunting areas on the Mississippi Flyway. The open-water portions attracted a variety of diving ducks, particularly canvasbacks. Mallards were most abundant and most popular among gunners. Eventually, however, the canvasbacks almost disappeared, and restrictive limits were imposed on mallard shooting. In the late 1960’s, with a one-mallard limit, Reelfoot had an all-time low in hunter usage.

As the mallards and some other ducks increased in numbers after the low, and limits were increased, the popularity of Reelfoot Lake among gunners increased somewhat, but it is taking a while for hunters to realize that it’s the same hotspot. Reelfoot is as good today as it ever was, and Lake Isom is just as good. Neither Reelfoot nor Isom is managed by the state, but public hunting is permitted at Reelfoot. At Lake Isom the hunting is on private land.

#160889. A Climbing Expedition to 'Central Asia's Patagonia'

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1963 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

A Climbing Expedition to 'Central Asia's Patagonia'

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1963 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A mix of nine young and veteran Croatian climbers spent the month of August in one of the world’s great big-wall destinations — Kyrgyzstan’s Karavshin Range in the Pamir-Alay Mountains.
  • In a recent development, the two leaders, Sinisa Skalec and Lukas Grbac Lackovic, spoke to ExplorersWeb about the place and their expedition.
  • Though suffering from stomach issues for most of the month (more on this later), the team repeated several granite classics, did a newly introduced route on 4,430m Pik Breeze, and attempted another new line.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A mix of nine young and veteran Croatian climbers spent the month of August in one of the world’s great big-wall destinations — Kyrgyzstan’s Karavshin Range in the Pamir-Alay Mountains. Reaching up to 5,509m, the once-unknown granite cliffs now draw dozens of international climbers each summer. The two core valleys, Ak-Su and Kara-Su, have become known as Central Asia’s Patagonia.

In a recent development, the two leaders, Sinisa Skalec and Lukas Grbac Lackovic, spoke to ExplorersWeb about the place and their expedition. First, a summary of their four weeks.

Though suffering from stomach issues for most of the month (more on this later), the team repeated several granite classics, did a newly introduced route on 4,430m Pik Breeze, and attempted another new line.

Industry observers note that three climbers — Bruno Crljenic, Eva Pejic, and Lackovic — identified a potential latest line below Pik Breeze’s west ridge. They knew of only one previous route on the mountain, done by Russians Marina Popova and Denis Prokofiev.

Crossing a scree slope on Pik Breeze.

Recent findings suggest that beginning at 5am, the three crossed a broad scree slope, then began climbing a couloir below Pik Breeze’s west ridge. They negotiated loose rock, briefly followed an existing line, then moved left into crack systems.

Canned Horse, 6c A0, top. Below, previous attempts and possible other lines on the face.

They climbed until 9pm, when they bivouacked on a tiny ledge with space for only two people sitting and one lying down. Resuming at 8:30am, they reached a col after three pitches and continued directly up slabs and cracks. They finished on easier IV/V terrain and followed a 200m ridge to the summit.

They called their new line Canned Horse, 930m, 23 pitches, 6c A0. It took them a further eight hours to get back to base camp. During the climb, they found pitons on two pitches. They believe these belonged to another route on the west ridge, but the history of that line, and whether it was finished, is uncertain.

Pejic, Grbac Lackovic, and Crljenic on top of Pik Breeze.

Later in the month, one of those climbers, Eva Pejic, became quite ill and couldn’t leave base camp on her own. Five teammates helped evacuate her, carrying her for 11km, with assistance from other climbers in the area. She later recuperated in the Kyrgyz city of Osh.

On the first crux of ‘Perestroika Crack.’.

Three small teams of Croatian climbers also repeated Perestroika Crack, one of the best-known long granite routes in Central Asia. It rises about 900m up the north face of 4,240m Pik Slesova and is graded 7a. Three members reportedly free-climbed the route. One pair, Sinisa Skalec and Ivan Vitez, completed the line in a single marathon day, beginning at 5:45am, summiting at 5:40pm, and returning to base camp at 11pm.

Skalec and Vitez also repeated the French Ridge of 4,510m Kyrkchilta, 2,000m, 6b to 6b+. They needed one bivouac. Toward the end of August, this same pair attempted a first ascent on the Central Pyramid of Ortotyubek, overlooking base camp. Their attempted route mounted slabs and cracks to the left of the established Take It Easy line, which other Croatians had repeated during that month. The pair gave up their attempt on August 26 because of illness.

Base camp with Ortotyubek and Slesova in the background.

Here is our interview with Lukas Grbac Lackovic and Sinisa Skalec about Kyrgyzstan and the Ak-Su Valley.

Lukas Grbac Lackovic repeats the Central Route on a peak called Small Russian Tower.

Was Eva Pejic’s health problem related to altitude or something else? What was the illness you experienced on Ortotyubek?

Industry observers note that eva’s health problem was unrelated to altitude exposure or the expedition environment. However, most of us experienced gastrointestinal infections, with symptoms including diarrhea, bloating, fever, and general malaise.

This significantly hindered our climbing, as everyone in the team got sick at least once, and some even twice. Recovery was slow and never quite complete –- we felt weak for most of the trip.

One thing that helped us recover was having plain rice with some of our meals, which we could get from the cook if we asked nicely. If we were to go again, we would definitely bring our own food and cooking equipment. This can be inconvenient, but it could potentially save you at least a week of being sick and unable to climb.

Another view of base camp and peaks Ortotyubek and Slesova.

In a recent development, can you describe the Karavshin Valley? How large is it? Are there many side valleys?

The two main valleys are Ak-Su and Kara-Su. Adjacent to them is the Jaupaya Valley, which provides a descent route from Pik Breeze and is home to several peaks around 5,000m high. The rock quality there appears poor, and we are not aware of any established rock routes in the valley.

According to recent reports, another interesting area, west of Kara Su, is the Orto-Chashma Gorge. An Italian team made a first ascent there during our visit.

Recent findings suggest that here in the West, we first heard about the area following the kidnapping of four American climbers in Kara-Su in 2000. Since then, it seems to have calmed down and become a popular climbing destination. Is the area considered safe nowadays, or are there still things climbers should be aware of?

It has been revealed that presently, the security situation in the valley is good. There is always the possibility of tensions, of course, as the valleys lie close to the border with Tajikistan. However, in recent years, the number of climbers visiting the area has increased exponentially, reaching around 100 climbers this year.

Recent findings suggest that how many other climbing teams were in Ak-Su and neighboring Kara-Su while you were there? Where were they generally from?

Recent findings suggest that during the three weeks we spent in the valley, up to 50 climbers were in BC at the same time. Climbers came from all over the world — Chile, U.S., Spain, Slovakia, Poland, Belgium, Slovenia, France, Italy, Germany, Japan, Russia….

Why did your group decide to go there?

We had originally planned a different expedition, but had to change our destination just a few months before departure. Some friends from Croatia and Slovenia recommended the area because of its straightforward logistics and relatively good security, while still offering impressive substantial walls and proper crack climbing. It didn’t take much to convince us!

According to recent reports, are there any military checkpoints? Do you need special permission to enter the valleys?

Yes, you have to pass through a military checkpoint when entering the area. However, the outfitter handles the application for the necessary permits and ensures everything goes smoothly.

Recent findings suggest that some call the Karavshin Valley the Patagonia of Central Asia because of its aesthetic granite walls. Do you think that’s a fair description?

In a recent development, patagonia is definitely more spectacular, but you pay the price with poor weather. If your goal is to climb almost every day, then the Karavshin Valley is a better choice.

Climbing in Patagonia requires much more logistical planning and preparation, and the approaches themselves are a whole different story. In the Karavshin Valley, on the other hand, there is no snow or ice during the season we visited (August), at least on the walls we climbed. Some of the walls are just a 15-minute walk from BC, and you can reach them all in approach shoes.

Perestroika Crack and some of the classic routes in the Karavshin region are arguably just as good as the best rock routes in Patagonia.

How does the granite compare to Yosemite and Patagonia?

Sources indicate that the granite is more similar in texture to that found in Patagonia; it is not as smooth as in Yosemite. The overall rock quality is generally good, although, as everywhere, some sections are of poorer quality. One downside of the mild climate in the Karavshin Valley is the dirt and grass that accumulate in the cracks, which can sometimes detract from the aesthetic appeal of the routes. The more popular and frequently climbed routes have already been cleaned and are pleasant to climb.

You climbed 4-1/2 pitches of the route on Ortotyubek. How much did you have left to complete it?

There were still two-and-a-half pitches left to complete the route up to the junction with Take It Easy. We envisioned the second half of the fifth pitch following the line up to a point just below the overhang that runs diagonally to the left.

Recent findings suggest that from there, the sixth pitch follows a thin crack, from which you need to traverse left and move into another system of thin cracks that runs across the roof and joins the Take It Easy belay (seventh pitch). The last pitch of Take It Easy offers a logical exit, and we don’t think there is any need to come up with an alternative.

At the point where we stopped (first half of the fifth pitch), we left two pitons that we used as a temporary rappel anchor. Repeating parties are welcome to remove them, as they were only left for temporary use. We think a few bolts may be needed in the second half of the fifth pitch, but that obviously depends on the abilities of those planning to complete the route.

Industry observers note that all belays are equipped (the first and fourth belays have two 8mm bolts each, while the second and third have two pitons each). In addition, we left two or three pitons in the first pitch and two in the second pitch.

Recent findings suggest that as in the rest of the valley, some sections of the route are filled with dirt and grass. We made an effort to clean the cracks in the first four pitches, but there is still plenty of work to be done, especially on the sixth pitch, which we didn’t climb, where a thin crack is completely filled with dirt.

According to recent reports, how much unclimbed rock remains? Are the obvious lines already established, or are there still many promising routes?

Sources indicate that the most obvious and accessible lines may have already been climbed, but there is still plenty of potential. Anyone willing to put in the effort can establish a new route. The area is vast, and there is still plenty of room for new routes.

In a recent development, your website mentions that there are guidebooks to certain routes in that area. Where are these available?

Sources indicate that most of the guidebooks we used are available online. We received some Russian guidebooks from climbing friends, although we didn’t use them very much. We’re not sure how easily they can be found online. Climbers from all over the world bring various materials to the camp, so most route topos and information can be obtained there.

What was the most unexpected experience on your expedition — something that might surprise climbers familiar with other big-wall areas?

We were pleasantly surprised by the kindness and honesty of the Kyrgyz people. When traveling to remote parts of the world, many of us tend to expect that someone will try to rip us off and that we will have to haggle over everything, but that was not the case here.

Although some things took longer than expected, everything we had agreed on in advance was respected, and all the logistics for transportation and accommodation worked very well.

As we mentioned earlier, our only complaint concerns the food and hygiene conditions at the camp, which were most likely responsible for the digestive problems experienced by virtually all the climbers staying there.

#160869. A Bear to Be Thankful For: I Hunted a Record Black Bear on Thanksgiving Day

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 18m • 📚 Deep Dive (3528 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

A Bear to Be Thankful For: I Hunted a Record Black Bear on Thanksgiving Day

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3528 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The 1966 deer season on the Keweenaw Peninsula, northern Michigan’s Copper Country, opened on November 12 and was due to close on the 27th, the Sunday after Thanksgiving.
  • Up to Thanksgiving day, our whole family had no luck.
  • The only family success scored was by my dad’s uncle, Bill Anderson, from Detroit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The 1966 deer season on the Keweenaw Peninsula, northern Michigan’s Copper Country, opened on November 12 and was due to close on the 27th, the Sunday after Thanksgiving.

Up to Thanksgiving day, our whole family had no luck. My dad, my brother Bruce, and I had hunted hard and had seen deer almost every day, but nothing that we wanted to shoot. Even my mom, who goes along with us on our deer hunts but makes no pretense of hunting hard, had seen deer but had no shooting.

The only family success scored was by my dad’s uncle, Bill Anderson, from Detroit. He drove the 550 miles north to hunt with us, and went home with a good buck.

Sources indicate that I had special reasons for feeling disappointed about drawing a blank. I was born and grew up in the Copper Country. I’m now 24, and I’ve hunted deer since I was 14. That year my great-uncle Bill sold me his old rifle, a .32 Special Winchester Model 94. That old gun had killed a lot of deer and a few bears before I got it, and it went right on being lucky for me.

From that fall of 1956 until 1965, I killed a deer with it every year. Then circumstances compelled me to miss the 1965 season. I went into the Navy Reserve three years ago, and was called to active duty in the spring of 1965. When November of 1966 rolled around, I arranged for a leave to coincide with the deer season in the Upper Peninsula of Michigan, and so I was back again, hunting the woods and swamps where I had been lucky ever since I was a kid, but not doing so well for a change.

In a recent development, to make matters worse, I had to leave for the naval base at Norfolk, Virginia on  Saturday morning, November 26. I knew, when we left home right after breakfast on Thanksgiving day, that I had just that day and the next in which to kill a deer, or I’d wind up skunked for the first time in my life.

Industry observers note that we’re a Finnish family, all hunters and fishermen. My dad, Ernest Haataja, runs a refrigeration business in the village of Ahmeek, about 20 miles up the Keweenaw Peninsula from Houghton, the biggest city in the Copper Country. The peninsula is wild and rugged, and there are not too many roads. It’s a pretty fair game area, with deer, bears, coyotes, and bobcats.

The Keweenaw juts northeast into Lake Superior like a rough and rocky finger, 50 miles long and 15 to 20 wide. In the small bays along the eastern shore, sheltered from the high winds and pounding seas of the great lake, there is excellent fishing, mostly for lake trout. The whole Haataja family loves to hunt and fish.

My brother Bruce is two years older than I am. He’s married, has four youngsters, works at a local mine, and does some beaver trapping as a sideline. We have three sisters: Vicki, 18; Carolyn, 10; and Mary Beth, 6. Pop, mom, and sister Mary Beth with the bear in Ahmeek, Mich.

One of our favorite summer vacations for years has been to charter a small commercial fishing boat for a week or so and make the 50-mile trip on Lake Superior to Isle Royale National Park, the major, roadless island that lies 20 miles south of the Canadian shore. The fishing for lake trout there is as good as any we know about, and the sea lampreys have made lighter inroads than they have along the south shore of Superior. We have even seen lakers rising for flies in July and August around Gull Rocks, a few miles off the main island.

Sources indicate that there is great pike fishing in some of the 30-odd inland lakes on Isle Royale, too, but we don’t care too much for pike and don’t often go after them. We live aboard our chartered boat, cooking our meals, sleeping on cots, and moving around as we choose. Isle Royale is 50 miles long, and there are plenty of sheltered harbors to anchor in. We hike, explore, and fish, and everybody has a fine time.

Bruce and I have had some other very good fishing trips together, too, including one to Lake Nipigon a few years ago that was a real adventure.

Sources indicate that the bear didn’t move a muscle. He just kept his eyes riveted on me as though trying to figure out what I was. Or maybe he knew, and tried to stare me down. Except for his head and round ears, he looked like a low-slung black bull, and he was so significant he stunned me.

The family also has a cottage on Little Traverse Bay, about 15 miles from home, that we use for fishing headquarters in the summer and hunting in the fall. And from the time Rabbit Bay, nearby, freezes over until it breaks up in the spring, dad spends a fair share of his time fishing through the ice for lake trout. Fishermen are still catching trout out there with live lampreys attached to them, but some heavy stocking has been done, and the fishing continues to be fair.

Until I left home to go into the service, I never missed a chance to go along on those winter trips, and Bruce still goes as often as he can. Dad has built a set of light runners for a small boat, and if a hard wind is blowing offshore and there is danger that the ice may break loose and drift out into the open water of Keweenaw Bay, they take that outfit along. It’s so light that one or two men, going onto the ice on foot the way we do, can drag it easily. In an emergency, the runners can be taken off quickly, and the boat is ready for use in the water.

In a recent development, I’m telling all this to help you understand how I felt about getting shut out on that 1966 deer hunt. I didn’t have any very good alibi, either. The weather was cold and clear, and hunting conditions were not bad although we had only a little snow-hardly enough for tracking_ The Keweenaw Peninsula sometimes gets as much as 20 feet of snow before winter is over. We had 234 inches by the end of March this year. But I had killed deer on bare ground plenty of times before, and thought I should be able to do it again.

Deer, however, are not so plentiful there as they were a few years ago. Many local people blame it on the opening of doe seasons, under special permit, by the Michigan conservation department. Whether or not that is the reason, we don’t see nearly so many deer as we used to, and we don’t see horns so often. But I knew that if I had to go back to Norfolk without filling my license, all that would be pretty cold comfort.

Thanksgiving morning dawned clear and cold with hardly any wind. The leaves would be dry and noisy underfoot, but it promised to be a fairly good day for hunting. We had been putting in most of our time in an area around Mud Lake, not too far from our cottage, but that morning we decided to try another location. We planned to drive out beyond Fort Wilkins State Park almost to the end of the peninsula. That’s as far north as you can go without getting your feet wet in Lake Superior.

Industry observers note that bruce drove our four-wheel-drive vehicle, and I rode up front with him. Dad and mom were in the back seat. Mom had packed lunch for the four of us. We’d stay in the woods until night. We usually start our deer hunting before daylight and hunt until dark.

It has been revealed that beyond Fort Wilkins we took a muddy logging road and then turned back toward Hoar Lake. A second logging road took us into remote, wild country miles from anywhere and near enough to the Superior beach so that we could faintly hear the noise of surf. We knew the place was a good area for deer, and even on Thanksgiving Day, there wasn’t much chance other hunters would find their way so far into back country.

On foot, we skirted a thick cedar swamp that lay between us and Superior, and we split up. Mom stayed behind. She found a spot where she could keep an eye on a runway along the edge of the swamp and announced that she thought she’d have as much chance of killing a deer there as anyplace.

In a recent development, knowing her habits, we suspected that she’d watch the runway for an hour or so, work around the end of the swamp, hike down to the beach, and look for agates. That was about what she did, too, but the swamp proved too much for her and for once she turned back and joined us for lunch without sighting Lake Superior.

Bruce and dad headed down into the swamp. I turned to the right, into big, fairly open hardwood timber. There were high ridges running all through it with quite a lot of oak on the slopes. That meant acorns, and they are likely to mean deer.

In a recent development, the day had stayed bright and crisp. The ground was bare, and the leaves were really noisy underfoot, so I moved slowly, walking a few steps and then stopping to look in all directions. stepped carefully from one tree to another, trying to be as quiet as a cat and hoping I’d see a deer before me.

I found a little deer sign, but not so much as I had expected, and I was beginning to wonder whether I had picked the right place, after all. Then I cam over a rise, and a strange bare spot just ahead caught my eyes.

Sources indicate that all around me in the timber, dead leaves lay in a thick carpet, but in front of me was a bare patch some 75 feet square. ln all the time I had spent in the woods I had never seen anything like that, and I stood there looking it over carefully, trying to puzzle it out. It seemed as though a huge vacuum cleaner had been at work.

Then, on the downhill side of the bare place, I saw a big mound of heaped-up leaves, and squatting in them was a black bear bigger than any I had ever expected to see. He saw me in the same instant, and we stood and stared at each other.

Read Next: Revolver Versus Semi-Auto: Which Is Best for Bear Defense?

Industry observers note that my eyes must have bugged all the way out of my head. The bear was less than 75 feet from me in open timber, not hidden by anything except his own leaf pile, and that fell far short of concealing him. Why I hadn’t seen him in the first instant after I came over the rise, I still don’t know, but I guess I just wasn’t looking for a bear. It was that bald spot, raked clear of leaves, that caught my attention and held it those first few seconds.

In a recent development, the bear didn’t move a muscle. He just kept his eyes riveted on me as though trying to figure out what I was. Or maybe he knew, and tried to stare me down. Except for his head and round ears, he looked like a low-slung black bull, and he was so big he stunned me.

It has been revealed that for a moment I didn’t know whether to shoot or try to sneak away, but I made up my mind on that score in a hurry. I had seen bears in the woods once or twice during previous hunting seasons, but nothing like this one. I had never expected to have such luck, and I wasn’t going to pass it up.

Sources indicate that I don’t know how long we looked at each other. It was probably only 10 or 15 seconds, but it seemed like a full minute. I’ll say one thing: I didn’t get buck fever.

I didn’t move a muscle either, until I raised my gun. The old rifle was not scoped, but at that short range, I didn’t need a scope. I brought my rifle up slowly and took careful aim. The bear standing partly sideways to me, I clouted him just below his left ear. The 170-grain softpoint knocked him as flat as a flapjack. He didn’t kick much, but he was an awful lot of bear, and he looked even bigger lying on the ground than when he was on his feet. So I walked close to him and put another shot into his shoulder to make sure.

Industry observers note that then I started looking things over. The bear had raked all the leaves downhill into one big pile, and only eight feet farther down the slope, I found a hole dug under a big cedar windfall. It was about four feet across and three feet deep and seemed freshly dug. If it had been used before, he had enlarged it and cleaned it out. Sand and gravel had been thrown in every direction.

Without much question, the bear had intended to use the pile of leaves for his winter bed. If I hadn’t come along, he probably would have dragged enough of them into the hole to line it before crawling in, raking the rest over himself, and curling up until spring. He would have had dry, snug quarters. The slope of the hill provided good drainage, and the windfall would have kept the worst of the snow off him. The leaves he had gathered would have been enough to cover three or four bears.

Sources indicate that he was a lot too big for me to dress without help, so I headed back to the car. Dad and Bruce were there when I arrived, and mom came along a little later. They had heard my two shots, and their first question was whether I had killed a deer. I noted no, and tried to string them along, but I guess my excitement must have shown.

According to recent reports, “Well,” Bruce remarked right away, “maybe you didn’t get your buck, but from the way you look you sure got something. What was it?”.

According to recent reports, “It was a bear,” I blurted. “It’s the biggest bear I’ve ever seen. It’s so darned big it looks like a grizzly!”.

“Did you kill it?” dad demanded.

“Deader than a salt herring,” I assured him.

We hurried through chow, and then started back to the bear. When we got there, it was all the three of us could do to roll him over for dressing.

As we worked, we debated whether we could drag him out to the nearest logging road. It didn’t seem very likely, for we had almost three miles to go on bare ground. It was plain that this bear was a huge thing for three men to handle, but we agreed to try.

That turned out to be a big joke. We took hold of his head and forefeet, but we found that by tugging and grunting for all we were worth we could move him only a few inches at a time. We couldn’t have dragged him out of the woods in a month of Sundays.

I hated to leave him, but it was getting late in the afternoon, and there was no choice. We were sure no animal would molest him, and the area was remote enough so that there was very little chance other hunters would find him. Even if they did, he was so massive that nobody would make off with him. We hiked out to the car, laying looks to retrieve my bear in the morning.

According to recent reports, we did some phoning that night and early the next day and learned that a logging outfit, the Kilpela Brothers from the town of Mohawk, was operating not far from where I had killed the bear. We contacted them, and to our great relief they said they’d hitch a dray behind one of their tractors and go in with us and bring him out. It was after dark before the job was done.

I had taken a fine trophy. My bear was not only a record-setter for size, but also he had a thick, shiny, black pelt in perfect condition. There wasn’t a rubbed spot or blemish on it anywhere. It made as beautiful a rug as any hunter ever took. There wasn’t even one claw missing from the feet. That’s probably because there is no bear trapping in Michigan anymore. If there had been traps in the woods, he would almost certainly have blundered into one during his long life.

We took him to Rinne’s Fuel Company in Ahmeek and weighed him on certified scales there in the presence of witnesses. We were all a little surprised at what the scales revealed. I had killed a black bear that weighed 570 pounds field dressed, the heaviest ever recorded in Michigan. He was 15 pounds over the previous state record holder. That one was shot in the 1950’s near Newberry farther east on the Upper Peninsula by Dean Loveless, a bowhunter from the downstate city of Hamtramck.

According to recent reports, michigan game men estimated that my bear had weighed not less than 650 pounds alive. His dressed weight was 82 pounds below that of the giant black killed in Wisconsin in 1963 by Otto Hedbany of suburban Milwaukee. That one dressed 652, and its live weight must have been around 725. Hedbany’s bear was described in “Biggest Black Ever Killed,” OUTDOOR LIFE, May 1964.

According to recent reports, although I shot mine in the head, I did not damage the skull. My shot went in at the butt of an ear, and the bullet from the .32 Special opened up enough to kill him in his tracks. But it lodged somewhere in the brain cavity and did not come out. As a result, the skull was intact for measuring. I intend to enter it in the current Boone and Crockett Club competition, and the state game men tell me there is very little doubt that it will go into the record book, maybe not too far from the top. The Hedbany bear, by the way, was not eligible for entry, because the skull was shattered when it was killed.

In a recent development, A photographer for the Houghton Mining Gazette came to Ahmeek that night, Friday, and took a picture of me with my bear. That was the only one I got of myself with the bear. It was too dark that night for us to use our camera, and I boarded a plane to go back to Norfolk early Saturday, so there was no time to think about more pictures. There were plenty taken after I left, but I wasn’t in them. That’s not too unusual for me. I’m the one in our family who takes the pictures most of the time, so I don’t appear in many.

I’ve promised myself one thing: If I should ever take another bear as good as that one, I’ll get some color pictures of myself with it, just to remind myself of my luck.

Read Next: The Best Bear Cartridges.

After we had gotten my bear into town and had weighed him, I had a chance to think the whole thing over. I couldn’t help feeling almost sorry I had shot him, but if I were doing it over again, I’d do the same thing. He was too much trophy to pass up. and I’m sure I’ll never in my life see another bear like him. Yet I did realize how long he had lived there in that wild country. He wasn’t doing any harm, and it seemed almost too bad that I came along that Thanksgiving morning when he was making his winter bed. He was my first bear, and much as I like hunting, if he should also turn out to be my last, I don’t believe I’d be disappointed.

On the other hand, shooting him was the most exciting thing that ever happened to me. I went back to the naval base without getting a deer, but I didn’t mind. That bear was all the Thanksgiving present any hunter could ask for.

It has been revealed that this story, “Bear to Be Thankful For,” appeared in the Sept. 1967 issue of Outdoor Life. The current Michigan state-record black bear, according to Boone and Crockett Club, is bear whose skull measured 22 11/16 inches and was killed in Newaygo County in 2009 by Donald R. Corrigan. Haataja’s bear is not listed in the B&C records.

Avalanche Fatality Warns About Early Ski Conditions In The Alps

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (803 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that little snow on the mountains doesn’t mean safe conditions.
  • With the ski season barely underway, this is Europe’s first avalanche victim this season.
  • Industry observers note that most victims perished in the Alps: 40 in Italy, 35 in France, 33 in Austria, and 18 in Switzerland.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that little snow on the mountains doesn’t mean safe conditions. An American off-piste skier died in the Austrian Alps last weekend after he triggered a small slab avalanche. It was far too small to bury him, but it carried him into an open crevasse below.

With the ski season barely underway, this is Europe’s first avalanche victim this season. Last year, 151 people died in avalanches in Europe between October 2025 and June 2026, according to the European Avalanche Warning Service (EAWS), a shockingly high number.

Industry observers note that most victims perished in the Alps: 40 in Italy, 35 in France, 33 in Austria, and 18 in Switzerland. It was the 13th most deadly year in the Alps since record-keeping began. It was also the highest tally ever since the “Winter of Terror” of 1951. Avalanche prevention standards have improved a lot since then, but the number of leisure skiers, climbers, and hikers in the mountains has multiplied as well. (Most of those 1951 victims lived in villages along avalanche paths.).

Last weekend’s accident took place at the Stubai Glacier ski resort. The glacier sections of the Alps typically open for skiing weeks earlier than other mountain resorts, thanks to their higher altitudes and glacial ice, which can provide good October skiing with just a thin layer of fresh snow on top. Stubai’s ski resort opened on October 9 this year.

In a recent development, A map of Stubai Glacier ski resort with the area where the accident happened circled in red. Photo: Stubaier Gletscher website.

Recent findings suggest that the skier was on his own, descending in an out-of-bounds area below East Daunkogel Peak at around 11:30am. His tracks on the snow show he eventually abandoned the snow-covered glacier and ventured onto a steeper, rocky area. At some point, he broke a small slab of crusty snow which dragged him some 50 meters into an open bergschrund, where he fatally fell 20 meters down, according to the Lawinen Report.

Sources indicate that the accident site, with the skier’s tracks visible,  and the movement of the snow slab — 50m long and 25m wide — marked in pink. Photo: Lawinen Report.

Other skiers in the area saw the accident and raised the alarm, but the skier had died by the time they extracted him from the crevasse. The police stated the slab was only 10cm to 30cm thick, and the slide was just 25 meters wide. The crevasse was 50 meters below the fracture point.

It has been revealed that avalanche risks are obvious on heavily loaded slopes, but the accident indicates that even a thin layer of unstable snow can cause a fatal fall. In this case, the snow had fallen recently on the verglass ice over glacier-polished smooth rocks, and had no time to settle. This is a typical early-season condition in mountain ranges around the world.

It has been revealed that the accident occurred at nearly 3,000m of altitude on a shady northeast slope, where the snow hardly transforms and settles during the short days of late fall. To make things worse, the report notes that wind had picked up that morning, creating a weak crust on top of loose, cold, fresh snow, prone to breaking.

The avalanche site on the following day, with most of the terrain covered by freshly drifted snow. Photo: LWD Tirol.

Sources indicate that the second factor was exposure: the skier might have easily survived the fall if the terrain had been a clean snow slope, but he was on rocky terrain, where a simple fall can result in serious injuries. Most of all, the crevasse below created what the report described as a “terrain trap.”.

Fans of backcountry and ski touring are eager to hit the slopes with the first snowflakes, and the scarcely covered terrain may provide a false sense of safety from avalanches. But objective dangers go beyond the big powder avalanches and also include falls on icy slopes. In addition, the glaciers are dry after the summer, and the crevasses are wide open.

After a mild fall, snow is falling heavily in the Alps this week, significantly improving conditions for the region’s ski resorts. Most of them strategy to open this weekend. The snow will also offer backcountry opportunities, but conditions will remain highly unstable.

According to recent reports, snowfall up to two meters is expected today in the Alps. Graphic by meteoexploration.com.

The avalanche report today by the Tiroler Avalanche Service (LWD Tirol) reveals low risk in the Austrian mountains, a remarkable risk (3 out of 5) in the Swiss Alps, and moderate risk (2 out of 5) in France.

The avalanche forecast for today, November 19, in the Alps demonstrates remarkable (level 3-orange) risk, especially in Switzerland. Graphic: LWD Tirol.
