Townsend Whelen’s Favorite Big Game Hunting Cartridges

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (4055 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs.
  • According to recent reports, townsend Whelen, who was one of Outdoor Life’s first shooting editors and one of the founders of the legendary gun maker and outfitter Griffin & Howe, wrote extensively about substantial game hunting from the early 1900s until his death in 1961.
  • He opined at length on the best cartridges for massive game hunting, though he approached the topic with a characteristic open-mindedness.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

According to recent reports, townsend Whelen, who was one of Outdoor Life’s first shooting editors and one of the founders of the legendary gun maker and outfitter Griffin & Howe, wrote extensively about substantial game hunting from the early 1900s until his death in 1961. His articles on rifles, ballistics, cartridges, optics, and marksmanship have endured through the decades, thanks to his concise, informative prose that was based on years of practical experience as a hunter, competitive shooter, and career army officer.

He opined at length on the best cartridges for massive game hunting, though he approached the topic with a characteristic open-mindedness. He was willing to consider and try new rounds as they became available, and loved to test out new equipment in the field and report on their results.

Sources indicate that I’ve unearthed Whelen’s favorite hunting cartridges by reading through his archived stories and books. One way to think of this list is as a snapshot of some key milestones in ballistic history, as well as an over-the-shoulder peek at the hunting rounds Whelen viewed as state of the art over his decades-long career. Many of his observations embody timeless wisdom and are still relevant today.

You’d think that among the cartridges he touted the .35 Whelen, which bears his name, would be included. After all, taking the .30/06 case—which was technologically advanced for the time—and necking it up for hard-hitting .358-caliber bullets was a winning combo.

Industry observers note that for not much increased recoil the .35 Whelen launched bullets from 180- to 250-grains and rapidly gained a reputation as a solid massive-game killer. (Most .35 Whelen loads feature one of four bullet weights: 180, 200, 225 and 250 grains).

It has been revealed that whelen mentioned the round in passing—notably to give credit to James Howe (of Griffin & Howe) for designing it—and briefly touched upon others’ accounts of it in the field. But if he ever hunted with it, or even shot it much, he didn’t document the experience. As far as I’ve been able to learn, he never messed with the round in any meaningful way—other than doing some hand loading for it—and its exposure to the general reading public was through other writers of the time like Elmer Keith, who hunted with it extensively and was a fan of the 250-grain spitzers.

READ NEXT: Two Rifles for the Ages, Chambered in .35 Whelen.

This blind spot to his eponymous cartridge extended to the .400 and .375 Whelens, which Howe developed at the same time, though they never caught on the way the .35 did. If I had to guess, I would say that Whelen’s modesty, refined upbringing (he came from Philadelphia aristocracy), and soldierly sense of decorum precluded him from overtly praising the cartridge, rather than the existence of some undisclosed antipathy toward it. To ballyhoo something bearing his name would be unseemly.

The list of cartridges Whelen recommended for substantial game evolved over the years. His career spanned an era of explosive growth in cartridge and bullet development as well as the adoption of such marvels as telescopic sights.

In a recent development, for this reason, his earlier writings (from 1906 to the mid 1920s) prominently featured cartridges like the .30/40 Krag (aka the .30 Army), the .30/30 W.C.F. (aka .30/30 Win.), 7mm Mauser, .250 Savage, and their peers. Later on, he became a fan of rounds such as the .270 Win., .257 Roberts, and .348 Winchester. Throughout his long career, however, he never wavered in his praise for the .30/06 and the .375 H&H (with some qualifiers) when the topic of major-game hunting turned to cartridge selection.

It has been revealed that whelen’s career as an authority on hunting and shooting marched in lockstep with the creation of the .30/06 and its rise to prominence. He was intimately familiar with the round and could rattle off technical details in his sleep concerning its history, refinements, the pros and cons of the numerous available loads, and its qualities on the battlefield and for hunting.

He worked with the cartridge both in his capacity as a sportsman and as an army officer—particularly after World War I when he transferred from Infantry to Ordnance, eventually becoming the commanding officer at Frankfort Arsenal and the director of research and development at the Springfield Armory.

Sources indicate that he hunted extensively with the .30/06, killing all manner of massive game during his many adventures. One of his preferred projectiles was Western Cartridge Organization’s 180-grain open point boat tail bullet, with which he killed a grizzly bear, three moose, two caribou, two bighorn sheep, four mountain goats, and six deer.

It has been revealed that he documented his experience with this bullet in particular because of occasional reports of 180-grain bullets failing on game. He wasn’t buying it.

“There has never been even a suspicion of a failure on any of the game I have shot with it,” he wrote. “Many other sportsmen have had a similar experience.”.

Industry observers note that he found the bullet delivered good accuracy as well. “In my own rifle it was averaging about 2-inch groups at 100 and 4 inches at 200, and I got one moose killed clean at 325 yards and two goats killed likewise clean at 325 and 350 yards,” he noted.

On bigger game, many hunters gravitated toward 220- and 225-grain bullets back then, and the relative killing power of those bullets when compared to the wimpy 180s was a hot topic of discussion.

Whelen gives the heavier bullets their due, in particular the 220-grain soft points: “This bullet has made a very enviable reputation for fine killing power on larger game, and particularly on moose and Alaskan brown bear.”.

But when it came to terminal ballistics, a topic he was better versed in than most, he didn’t go along with the accepted wisdom that bigger meant better.

It has been revealed that “It is generally supposed that the 220- and 225-grain bullets are more reliable killers on our larger game than those of 180 grains. I am not so sure of this,” he said. “I would put them about on a par with the best of the 180-grain bullets up to 200 yards. Beyond that distance the trajectory of the 220 grain bullets becomes too curved to surely hit a deer or animals of that size.”.

In his opinion the effectiveness of those heavy bullets topped out around 225 yards, while the 180s and 172s could hit accurately and kill game to 350 yards.

If he sounded like he held strong opinions on the .30/06 that’s because he did. He never hesitated to discuss—and defend—its effectiveness on game, but he also didn’t hold back critiques either.

It has been revealed that for instance, he took ammunition manufacturers to task in the 1930s for allowing the general quality of .30/06 ammo to slip. He had three “fine scope sighted rifles of Springfield, Winchester, and Remington makes” in his collection and gathered data that showed accuracy had fallen off from an average of 1 ¾ to 2 inches at 100 yards to 3-inch groups, while at 200 yards ammo that used to print 3 ½- to 4-inch groups now couldn’t shoot better than 7 inches.

READ NEXT: .30/06 Cartridge Review.

He felt ammo makers were neglecting the round in favor of newer offerings that were in the limelight and used the power of his platform at Outdoor Life and other publications to chastise those companies.

“With such ammunition a fine .30/06 rifle is no longer a 350-yard rifle, but rather a 225-yard arm for sure hits,” he said.

The reason for his bluntness was that he hated the idea of the .30/06—which he noted is “never a mistake”—not living up to its potential as our best all-around major game cartridge.

Not many deer hunters today would list the .250 Savage among their top picks for whitetails—assuming they’re even aware of the cartridge’s existence. A lot of them would dismiss it as underpowered, though that would have come as a shock to Whelen. I guess whitetails have become more bulletproof since his day.

But when ballistic visionary Charles Newton created the .250-3000 in 1915 for the Savage 99 lever action, he gave American sportsmen their first high-power round capable of pushing a bullet at 3000 fps.

To be clear, Newton favored 100-grain bullets in the round with a muzzle velocity of 2800 fps, but Savage wanted to break the 3000-fps barrier and loaded it with 87-grainers which would do just that.

A lot of hunters jumped on the .250 Savage bandwagon and rapidly demonstrated its worth in the woods.

In a recent development, “It has proved to be a very good deer cartridge,” Whelen wrote. Adding, “from hundreds of reports from the game fields it is quite clear that it gives a much larger percentage of instantaneous kills on deer with the first shot than does the .30/30 cartridge.”.

Whelen shot the .250 with 87- and 100-grain bullets, developing handloads for both. He favored the lighter bullet for small game, and the 100-grainers for varmints and deer.

READ NEXT: Best Deer Hunting Cartridges.

When he first recommended the .250 Savage for deer, the .257 Roberts hadn’t been developed yet. By his own admission in later years, he felt anything the Savage could do the Roberts could do better.

“I think that a well-informed rifleman would hardly choose this cartridge because the .257 Roberts cartridge slightly excels it in every respect,” he mentioned.

According to recent reports, I’m taking a bit of liberty with this one, as when Whelen wrote about mule deer earlier in his career he advocated the .30/30 W.C.F. as a minimum acceptable cartridge and, as he often did, defaulted to the .30/40 Krag with a 220-grain bullet as optimal. That remarked, he did throw in a qualifier that any cartridges for other Western game would serve well on muleys.

After the .270 Win. came on the scene, Whelen became a huge fan, calling it “one of the finest cartridges we have for American significant game shooting—a very remarkable load.”.

He extolled the killing power and flat shooting characteristics of Winchester’s 130-grain spitzer bullet and described how a moose he shot with it “was killed more instantaneously than I have ever seen a moose killed before or since.”.

It has been revealed that his Winchester Model 54 was the most accurate big game rifle under 10 pounds he owned—capable of printing 10-shot groups at 100 yards measuring 1 7/8 inches, and 4-inch groups at 200. Relative to harder-kicking cartridges like the .30/06, the soft-shooting .270 lent itself to “fine practical accuracy.”.

As much as we link Jack O’Connor and the .270 Win., there’s little doubt as to Whelen’s perspective: “I think it is our best American major game cartridge in the hands of a rifleman who can avail himself of its flat trajectory and fine accuracy.”.

Sources indicate that when Whelen joined the Army in the late 1890s prior to the Spanish American War, the .30/40 Krag (aka the .30 Army and .30 US) was the standard glitch round. It didn’t serve in that role long. It was adopted in 1892, replacing the .45/70 and then was ousted by the .30/03 (which later became the .30/06) in 1903.

According to recent reports, but like most cartridges employed by the military it became a hit with the sporting public, and as one of our first domestic smokeless powder rounds hunters took a shine to it. It shot a metal jacketed round nose 220-grain bullet at 2000 fps from a 30-inch barrel, which was hot stuff back then. In a carbine configuration with a 22-inch barrel, the velocity dropped to 1960 fps, which was still impressive for the time.

In 1899, a hunter killed the world-record Rocky Mountain elk with a .30/40 Krag, which cemented its reputation as good medicine for wapiti.

READ NEXT: Best Elk Hunting Cartridges.

Whelen liked the .30/40 Krag for elk, too. When he expressed this opinion in his book, American Big Game Shooting, he felt it was the minimum one should attempt to hunt elk with and made a point of emphasizing the use of the 220-grain bullet rather than some of the lighter projectiles available.

That said, in 1923 he gushed about the capabilities of the .30/40 Krag with a 180-grain open point bullet, declaring it “the most useful and all around successful cartridge ever made for the American sportsman.”.

This round is all but forgotten today, having been consigned to the ballistic graveyard in 1936 when Winchester ditched it, along with the Model 1895 rifle that it was chambered in.

But from 1903, when it was developed, through the Roaring 20s the .35 Winchester had a respectable run as a substantial-game round that fell in between the .30/30 and the .405 Winchester, both of which are still produced today.

Sources indicate that like the .30/30 and .405, the .35 W.C.F. is a rimmed bottle-neck cartridge that shoots soft-pointed lead bullets from lever actions. Launching a 249-grain lead cast bullet at 1,500 fps would be plenty potent for moose, which is why Whelen mentioned this cartridge in American Big Game Shooting.

READ NEXT: Best Moose Cartridges.

Of course, being a magnanimous sort, Whelen also lauded the .30/06, the .405, and later on cartridges like the .270 Win., as good options for moose hunters.

According to recent reports, nowhere does Whelen reveal his level-headed style of analysis more than when discussing hunting large bears. He loathed exaggeration as much as he loathed excessive recoil, so when discussing the best all-around bear cartridges he walks a fine line in terms of his recommendations.

On the one hand, he discusses how tales of the ferocity of grizzly bears are vastly overstated—but without minimizing their toughness. “Today there is little danger attending the hunting of the grizzly for a fairly good shot, equipped with a modern rifle of fair killing qualities,” he stated. “However, a grizzly can carry away an awful amount of lead, and from the standpoint of obtaining the bear as well as for protection, a powerful rifle is desired.”.

What qualified as “powerful,” according to Whelen, were the .30/40 Krag, .30/06, .405 Winchester, .35 W.C.F., and the .375 H&H.

Industry observers note that he rightly noted that the .375 H&H was a cut above those other rounds. At one point he described a scenario where when hunting large coastal brown bears in thick cover around salmon streams carrying a stopping cartridge like the .375 H&H was the way to go.

But he also understood the limitations of the round in terms of practical accuracy for most hunters.

“The recoil is not severe to the thoroughly trained rifleman, but is rather heavy for the novice and the ordinary sportsman,” he said. He goes on, “I find that in many cases sportsmen have selected a rifle for this cartridge because they have had failures with the .30/06 cartridge. In almost every case of this kind, if we analyze the seeming failures with the latter cartridge we find that they are due either to a lack of skill in marksmanship, or else the wrong type of .30/06 cartridge was chosen for the game in question. The .375 Magnum cartridge will not in any sense make up for any lack of skill in marksmanship.”.

READ NEXT: Best Bear Hunting Cartridges.

He continues to hammer home this point, saying that a typical sportsman will be ill served trying to overgun for any animal, and is better off shooting a milder round with an appropriate bullet.

“It is certain that if one is a poor or only ordinary shot, he will shoot much worse with a rifle taking the .375 Magnum cartridge than with one less heavily loaded, due to recoil.”.

That perspective is as valid today as it was more than 70 years ago.

This entry requires a bit of a caveat. First off, when Whelen first wrote about hunting black bears in American Major Game Shooting, he didn’t offer a recommendation as to which cartridge to use. It is the only animal in that book that he declined to list one for.

It has been revealed that his reason for doing so was because he didn’t care to hunt them himself and wanted to see them protected by adequate game laws. At the time, bear hunting was largely unregulated and they were regarded as vermin. “The black bear is the only species of American game that I have not shot, and I never want to,” he remarked.

Industry observers note that “The black bear is the most amusing, ludicrous, human, and understandable of our wild animals, and in captivity it makes a most interesting pet…. It is entirely harmless, except on rare occasions, and it should be protected by proper game laws and permitted to survive,” he wrote.

That remarked, the book, which he did in conjunction with the Western Cartridge Company, had a picture of the above-mentioned .35 Winchester Cartridge under the black bear entry, which was a good all-around big-game woods cartridge.

The rise in popularity of the .35 Remington no doubt hastened the .35 Winchester’s demise. It was initially offered in Remington’s Model 8 autoloading rifles and was later chambered in Remington Model 14 and 141 pump actions and the Model 30 bolt gun. Marlin started chambering it in their lever-actions in 1953.

All this is to say that Whelen recognized the capabilities of the .35 Remington as an all-around option for deer, bear, and other animals.

“It is a good cartridge of moderate power and range for use on all American big game. It kills very well at medium ranges, being in this respect much superior to cartridges of the .30/30 class,” he mentioned.

Industry observers note that he felt the cartridge was a good match for the Remington Model 141 in particular. “Deer will be killed much more quickly and reliably than with the other cartridges adapted to this rifle, and (in the rifle it) is by no means out of the running for moose, elk, or large bear.”.

According to recent reports, among all the cartridges Whelen spent time with, the quarter-bore “Bob” was his all-time favorite. He was in touch with Ned Roberts during the development of the .257 Roberts in the mid-1920s and encouraged him to call it the “.25 Roberts” in light of the effort he put into creating the round, which is based on a necked-down 7×57 Mauser.

In a recent development, “I think that no man has ever spent so much time in perfecting a cartridge as Mr. Roberts spent on this one,” Whelen wrote.

Whelen who was an avid varmint shooter and one of the driving forces behind the development of benchrest shooting, loved small, accurate cartridges so it is no wonder he took to the Roberts when it was introduced.

He favored 100-grain bullets for their flat shooting and hard-hitting capabilities on woodchucks out to 300 yards and on crows to 200 yards.

“I do not know of a finer long range varmint cartridge than this, particularly with hand loaded cartridges,” he mentioned.

Industry observers note that he didn’t feel it was limited to popping chucks, however. “It has been proved innumerable times that the full charged cartridges loaded with 100- and 117-grain bullets give excellent results on deer, and we therefore here have a most excellent all-around cartridge which a rifleman can use all year round for small game, varmints, and target, and then take into the substantial woods after deer in the fall,” he mentioned, adding that other than for moose and elk it was a good option for other game, including antelope.

Read Next: Best Antelope Cartridges.

Because of its light recoil, relatively soft report, excellent accuracy, and—for the time—wide bullet selection he remarked it would get the nod as the one cartridge he’d pick if could only shoot one.

“I consider it a very fine cartridge, and if I had of necessity to confine myself to one rifle only I would choose it in this caliber,” he mentioned.

Whelen didn’t mince words when it came to hunting sheep and goats. He knew through first-hand experience how challenging those animals are, both in terms of the terrain that needed to be traversed to get to them and the difficult shots a hunter was often confronted with.

In a recent development, “The hunting and stalking of them is so difficult that the head of a big ram killed by fair stalking is the most prized trophy that can fall to the rifle of the American hunter,” he said. “Often the stalk ends with the hunter quite a long distance from his game with no chance of getting closer unobserved…for this reason a rifle adapted to a cartridge of very high velocity and extreme accuracy at long ranges is most desirable.”.

The two cartridges he touted as most capable for this work were the “.30 caliber Model 1906” shooting a 180-grain “Open Point” and the 7mm Mauser shooting a 139-grain open point.

In his personal 7mm Mauser he was able to swap between 175-grain expanding bullets for large game and the 139s when it came time to go after deer, sheep, goats, antelope and varmints.

When zeroed with the 139s at 100 yards, the 175s shot to point of aim at 200 yards, giving him the confidence to swap ammo as needed on the fly.

But he warned his readers not to count on that trick working in their personal guns.

In a recent development, “Sometimes such a combination can be worked out for certain rifles, and for some it cannot be accomplished. It is not so much a matter of cartridge, caliber, or make of rifle, as how the individual barrel vibrates with each load.”.

According to recent reports, one thing that’s clear to me is that Whelen would have been a fan of the 6.5 Creedmoor. He loved mild, accurate, and effective cartridges, particularly when loaded with the proper bullets, and didn’t hesitate to employ them on massive game.

It shouldn’t come as a shock then to see him sing the praises of the 6.5x54mm Mannlicher Schoenauer as a good choice for caribou.

“Caribou are often found in open or partly open country, and the careful stalking necessary to bring them to bag, with attention to wind, sight, and hearing, make their pursuit a splendid sport,” he noted. “As they are often in localities where it is impossible to approach very closely, a rifle which is effective at long range is very desirable, usually one firing a military or semi-military type cartridge.”.

He claims that caribou deserve a cartridge along the lines of what one would use for elk and lists the .30/06, 7mm Mauser, and 6.5mm Mannlicher as examples—all of which were standard concern military rounds at the time.

Whelen’s eclectic and open-minded approach to cartridges was a defining characteristic of his. So narrowing down a list of his favorite rounds is a bit tricky.

In a recent development, on the one hand, in 1923 he called the .30/40 Krag the “most useful” and “successful cartridge ever made for the American sportsman” that “will kill with a single shot any game in America.” He supported that statement with anecdotes of his own success with the .30/40 Krag in the field, including a one-shot instant kill on an 18-foot crocodile. Fast forward 17 years to 1940 and he doesn’t even mention the round in his thick tome, The Hunting Rifle.

It has been revealed that that was in part a function of the rapid pace of small arms and ammunition development at the time. Whelen’s job was to be on the cutting edge of all things ballistic, and he refused to stick with something out of a sense of nostalgia.

Industry observers note that that remarked, having read much of what Whelen wrote I’ve aimed to do him justice with the rounds I picked. All of the cartridges mentioned are ones he bestowed his imprimatur upon, though I will be curious to see what other fans of “Townie”—as he was called by his friends—think his favorites would have been.

    According to recent reports, today, November 19, the Yamanashi Prefectural Police announced that they had ended the search for Chinese climber Chen Jie, 25, according to the Japanese national newspaper Mainichi Shimbun. Chen disappeared November 8 on the main Yoshida Trail after continuing alone up 3,776m Mount Fuji during its closed season.

    Sources indicate that his two companions reportedly turned back because of deteriorating weather and inadequate equipment. Chen continued on his own without crampons or sufficient cold-weather clothing. His last video was sent that morning between 2,300 and 2,700m.

    His father subsequently traveled to Japan and offered a reward of RMB500,000 ($75,000) for information leading to his recovery alive, or RMB100,000 ($15,000) for recovery of his body.

    Industry observers note that ironically, Chen belonged to China’s Blue Sky Rescue Team, a volunteer search-and-rescue organization. His mother told local media that he had participated in rescues in China and had some mountaineering experience, including trekking and climbing in Nepal and Indonesia.

    #160854. Climbers Forge New Route on Mount Shiva Despite Limited Acclimatization

    📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (625 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

    Climbers Forge New Route on Mount Shiva Despite Limited Acclimatization

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (625 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Benjamin Bosshard and Philippo Sala will never forget their first experience above 6,000m and the fresh route they opened with Stefan Siegrist on India’s Bahai Jar, commonly known as Mount Shiva (6,142m).
    • Industry observers note that expeditions in the Indian Himalaya are usually quiet while they take place, because satellite phones and InReach devices are prohibited.
    • It has been revealed that siegrist had already visited the Chenab River Valley area in 2018 and climbed Shiva with Jonas Schild, but he still had designs on its unclimbed northwest ridge.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Benjamin Bosshard and Philippo Sala will never forget their first experience above 6,000m and the fresh route they opened with Stefan Siegrist on India’s Bahai Jar, commonly known as Mount Shiva (6,142m).

    Industry observers note that expeditions in the Indian Himalaya are usually quiet while they take place, because satellite phones and InReach devices are prohibited. After returning home, however, Stefan Siegrist reported the details, and the team’s cameraman, Christoph Detschmann, posted a video summary of the expedition:.

    It has been revealed that siegrist had already visited the Chenab River Valley area in 2018 and climbed Shiva with Jonas Schild, but he still had designs on its unclimbed northwest ridge. At the end of September, he, Sala, and Bosshard reached base camp in the Kishtwar massif.

    Recent findings suggest that the three Swiss climbers were prepared to endure a long period of bad weather while acclimatizing. To their surprise, a good weather window opened right away. It was too good to let go, despite not being properly acclimatized and Sala and Bosshard’s lack of altitude experience. The window was expected to last just three days. After many “discussions and doubts,” they left base camp on October 3.

    It has been revealed that sala had a headache during the first night, but the following morning, they were all totally focused on the climb, and the tension disappeared. “We assumed that we were unlikely to reach the summit on this attempt, and that we would therefore be wasting our only chance before a major storm [brought] the season to an end,” Siegrist explained. “So from then on, the idea was simply to climb higher and acclimatize, without any pressure.”.

    A moment of the climb, filmed from a drone by Christoph Detschmann.

    Sources indicate that along the way, they discovered they had left their stove at base camp. No problem in 2026: The expedition photographer used his drone to carry the stove up to them. The use of drones was a hot topic during the recent Piolets d’Or: To what extent are they compatible with alpine-style criteria? While most accepted that drones could scout routes or sections out of view of base camp, many considered using them to carry equipment up a face to be a red line.

    On Shiva, Siegrist indicates the delivery of the missing stove “proved essential to the success of the climb.”.

    Recent findings suggest that the climbers spent their second night at 5,250m at the base of the northwest ridge. On the following morning, they had to decide whether to continue or retreat. They all felt well, but starting the highly technical ridge was a point of no return. At the same time, Siegrist recalls, they realized they really had a chance to summit. And so on they went.

    Recent findings suggest that that night, they stopped at 5,700m in what Siegrist describes as a crucial moment. His partners had not been at that altitude before, and the latest forecast declared a storm the following day. They decided to wait and see what the morning looked like. No one slept at all that night.

    Sources indicate that the last meters before the summit. Drone image by Christoph Detschmann.

    The sky was still clear when the team set off again at 4am, so they chose to keep going. “After a while, we finally reached the final slope, just 300m below the summit,” Siegrist wrote. By now, they knew they were going to make it. They reached the top at 7:44am, six days after arriving in Base Camp, and just in time to hurry down as the storm approached.

    The climbers descended via the 1985 Japanese route (see topo below), and reached their base camp tents as it started to snow.

    #160849. Latest Update: How to Sharpen an Axe Like a Pro. Follow This Step-By-Step Guide

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1540 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

    Latest Update: How to Sharpen an Axe Like a Pro. Follow This Step-By-Step Guide

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1540 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs.
    • According to recent reports, many people have heard the story about two woodcutters chopping trees in the forest.
    • In a recent development, A sharp axe will have less glancing blows, cut deeper, and cut faster.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

    According to recent reports, many people have heard the story about two woodcutters chopping trees in the forest. One chops and chops and chops without stopping, while the other takes breaks frequently, but still manages to chop more wood. That’s because while the second woodcutter was “on break” he was sharpening his axe. Now, lots of corporate types use this story to try to teach something about productivity, or whatever, but the only real takeaway is that a sharp axe translates to less hard work.

    In a recent development, A sharp axe will have less glancing blows, cut deeper, and cut faster. I’m not interested in banging a dull hunk of metal into a tree for 15 minutes when I could get it done with a sharp axe in less than five. So, sharp axe good, dull axe bad. But how do you get your axe nice and sharp and ready to do some real work? Believe it or not, it’s not that hard, and it doesn’t require expensive tools. Here’s a step-by-step guide on how to sharpen an axe.

    Recent findings suggest that for this method, you really only need two tools. A flat file, and a “puck” style sharpening stone. The file should be a Mill Bastard file. These are commonly available at any hardware store, and if you get your technique correct, you don’t actually need a puck afterward. An 8” or bigger file makes this easier, but you can get the job done with a smaller 4” or 6” file. I sharpened my axe for this tutorial with a flat file for leveling chainsaw guide teeth, just to show that it can be done with a small file. (Plus my bigger file is getting dull and needs replacing).

    After you’re done with the file, you can move on to really honing and sharpening the edge with a puck-style sharpening stone. I use stones from Straight Grain Supply because they are dual grit, and the rubber band makes for a good grip. The stones come in a variety of grits, and can be used alone without a file if you like. I use both because the file removes damage faster, and the pucks give a finer edge with the higher grits. For these stones, I keep a bowl of water and an old toothbrush handy. Letting them sit in water before sharpening helps to keep them from getting clogged up with metal particles. A quick scrub with the toothbrush and some water helps keep them clean and cutting properly and it extends their effective life.

    In a recent development, if you have a vise, that can be helpful if there is damage that needs to be sharpened out, but it’s not necessary. If you don’t have a vise, having a longer file is much more important. More on that later. The last thing you will need is a dull axe. I used my “beater” axe for this story. It’s been used as a wedge and it’s been beaten and deformed. It has smashed more than a couple rocks while taking out roots. It had some serious damage, so I thought it would be useful to show how effective the file is. As a final note, I recommend wearing a pair of work gloves for this because your hands and fingertips will be very close to the edge.

    Sources indicate that first, you will take your file and set your edge angle and thin out the cheek of the axe. The cheek is the portion of the blade just behind the edge. You can thin this out if you want the axe to chop deeper into the wood. If you have to bring the edge back for significant damage, you should file the cheeks down a bit to keep the cutting performance. Make sure you are sharpening the whole bevel, not just a tiny portion near the apex of the edge. With a longer file, you can ball up an old rag or t-shirt and put it on the axe head and rest the tip of the file on it as you make your cuts with the back of the file. Make the rag thick or thinner so you can match the angle of the bevel. The rag acts as a pivot point for the file and allows you to keep pressure on the axe head so it won’t move around.

    With a shorter file, this method won’t work, and a vise really comes in handy. For wood handled axes, rubber jaw protectors, rags, or leather can be used to protect the wood in the vise.

    Pull your file across the edge from one end of the blade to the other. These files don’t just cut with the file moving from tip to handle, they cut laterally as well. You will feel the file bite into the material. Lift the file and go back and make another lateral pull.

    Industry observers note that make passes until all damage is removed, and you feel a burr on the entire edge. Flip it over and do the same thing to the other side. After you have apexed the edge on both sides, you should have a pretty sharp axe, and you can stop here if you want. With just a file, you can achieve a great working edge. But, I like my stuff really sharp, so I continue on to the stones.

    It has been revealed that once you have removed the heavy damage and re-profiled the edge with your file, you can refine the edge with progressively finer grit stones. If you don’t have a file, you can use a coarse stone to profile the edge, but it will generally take more time, especially if there are some deeper chips or rolls in the edge.

    After your stones have soaked in the water a bit, “scrub” the entire beveled edge with the puck using small circular motions to refine it. Hold the puck with your fingertips and keep them away from the edge. You will see the scratch pattern from the stone taking away the tooling marks from the file.

    Give your stone a dip in the water every so often to keep it clean. When you have removed the marks from the file on the whole edge, repeat for the other side. Then, get the next grit stone, and repeat this process on each side. Scrub until the scratch pattern from the previous grit stone is gone. I usually use the medium grit after the file work and progress to a fine grit. Straight Grain Supply makes two-sided stones in 80/220 grit, 220/400 grit, and 220/600 grit. I use the 220 grit and then progress to my 400 grit side. I have used the 80 grit side for damage before, and it will remove material fairly rapidly, but I still prefer a file for initial shaping. After you have done both sides with medium and fine grit, your axe should be ready to go, and will be taking on a nice shiny, somewhat polished appearance. If you have a leather strop, you could make a few passes on that just to remove any small burr that might remain and further polish and refine the edge, but the bur will be gone on the first chop or two anyway. I strop mine because I have one, and I like the edge to be shiny after I’m done. If you want the best edge possible, take your time with these steps. It will be worth it when you start chopping.

    Recent findings suggest that once you profile and remove damage on an axe, maintaining that sharp edge shouldn’t take much effort at all. After each use, take a minute or so and hone each side with your finest grit puck stone before you put the axe away, and you will generally be able to go a long time before you have to sharpen it again. Now, if you happen to hit a rock or nail or something else that damages the edge beyond small nicks, then you will have to go through the whole process again. A little maintenance after each use will keep your axe cutting well between sharpening, and prolong the life of the axe head. If you maintain it with a file every time, you will remove more material than needed and wear out the bit of the axe sooner. An ounce of prevention is better than a pound of cure.

    Read Next: Best Camping Axes, Tested and Reviewed.

    Sources indicate that A little time spent learning how to sharpen an axe will pay dividends when it comes time for chopping. For me, few things are as frustrating as a tool not performing the way it is supposed to. The thing is, you might not think your axe is even dull, but if you take the time to sharpen it, you will be amazed at the difference in cutting performance. Invest a little in sharpening and save a bunch of hard work down the road. Keep your axes sharp.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Two Germans, aged 15 and 18, spent almost 20 hours on Austria’s highest mountain before being evacuated by helicopter on November 15.
    • Initially, police reported that the pair had reached the 3,798m summit and become lost while descending.
    • Industry observers note that their ordeal began around 11pm on Saturday, November 14.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Two Germans, aged 15 and 18, spent almost 20 hours on Austria’s highest mountain before being evacuated by helicopter on November 15.

    Initially, police reported that the pair had reached the 3,798m summit and become lost while descending. The younger climber disputes this, saying they turned back near an alpine hut at 3,454m because his companion felt ill.

    Industry observers note that their ordeal began around 11pm on Saturday, November 14. The pair had no previous experience with such a serious mountain but had prepared by reading websites, watching videos, training physically, and asking others for tips. They did carry crampons, an ice axe, a helmet, a rope, a belay device, and extra clothing.

    It took them a long time before they decided to turn around. The descent went well at first, but one spot seemed too dangerous to them. To get around it, they followed someone else’s tracks in the snow, but these suddenly disappeared. While looking for a way, they got stuck in deep snow. The older boy called for help at around 6:30pm on November 15, according to Austria’s public broadcaster, ORF.at.

    Recent findings suggest that at first, rescuers tried to guide the pair down by phone. More than two hours later, the boys were still stuck, so a helicopter was dispatched. The rescuers found the pair, exhausted, disoriented, and hypothermic, at around 2,800m.

    Industry observers note that A rescue helicopter brings the teens to safety. Photo: Mountain Rescue KALS.

    Yesterday, rescue leader Peter Tembler criticized their lack of alpine experience and preparation. He told the German Press Agency that the pair lacked sufficient experience for the terrain and winter conditions. He also criticized their late-night departure.

    According to recent reports, according to Tembler, a section that normally takes four to five hours took them almost 12. Other climbers reportedly advised them against continuing.

    Tembler believes an increasing number of inexperienced people are attempting serious alpine routes, sometimes encouraged by social media accounts that downplay the difficulty. The disagreement has become a public debate about risk-taking, responsibility, and rescue operations.

    Recent findings suggest that as Austria’s highest peak, Grossglockner is a magnet for climbers of all stripes and has more than its share of controversy. In January 2025, a man abandoned his less experienced girlfriend high on the mountain. She froze to death, and an Austrian court later convicted him of manslaughter for leaving her behind. This summer, an altercation occurred on Grossglockner in which a guide insulted a passing climber and nearly pushed him off a cliff. At the same time, veteran alpinists are still setting bold new routes here.

    According to Der Standard, Grossglockner gets 8,000 to 9,000 ascents each year, with an average of two dozen rescues annually. Between 2005 and 2025, 29 climbers have died on the mountain.

    This Massive Swordfish Smashed the State Record, But It Was Disqualified Over a Technicality

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (738 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Jake Kinzie had a crew of three buddies aboard his 28-foot boat while fishing off Ocean City, Maryland the morning of November 11.
    • Swordfish action has been good this year along the Atlantic Coast.
    • In 1,000 feet of water, they put out a swordfish squid bait on a 10/0 Mustad hook, taken deep with a strobe light attached to the leader to get the attention of a heavy fish.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Capt. Jake Kinzie had a crew of three buddies aboard his 28-foot boat while fishing off Ocean City, Maryland the morning of November 11. The anglers ran 60 miles out to fish the deep “Poorman’s Canyon” for prized swordfish — and they would end up catching the largest sword in state history.

    Swordfish action has been good this year along the Atlantic Coast. And the “Way Out” crew had caught a couple big swords earlier off Ocean City.

    In 1,000 feet of water, they put out a swordfish squid bait on a 10/0 Mustad hook, taken deep with a strobe light attached to the leader to get the attention of a heavy fish.

    “Jake is an old friend I’ve known for over two decades,” Capt. Keith Jacobs tells Outdoor Life. “We were with our other buddies Joe Spayd and Blaine Beyer, and about 2:30 p.m. we hooked a deep, very large fish.”.

    In a recent development, spayd was on the rod, fighting the tough swordfish for about three hours. It never jumped, and the anglers never saw it until late in the fight.

    “We knew it was huge because it was so powerful,” says Jacobs, a professional boat captain and owner of “OC-anic,” a fishing gear and apparel firm. “But we figured it was only 300 pounds or so until we saw it near the boat as the sun was setting.”.

    It has been revealed that jacobs noted it was all they could do to keep the swordfish from getting close to their boat and perhaps breaking the 80-pound test braided line on the Daiwa reel that Spayd used. He fought the fish from a gunnel rod holder on a swivel.

    “Jake had to spin the boat a lot to keep the line from rubbing against the boat hull,” Jacobs says. “Three hours into the fight we got the fish close to our boat, but it was still full of fight.”.

    It has been revealed that while Spayd stayed on the rod battling the sword, Beyer hit the fish with a harpoon dart. The metal dart head, with a heavy line fitted to it, detached from the pole.

    “Then I hit the fish in the head with a big gaff – which wasn’t such a good idea,” states Jacobs. “It went crazy and ripped the gaff handle out of my hands and we lost it overboard.”.

    Jacobs hit the fish with another gaff to help control and kill it.

    Industry observers note that “We struggled to get a tail rope around the fish,” Jacobs states. “All that time lines were crossing, we’re wet, tired, the fish is thrashing beside the boat – and it’s getting dark in three-foot seas.”.

    Recent findings suggest that finally, the anglers secured the massive swordfish with a tail rope. After the fish died, they had to haul it into their 28-foot boat.

    In a recent development, “We didn’t have a block-and-tackle or come-along, so we had to grab it and haul it over the stern and around the boat’s two outboards,” Jacobs indicates. “We had to do it twice, because a fin got wedged in one of the outboards.

    According to recent reports, “We were exhausted when we finally got it in the boat. It took up about half of the deck space. That’s when we headed back in to Ocean City.”.

    The anglers arrived at Ocean City’s Snug Harbor waterfront neighborhood about 9 p.m. There the 12-foot long fish was hauled out of their boat with a crane and weighed on a digital scale at 558 pounds.

    It topped the largest swordfish caught by a sport angler by 165 pounds. That fish was boated in 2022 by angler Jeff Jacobs and weighed 393 pounds.

    Read Next: Maine Tuna Fisherman Accidentally Catches Record-Setting Swordfish.

    The anglers covered their 558-pound swordfish with fish bags and ice, and the next day contacted authorities to enter it as a state record catch.

    Industry observers note that “But we learned that because we used an electric Daiwa reel it doesn’t qualify as a Maryland record,” Jacobs claims. “Other states have record fish that are certified if electric reels are used by sporting tackle anglers.

    “The tackle we used – even with electric reels – is far different than what commercial fishermen use.

    “I wish Maryland had another records division that allows electric reels for heavyweight marine gamefish like swordfish, tuna, and giant marlin.”.

    #160843. LaCrosse Alphaburly Aero 2000 Boot Review: The Warmest Boot LaCrosse Has Ever Made

    LaCrosse Alphaburly Aero 2000 Boot Review: The Warmest Boot LaCrosse Has Ever Made

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (838 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs.
    • Industry observers note that insulated rubber boots are warm and waterproof.
    • Recent findings suggest that last week I got the chance to field test LaCrosse’s new Alphaburly Aero 2000 insulated rubber boot on a whitetail hunt in Saskatchewan.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

    Industry observers note that insulated rubber boots are warm and waterproof. But they’re also heavy, hard to walk in, and uncomfortable to wear for a long period of time — or at least they used to be.

    Recent findings suggest that last week I got the chance to field test LaCrosse’s new Alphaburly Aero 2000 insulated rubber boot on a whitetail hunt in Saskatchewan. The program for this kind of hunt is as follows: A cheery Canadian guide drops you off at a ground blind somewhere way back in the bush; you sit there overlooking a small shooting window from dark to dark; you never leave the blind because the biggest buck of your life could show up at any moment.

    Temperatures on this hunt ranged from the mid 20s to low 40s, which is chilly but not as cold as we were hoping for (temps in the teens with a good foot of snow really get the bucks moving during daylight up there, or at least so I’ve heard).

    In a recent development, this was the perfect testing ground for a rubber boot that’s designed for cold-weather deer hunting, among other duties. Here’s how the upcoming LaCrosse boots held up.

    It has been revealed that the heart of the Aero line is the ETPU midsole, which borrows its design from the high-performance running world. The midsole returns energy as your foot strikes the ground (or more simply put, the boots are springy). The effect is that the boots are incredibly comfortable to walk in. If you’ve ever walked, say a mile or so in heavy boots, you know that they can wear out your legs and feet quickly. But with the new LaCrosse design, the weight of the boots is offset by the springiness of the midsole.

    It has been revealed that but your feet won’t stay comfortable long if they’re cold. It’s common for rubber boot wearers to get sweaty feet early in the day, and then freeze later on. To combat this, LaCrosse is using a completely newly introduced type of insulation called Solarcore. This is a kind of aerogel, which is woven into the interior of the boot. It’s promoted as a very light, very warm kind of insulation. In fact these boots are up to a pound lighter than other insulated rubber boots in their class. That lighter weight makes them easier to walk in as well. Importantly, Solarcore also repels water, unlike Thinsulate. So if your feet do get sweaty or wet inside the boot, that moisture doesn’t soak into the insulation.

    Recent findings suggest that there is a Pro version of the boot, which is all rubber, but I prefer the neoprene. I think it’s more comfortable on those long, all day sits.

    There’s also an 800g insulation version of the boot if you don’t anticipate hunting in very cold weather. If you’re going to mostly be hunting in the mid-20s and 30s, I’d say you’d be fine with the 800g boot. If you’re hunting in temps below that, or your feet get cold easily, go with the max insulation.

    During any long sit in the cold, your feet and hands are most likely to get cold first. But over the four days that I hunted, essentially sitting still for 10 hours at a time, my feet never got cold. I wore a light wool sock with a heavy wool sock over it. No foot warmers. No heater. I was impressed with how well the Solarcore insulation worked.

    Sources indicate that after the Saskatchewan hunt I took the boots to my family deer camp in Wisconsin and did a morning of still hunting with them. As advertised, they were extremely comfortable to walk in. I stepped in a stream that was shin deep and stood in it for about 2 minutes (just as a test) and experienced no leaks.

    Recent findings suggest that only time will tell how these boots will hold up over the long term. I think one benefit of the full rubber Pro version is durability. Any sort of neoprene can wear out with hard use. So if you’re planning on hiking in these boots in any sort of rugged terrain, you’d want to go with the Pro version.

    These are expensive boots, but they are jam packed with new technology. They are a true upgrade from basic insulated rubber boots that we’ve all worn in the past. If you hunt in cold weather, if you want to walk comfortably in rubber boots, or if your feet get cold easily, the Alphaburly Aero 2000 is a good option to consider.

    I’m a Midwesterner who likes winter and I think I could wear these boots in zero degree temps without fear of getting cold. If you really wanted a bulletproof setup, pair these boots with a pair of heated socks and never get cold feet again.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    This episode of the storm-chasing TV series Storm Rising is titled “High Plains Insanity.” Produced by National Geographic, it follows Reed Timmer and Mike Theiss as they attempt to navigate and document an increasingly unpredictable storm season.

    Sources indicate that the storm-chasing segments are filmed like an action movie but, as Timmer makes clear, thrills are not the primary objective. As the climate changes and disrupts weather patterns, tornadoes are no longer limited to traditional seasons and ranges.

    “That’s why we need to be on the ground directly in the path of these tornadoes,” Timmer explains, “to record data that no one else is getting.”.

    In a recent development, driving into a potential tornado in Montana. Photo: Screenshot.

    Industry observers note that with hurricane and tornado seasons now overlapping, the duo is forced to split up to cover the widest possible area and collect the most data. For the tornadoes, this means deploying a probe into the funnel.

    It has been revealed that up north in the High Plains of the U.S. West and Midwest, Timmer and his dog Gizmo narrowly miss storm after storm. Gizmo is better organization but is a very poor navigator, while Timmer isn’t much better. He constantly makes wrong turns as he tries to navigate, drive, and prepare equipment. He does take the time to explain the basic weather science behind what he is failing to catch, such as the conditions that created the baseball-sized hail pummeling his windshield.

    Timmer and Gizmo drive through the aftermath of a powerful tornado in the Black Hills of North Dakota. Photo: Screenshot.

    Industry observers note that in Florida, Theiss sleeps in his car to maintain a constant vigil along the coast. Our current scientific abilities, he explains, allow us to track the movement of hurricane systems with decent accuracy. But predicting their strength is much more difficult. Systems can suddenly turn deadly or fizzle out with equally short notice. In this case, the terrible-looking storm comes to nothing. He heads back up north to rejoin Timmer and Gizmo.

    Industry observers note that gizmo buffeted by fierce winds. Photo: Screenshot.

    Sources indicate that the reunited trio prepares for a final effort, complete with a windshield-replacement sequence. They immediately drive into the gathering storm, passing through a hail core which, of course, destroys the new windshield. The Lord giveth and taketh away, et cetera. Soon they’re racing on a near-empty tank, as the powerful storm threatens to touch down at any moment.

    According to recent reports, it’s their last chance this season to deploy the probe. When, after a long, tense chase, they actually manage to do it, both erupt into cheers. Gizmo appears unmoved, despite the fact that this ground probe, deployed in a storm of this type, in this area, has never been deployed before and is sure to yield valuable scientific data.

    #160839. Mountain Lion Is the Ultimate Underrated Game Meat. Here’s How to Prepare It

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

    Mountain Lion Is the Ultimate Underrated Game Meat. Here’s How to Prepare It

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1205 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, luke Ellsbury and his 16-year-old daughter had chased the lion for miles through a foot of snow in some of northwest Wyoming’s harshest country.
    • “There was no good horse trail or anything to travel in and out,” Ellsbury indicates.
    • It has been revealed that at that point, some lion hunters may have chosen to take the skull and cape and leave the meat, a practice that’s legal in some states like Wyoming and one that’s presently being leveraged to ban “trophy” mountain lion hunting in Colorado.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, luke Ellsbury and his 16-year-old daughter had chased the lion for miles through a foot of snow in some of northwest Wyoming’s harshest country. Their bluetick-English coonhounds finally treed the cat on the far side of a steep ridge, about 7 miles from their truck. By the time they tagged the lion, they’d already been running for well over half the day, and they still had to skin and field dress it.

    “There was no good horse trail or anything to travel in and out,” Ellsbury indicates. “Just getting to a lion is a lot of work.”.

    It has been revealed that at that point, some lion hunters may have chosen to take the skull and cape and leave the meat, a practice that’s legal in some states like Wyoming and one that’s presently being leveraged to ban “trophy” mountain lion hunting in Colorado. Anti-hunters there are trying to persuade the voting public that hunters don’t eat mountain lion meat.

    But Ellsbury, like plenty of cougar hunters, wanted the meat from his mountain lion. So, he and his daughter and two friends carefully removed the animal’s backstraps and quarters and packed them out, making the long haul back on that cold January day and reaching their truck after dark. Lion meat, Ellsbury says, is worth the work. Two years later, he’s still savoring the remaining packages of that lion’s meat. He made burnt ends out of it recently. “I’ve eaten my fair share of lion, and I really like it,” he says. “It’s pretty versatile and mild tasting.”.

    In a recent development, ellsbury, a large carnivore biologist for the Wyoming Game and Fish Department, longtime houndsman, and former guide, doesn’t blame people for being gun shy about eating mountain lion. It is a cat, after all. But he and others insist it’s worth trying. And not unlike other wild game, from moose to bighorn sheep and chukars to sandhill cranes, mountain lion meat is best consumed while keeping a few best practices in mind. Here’s how to prepare and cook mountain lion meat.

    It has been revealed that yes. Although mountain lion meat certainly isn’t as popular as wild game like whitetail deer or wild turkey, it is edible, tasty, and safe to eat when prepared properly. The meat from mountain lions and other predators, like black bears, has long carried a stigma because these critters eat other animals, which brings unfounded concerns about taste and safety. In reality, mountain lion meat tastes great, it’s lean, and relatively easy to cook, says Luke Worthington, a Wyoming hunter, guide, and founder of the Wyoming Houndsmen Association.

    “It tastes a lot like pork,” Worthington tells Outdoor Life. “I do the old shake and bake with it, where I cube it up and put it in shake and bake and fry it.”.

    According to recent reports, and that stigma around mountain lions has changed dramatically over the last 15 to 20 years. Worthington says his clients are becoming more interested in hauling out lion meat to take home. He credits a growing movement focused on eating other, more nontraditional types of wild game.

    Recent findings suggest that “I tell people, ‘This is good meat and edible meat, and it’s worth it. If you kill an animal, it’s worth taking the meat,’” he indicates. “The least you can do is try it.”.

    Most people who’ve eaten lion say the meat tastes much like a lean pork, with a mild or almost sweet flavor that is well suited to picking up other flavors in marinades, rubs, or sauces.

    Sources indicate that ellsbury also notes that while the fat from a deer or elk can be waxy and unpleasant tasting, lion fat — like bear fat — can be quite good. He likens lion fat to pork fat, although the two animals have vastly different quantities. (Lions are much leaner.).

    A common concern that many people have with lion and bear meat is trichinosis, a food-borne disease caused by a parasitic worm that lives in meat-eating animals. The worm doesn’t seem to bother mountain lions, but it does affect humans and can be fatal if left untreated. Historically, most people contracted trichinosis from eating undercooked or raw pork, but advances in commercial food and farming regulations have largely lowered the risk, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. There is still a risk with meat from mountain lions, wild boar, and bears, but it’s minimal: the CDC reports that the U.S. only sees about 15 confirmed cases per year.

    Industry observers note that while the risk of contracting trichinosis to humans is low, it still exists. That means hunters need to be sure they kill those parasitic larvae before eating.

    Read Next: 6 Wild-Game Rituals That Are About Much More Than the Meat.

    To safely prepare mountain lion meat, don’t cook it rare or medium-rare. Instead, cook it thoroughly to an internal temperature of 165 degrees Fahrenheit. The CDC also notes that “Curing (salting), drying, smoking, or microwaving meat alone does not consistently kill infective worms. Homemade jerky and sausage were the cause of many cases of [trichinosis] reported to CDC in the past.”.

    Sources indicate that because most lion hunters want the cape, Worthington recommends carefully skinning the animal before beginning to remove meat. From there, butchering a mountain lion is similar to quartering and butchering an ungulate. Just be sure to field dress your lion as quickly as possible. Because lions eat other animals, their guts can cause the meat to spoil quicker than a deer’s, Worthington notes.

    For hunters who are unable to pack out an animal whole, consider the gutless method and remove the front and hind quarters, backstraps, and edible portions of the neck.

    Worthington cautions that, depending on the size of the cat, the front shoulders may not offer much meat, and the backstraps are often about as round as a hefty bratwurst. But he states they’re still worth saving to cook later.

    Dan Thompson, Wyoming Game and Fish Department’s large carnivore section supervisor, cautions hunters to avoid a lion’s anal glands when skinning and field dressing the animal. The glands, used by cats and dogs to mark their territory, are pungent and can ruin the meat if punctured.

    To prevent accidental infection from trichinosis, wear disposable gloves when handling the lion and meat, and wash your hands thoroughly when you’re finished.

    Sources indicate that consider dividing meat into roasts, steaks, and ground burger. Ellsbury and Thompson both recommend slow cooking roasts in a crock pot with carnitas seasonings to make tender tacos, or with barbecue seasonings to create pulled lion sandwiches.

    You can also marinate and grill steaks. But while you need to make sure the internal temperature reaches 165, be careful not to overcook lion meat as it can easily dry out and become tough.

    Recent findings suggest that if you’re looking to impress someone who might be skeptical of mountain lion meat, Thompson recommends this recipe for pork stuffed mushrooms by Steph Gaudreau. As with other recipes, you can easily substitute ground lion meat for ground pork.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Richard Carlos Skidmore, 66, of the United States, was found dead in his tent on Mera Peak on Sunday, November 22, after summiting the 6,476m mountain the previous morning.

    According to Solukhumbu district police, he reached the summit at approximately 10am on Saturday, November 21, and descended to the high camp at around 5,800m, where he spent the night.

    He was found dead the next morning. Past Mera Peak climbers have suggested on social media that it was unusual to overnight in the high camp after summiting so early in the day.

    His body was evacuated by helicopter to Kathmandu for an autopsy. The cause of death remains undetermined. An initial report raised the possibility of altitude-related illness or a cardiac event, but neither has been established medically.

    It has been revealed that skidmore previously summited Lobuche Peak in 2024, according to the Everest Chronicle and the Italian Alpine Club’s publication Lo Scarpone. So he had previous Himalayan climbing experience above 6,000m.

    In a recent development, the Himalayan Database does include Mera Peak, but its coverage of popular trekking peaks is selective. However, it notes that since 2018, four people have died on Mera Peak, not counting Skidmore.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Three Polish climbers have established a fresh line on the north face of one of the Tien Shan’s best-known climbing peaks.
    • Michal Makowski, Robert Paluch, and Rafal Zając took 11 hours to climb their newly introduced 850m line on 4,777m Free Korea Peak, in Kyrgyzstan’s northern Tien Shan Mountains.
    • Recent findings suggest that they named the route The Polish Barber, after pioneer American climber Henry Barber, who soloed the wall in 1976.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Three Polish climbers have established a fresh line on the north face of one of the Tien Shan’s best-known climbing peaks.

    Michal Makowski, Robert Paluch, and Rafal Zając took 11 hours to climb their newly introduced 850m line on 4,777m Free Korea Peak, in Kyrgyzstan’s northern Tien Shan Mountains. They then spent a further 11 hours returning to base camp.

    Recent findings suggest that they named the route The Polish Barber, after pioneer American climber Henry Barber, who soloed the wall in 1976. Their line shares the first 250–300m with Barber’s, Makowski told ExplorersWeb.

    “According to the information I have, [the remaining 600-650m] was previously unclimbed and had never been attempted by another team,” remarked Makowski. “We reached the summit ridge and then began rappelling down from there.

    Corona Hut, the team’s base camp. Photo: Polski Związek Alpinizmu.

    Free Korea Peak — Pik Svobodnaya Koreya in Russian — was already famous among mountaineers in the former Soviet Union because of its 900m north wall. in 2018, Russian climber Valery Balesin suggested that it was no longer possible to find new lines on this well-known face, although advances in steep ice-climbing techniques have clearly opened new possibilities.

    “My friends and I researched Free Korea Peak and realized that part of the north face still has unclimbed terrain,” said Makowski.

    On the Polish Barber route. Photo: Polski Związek Alpinizmu.

    Their route was almost completely ice climbing. The crux came midway up the wall, when they faced a particularly steep section of ice that they graded at Alpine Ice 4+. The rest of the route was 3/3+. Fortunately, “protection on the Polish Barber was really good, except for the last 150m, where ice was pretty thin and crusty,” stated Makowski.

    Climbing by moonlight. Photo: Polski Związek Alpinizmu.

    Sources indicate that despite its former popularity, they had the valley almost to themselves during their week in camp. There was just one Russian group doing a tourist trek up nearby Corona Peak.

    A scrambly section on Free Korea Peak. Photo: Polski Związek Alpinizmu.

    Ukrainian Solos Newly introduced Route in Gokyo Valley, Near Everest

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Mykyta Balabanov of Ukraine has soloed a fresh route on the northeast face of Nepal’s Phari Lapcha (6,017m).
    • Balabanov is still trekking back to Lukla, but has given ExplorersWeb some details and photos about this impressive upcoming route.
    • Industry observers note that the Ukrainian set off on his own up an unclimbed line on the northeast face on November 19.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Mykyta Balabanov of Ukraine has soloed a fresh route on the northeast face of Nepal’s Phari Lapcha (6,017m). Also known as Machhermo Peak, it sits 24km west of Everest in the Gokyo Valley.

    Balabanov is still trekking back to Lukla, but has given ExplorersWeb some details and photos about this impressive upcoming route.

    Industry observers note that the Ukrainian set off on his own up an unclimbed line on the northeast face on November 19. He made two bivouacs on the way up and one more on the descent.

    “The level of difficulty is hard to tell, as always when solo, but I’d say it was around 80° on ice, M5+, 5c on rock, and lots of poor snow!” Balavanov said.

    He estimates the new route is 1,200m long, and spans some 850 vertical meters from base to summit.

    Rough topo of Balabanov’s solo route on the northeast face of Phari Lapcha. Photo: Mykyta Balabanov.

    Recent findings suggest that another side of Phari Lapcha saw action just one day before Balabanov, when U.S. guide Bennie Lieber led Canadian Emma Deguara up the Stone(d) Yeti route on the south face.

    It has been revealed that “I was not related to that climb, as I climbed alone after approaching from a different valley,” Balabanov explained. “However, I saw their tracks on the summit and spotted their bivy place at the bottom of the south face.”.

    Lieber and Deguara made the second ascent of their chosen route. “While the technical grade (M3, AI2+) is easily digestible, the room for mistakes, due to exposure, is zero,” Lieber said.

    Mykyta Balabanov and fellow Ukrainian Mikhail Fomino opened a new route on Ama Dablam in 2024, but they first became widely known for their new route on the Southeast Ridge of Annapurna III in 2021.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Russian team has returned to Everest, aiming to reach at least 7,500m, but high winds have again dashed their looks.

    The three-man team of Andrei Vasiliev, Sergey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov set off yesterday and reached their cached tent at 5,600m. As leader Vasiliev explained, they expected strong winds at summit altitude until Wednesday, but they intended to keep themselves in lower areas, where the wind speed was acceptable.

    However, the wind was too strong to go higher than 5,600m today, so they decided to stay put. MountainClub.com, which has access to the team’s InReach tracker, has posted a partial view of the climbers’ current location:.

    Recent findings suggest that we asked Jost Kobusch of Germany (also planning to climb the West Ridge of Everest this winter) about that location. He confirmed that they are midway up the vertical mixed section leading from the Khumbu Glacier to the Lho La Pass.

    This is the expedition’s fourth foray up the mountain. According to Vasiliev, it is also their last chance to acclimatize before a potential summit push. The Russians’ climbing permit is reportedly valid until December 15.

    Their future progress will depend on the wind. Multi-model forecasts indicate that winds are expected to decrease on Thursday but not to disappear. The chart by High Asia Avalanche Watch, which compares seven different weather models, predicts that winds will not drop below 45kph at the summit (on Thursday and Friday). They will then pick up again.

    Wind speed at the summit of Everest over the next two weeks, by High Asia Avalanche Watch.

    #160821. German Women Climb New Route on Sharphu VI

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (441 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

    German Women Climb New Route on Sharphu VI

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (441 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

    ⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that last month, five women with the German Alpine Club established a fresh route on the northwest ridge of Sharphu VI in eastern Nepal.
    • It has been revealed that in October, Steffi Feistl, Anna Gomeringer, Kristin Hinkelmann, Kathi Huber, and Fenja Kochl set up their base camp at 4,000m.
    • Their preliminary blueprint had been to attempt either Sharphu II or Sharphu VI, but Sharphu II’s condition looked too dangerous due to unstable rock, threatening seracs, and hazardous snow conditions.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that last month, five women with the German Alpine Club established a fresh route on the northwest ridge of Sharphu VI in eastern Nepal. It was only the second overall ascent of the 6,076m peak near Kangchenjunga.

    It has been revealed that in October, Steffi Feistl, Anna Gomeringer, Kristin Hinkelmann, Kathi Huber, and Fenja Kochl set up their base camp at 4,000m. A huge amount of snow had fallen earlier that season, guaranteeing arduous slogging in some areas.

    Their preliminary blueprint had been to attempt either Sharphu II or Sharphu VI, but Sharphu II’s condition looked too dangerous due to unstable rock, threatening seracs, and hazardous snow conditions.

    According to recent reports, sharphu II and VI. Photo: Xtreme Climbers/labels by Gunter Seyfferth.

    On the other hand, the northwest ridge of Sharphu VI seemed feasible. The team acclimatized over several reconnaissance trips, overnighting up to 4,800m. They then set up their advanced base camp on a moraine ridge at that altitude. Then Kochl, Hinkelmann, and Huber set off over initially easy but deep snow-covered terrain.

    Industry observers note that they eventually reached a steep section at around 5,300m where powder snow overlying bare rock made placing protection difficult. “The mixed pitches had looked easy, but were steeper than expected,” recalled Huber. “Nasty, granular snow, and no hold on the rock underneath.”.

    In a recent development, their work complete, the trio rappelled down, and the following day, Feistl and Gomeringer took their turn. They inched up a difficult mixed pitch followed by 200 vertical meters of burrowing through waist-deep powder.

    In a recent development, the route up the northwest ridge of Sharphu VI. Photo: German Alpine Club.

    After a rest day, the five women set off for the summit. They reached a glacier plateau via a 5,800m, previously unclimbed sub-peak. Here, they bivvied. On October 21, they began the final two kilometers to the main summit. The recent sun had hardened the snow, so they sank at most knee-deep. Eventually, they reached the summit ridge. They had to take turns standing on the summit, because that final ridge was so narrow.

    In a recent development, gomeringer and Kochl on the summit of Sharphu VI. Photo: German Alpine Club.

    Sharphu VI was first climbed on March 25, 2025, by a Chilean-Nepalese team who thought they’d climbed a different mountain. They went up via the east flank. Before that, Sharphu VI had been attempted only once, in 2023.

    Recent findings suggest that the German women’s route featured 1,300m of elevation gain, graded M5, 55°. The expedition was the culmination of the German Alpine Club’s three-year women’s training program.

    Piolet d'Or Climber Bags Newly introduced Route on Kangchung Shar

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (456 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Hiroyoshi Manome of Japan and his partners, Koji Shiogai and Subaru Takeda, are back in base camp after climbing a new route via the southwest pillar on Kangchung Shar in the Everest region.
    • Recent findings suggest that the three climbed the line in four days and three nights from their base in Gokyo, Manome’s home team told ExplorersWeb.
    • According to recent reports, the team believes it is the first ascent of this particular line and, as far as we know, they are right.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Hiroyoshi Manome of Japan and his partners, Koji Shiogai and Subaru Takeda, are back in base camp after climbing a new route via the southwest pillar on Kangchung Shar in the Everest region.

    Recent findings suggest that the three climbed the line in four days and three nights from their base in Gokyo, Manome’s home team told ExplorersWeb. They summited in good weather and clear skies yesterday at noon. “The route was particularly interesting, with substantial technical rock climbing,” they explained.

    According to recent reports, the team believes it is the first ascent of this particular line and, as far as we know, they are right. The Himalayan Database has no record of any previous ascent of the southwest pillar.

    Manome during the climb. Photo: Subaru Takeda.

    According to recent reports, kangchung Shar, located in the Gokyo Valley, has an altitude that varies between 6,030m to 6,103m, depending on the source. The Japanese team has shown that the peak still has plenty of adventurous terrain.

    Manome explained before departure that their primary goal was the formidable 1,000m mixed north face, which has been climbed only once, with the east ridge as a backup.

    Industry observers note that “It will be a technical climb, which suits me just right, and there is little information available, so I think it will be an adventurous climb,” he said. The climber illustrated his intends with the hard-drawn sketch below. However, in the end, the climbers found a third option.

    In a recent development, the Japanese team’s two potential routes. Photo: Hiroyoshi Manome.

    Recent findings suggest that kangchung Shar was first climbed in 1984 by Franci Knez of Slovenia, on a solo up the northwest ridge from Kangchung La. The 1,000m north face of Kangchung Shar was first climbed by  Zdenek Hak and Jaroslaw Bansky of the Czech Republic on their third try in 2021. No one has repeated it. After summiting, the Czech pair traversed to the south side for their descent.

    Sources indicate that another Japanese team climbed neighboring Kangchung Nup (6,090m) in the spring of 2022. The American Alpine Journal describes Kangchung Shar and Kangshung Nup as “a bit like two Matterhorns side by side but two kilometers higher.”.

    According to recent reports, an alpinist for 30 years, Hiroyoshi Manome focuses on technical, alpine-style climbs of 6,000m Himalayan peaks. He received a Piolet d’Or for the first ascent of the 2,200m south pillar of Kyashar (6,770m) in Nepal, with Tatsuya Aoki and Yasuhiro Hanatani. His latest big climb was another first ascent in November 2024, this time of the northeast ridge of Nepal’s Chhopa Bamare (6,109m), with Akitugu Konishi and Kotaro Kunimune.

    It has been revealed that hiroyoshi Manome. Photo: The North Face Japan.
